en: Now begins the latter portion of the glorious Saṭīkaliṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
The sages said:
"By what means, O Sūta, does Kṛṣṇa—the Lord of the lords of all gods—become pleased in this world?
You, who know the meaning of all things, ought to tell us."
Sūta said:
O best of Brahmins, in former times the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, possessed of great splendor, was questioned by Ambarīṣa; that I shall relate to you exactly as it happened.
Ambarīṣa said:
O sage of great intellect, you have reached the further shore of all dharmas;
O Mārkaṇḍeya, you are ancient and an expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas.
O you of great wisdom and noble vows, tell us here what is the most excellent and supreme among the divine attributes of the Nārāyaṇas for those who are devoted. LiP_2,1.4.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of his, he rose with palms joined in reverence,
remembering the god Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the infallible and imperishable.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O King, according to the proper method, to the meritorious practice consisting of Nārāyaṇa—
namely, remembrance, worship, and prostration performed with devotion.
That one supreme person, Janārdana, who is the Supreme Self, is said to be equal to each individual horse-sacrifice.
Since everything is liberated by taking refuge in Brahman,
I shall proclaim that single Dharma which has been seen and known by me.
Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a certain twice-born man named Kauśika,
who was constantly devoted to Vāsudeva and always delighted in the chanting of the Sāmaveda.
At all times— whether at meals, while seated, or on his bed— his mind should remain fixed upon Him,
repeatedly singing the noble deeds of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the sacred site of Viṣṇu, the unsurpassed field of Hari,
he sang there of Hari with proper rhythm, pitch, and tempo.

Having attained the yoga of devotion, which is distinguished by the combination of melodic scales (*mūrcchanā*) and notes (*svara*), as well as by the differentiation of intervals (*śruti*), he indeed took only alms there.
Then, seeing him singing in that manner, a certain twice-born man known as Padma gave him food at that time.
Accompanied by his family, the highly resplendent Kauśika, being delighted, sat there singing praises to Lord Hari while eating hot food.
That one named Padma remained listening, having emerged from time to time;
and by the turn of time, the disciples of Kauśika arrived.
Seven [should be chosen] from among Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, and those born of noble families of Brahmins who are superior in knowledge and learning, pure, and devoted solely to Vāsudeva.
To them as well, Kauśika Padmākṣa himself, together with his disciples and with a joyful mind, constantly provided food and provisions.
At Viṣṇusthala, he remained there singing of Hari according to the prescribed rites;
right there lived a Vaiśya named Mālava, who was devoted to Viṣṇu.
With a joyful mind, he constantly offered garlands of lamps to Hari;
his wife, named Mālavī, was likewise ever devoted to her husband.
Having smeared the entire area of Hari’s field with cow dung,
she remained there with her husband, well-pleased, listening to the most excellent song.
From Kuśasthalī, fifty Brahmins of celebrated vows arrived; they were indeed the most excellent ones who came for the purpose of singing the praises of Hari.
Accomplishing the tasks of the high-souled Kauśika,
those who knew the true nature of knowledge, the sciences, and the objects of experience remained there, listening attentively.
At that time, the singing of that Kauśika became renowned;
having heard it, King Kaliṅga approached him and spoke these words.
"O Kauśika, sing to me here once more today along with your hosts;
and you too, O people of Kuśasthalī, listen as well. (LiP 2.1.24)
Having heard that, Kauśika spoke to the king with consoling words:
"O Great King, it is not my tongue, nor is my speech always [under my control]."
"He praises no one other than Hari, nor will he ever speak of Indra or anyone else.
When this was said, his disciple Gautama Vāsiṣṭha [replied]: "Hari! 2.1.26.
Sārasvata, Citra, Citramālya, and Śiśu likewise spoke to the king exactly as Kauśika had said.
Those disciples, devoted to Viṣṇu, spoke thus to the king:
"O King, these ears of ours hear nothing other than Hari. (LiP 2.1.28)
"We hear of his fame as a singer, but not of any other praise.
Hearing this, the king became enraged and said, "Let them sing! (LiP 2.1.29)
"These Brāhmaṇas, who are my own servants, hear of my fame just as it is; why then do they not hear it while it is being sung from all sides? (LiP 2.1.30)
Thus addressed, the servants then spoke to the excellent king;
those brahmins, their path being blocked, were distressed when the singing had concluded.
The twice-born ones, Kauśika and the others, having understood the king's mental disposition, pierced each other's ears with wooden spikes.
"If this king, remaining in his own song, should forcibly sing us [the verses] himself," said the Brahmins, and being well-restrained, they cut off the tips of their tongues with their hands.
Then the king, greatly incensed, banished them from his own country;
taking all their wealth with them, they departed for the north.
Having reached the [western] direction, they were joined with the law of time by Time itself.
Seeing them arrive, O King, Yama wondered what should be done;
at that moment, Brahmā spoke to the lords of the gods.
"O you who dwell here, settle the brahmins beginning with Kauśika today as you please.
Bring those who constantly worship Janārdana through the practice of singing;
may prosperity be yours, if you desire divinity."
Thus addressed by them again and again as "O Kauśika," those guardians of the world were called "O Mālava" by some and "O Padmākṣa" by others.
Crying out, those gods approached, took them up, and swiftly went through the sky to the world of Brahmā in a mere moment.
Then, having seen Kauśika and the others, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
went out to meet them and honored them with a welcome according to custom.
Then, O best of kings, upon seeing the deed performed by Brahmā, there arose among the gods a tumultuous and exceedingly grave uproar.
The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, having restrained those foremost of gods and taking with him the sages Kauśika and the others, was surrounded by the deities.
Devoted to Vāsudeva, he quickly went to the world of Viṣṇu;
there, the god Nārāyaṇa was present along with the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa.
By the perfected masters of the yoga of knowledge, devoted to Viṣṇu, composed in mind, divine, equal to Nārāyaṇa, auspicious, and bearing four arms; ||| LiP_2,1.44 |||
He was attended by eighty-eight thousand great men, who were radiant, stainless, and adorned with the marks of Viṣṇu.
[He was surrounded] on all sides by us, by Nārada and others, by the stainless Sanaka and others, by various kinds of beings, and by celestial women.
Then, being served in the midst of that divine, auspicious, jewel-encrusted palace, which was a thousand yojanas in extent and enclosed by a thousand gates; LiP_2.1.47.
In a stainless and variegated celestial chariot, Hari sat upon a noble throne;
and Mādhava cast his gaze upon those who were intent on the welfare of the world.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, accompanied by Kauśika and others, arrived; having prostrated before him, he praised the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Then, having looked upon them, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa,
out of affection, addressed them all in order, saying, "O Kauśikas!"
When a great wonder had occurred, a great cry of victory arose in the kitchen;
then the Soul of the Universe said to Brahmā: "Listen, O Brahmā, to what is spoken by me."
These Brahmins of Kauśika, who reside in Kuśasthalī and are devoted to the goals and means of spiritual practice, have indeed set out for the welfare [of all].
"May these gods become my sādhakas— intent on hearing my fame, skilled in the meaning of the principles of knowledge, and devoted to no other deity."
Bearing a divine form, glorious, and listening to songs here, O Lord, remain forever according to your desire as long as the worlds indeed exist.
The Blessed One said to Padmākṣa: "Bhava, Mādhava, and Dhanada—having become the lord of riches—will indeed grant me [the boon] again at the proper time."
Dāmodara Hari spoke thus to Mālava and Mālavī:
"O Mālava, dwell in my world together with your wife for as long as time permits."
Bearing a divine form, O glorious Lord, listen here to the songs;
remain forever as you desire, for as long as the worlds indeed exist.
The Blessed One said to Padmākṣa: "Bhava, Mādhava, and Dhanada, having become the lords of wealth, shall indeed grant me [wealth] again at the proper time."
"Having come and seen me, rule the kingdom forever as you please.
Having spoken thus, Hari Viṣṇu said this to Brahmā:
By the singing of this Kauśika, my yogic sleep has departed;
and here at Viṣṇusthala, he praises me while surrounded on all sides by his disciples.
Cast out by the cruel and mighty King Kaliṅga,
he had his tongue cut off because he had somehow spoken of anyone other than Hari.
"He who has resolved, 'I shall not praise,' has already attained my world;
and these illustrious brahmins are likewise my devoted followers."
Then, having blocked their ear-cavities with stakes driven into one another, they thought, "We shall hear nothing else but the glorification of Hari. (LiP 2.1.63)
These brahmins shall attain divinity and my very presence;
indeed, Mālava, together with his wife, having cleansed my field, shall do so.
Having constantly and perpetually worshipped me with garlands of lamps and other offerings, he,
being self-restrained, listens to songs associated with my fame and deeds.
By that [act], he attained my eternal world as Brahmā;
that lotus-eyed one gave food to the high-souled Kauśika.
"He has attained the status of Lord of Wealth as well as my very presence.
Having spoken thus in that assembly, Hari, who is worshipped by the worlds, [remained there].
At that moment, she was attended by those skilled in the science of instrumental music, who knew the true nature of the strings of the lute and were eloquent with sweet-sounding syllables.
Slowly, with a gentle smile, the goddess Lakṣmī, adorned with various ornaments and singing, arrived as the beloved of Viṣṇu.
Surrounded on all sides by thousands of crores of women,
the leaders of the Gaṇas, armed with *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons and iron clubs, then beheld him.
Threatening Brahmā and the others, those sages and gods stood on all sides,
exultant and resembling mountains as they drove them away.
Indeed, we all set out together with Brahmā and the gods;
at that very moment, Tuṃbaru, the best of sages, was summoned.
He indeed entered into the presence of both the Goddess and the God;
having sat there according to the proper manner, he was filled with various states of ecstasy.
Delighted, he sang in melodious tones and struck the lute,
adorning himself with the finest divine ornaments set with various jewels.
Honored with divine and brilliant garlands, the best of sages,
Tuṃbaru, emerged delighted, as did the other ṛṣis and gods.
O subduer of enemies, having seen [Viṣṇu] being honored and departing as was appropriate,
the sage Nārada then observed the hospitable reception accorded to Tuṃbaru by Hari.
With a mind overcome by grief and eyes whose heart was tormented,
he fell into deep reflection there, his soul agitated by a swoon of sorrow.
"Alas! Tuṃburu has attained this yoga in the presence of the Goddess; fie on me, a fool and one devoid of sense!"—with these words, he indeed entered the mouth of Hari. (LiP 2.1.78)
"How shall I, who have been brought here by these beings to the presence of Hari, go back alive? Where indeed shall I go? Oh, what has been done by Tuṃburu!"
Reflecting thus, the brahmin sage undertook ascetic penance for a thousand divine years, remaining without breath.
Then, meditating upon Viṣṇu and remembering the hospitable reception of Tumburu, the wise man sat there weeping repeatedly, thinking, "Fie upon me! 2.81.
In that regard, O lord of men, hear what Viṣṇu did.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Account of Kauśika," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the divine Nārāyaṇa, having indeed bestowed everything upon him, [departed].
Then, through the conjunction of time, the Soul of the Universe made [the drum] equal to that of Tumburu.
O tiger among sages, such was the event that occurred in the past: Nārada sang the songs of Nārāyaṇa again and again, the most excellent of all.
Viṣṇu, propitiated by song, bestows fame, knowledge, and splendor,
as well as satisfaction and a dwelling place, just as he did for Kauśika.
And Hari bestowed upon Padmākṣa and the others the attainment of perfection;
therefore, O great king, you especially [should act] toward the field of Viṣṇu.
O King, worship consisting of singing, dancing, and so forth, accompanied by instrumental music and festivals,
should indeed be performed incessantly by men who are devotees of Viṣṇu.
And this Hari should always and eternally be heard;
likewise, the wise man who, endowed with devotion, causes [this] to be performed in a sacred field of Viṣṇu, [attains the highest goal].
As well as singing, dancing, and so forth, the stories of the narrations concerning Viṣṇu,
the recollection of past births, intelligence, and likewise the memory [of these] at the time of death.
O lord of kings, this is the truth: one attains union with Viṣṇu.
O King, I have thus told you that which you asked of me.
And what shall I say to you? Speak, O best among the upholders of dharma!
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Viṣṇu," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Ambarīṣa said: O Mārkaṇḍeya of great wisdom, by what yoga did you obtain [this]?
O highly fortunate one, the venerable sage Nārada [taught] the science of music.
At what time did Tuṃbaru attain equality [with Śiva]?
Tell me all of this, O Great-minded One, for you are omniscient. LiP_2,3.2.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I have indeed heard this matter from Nārada, who has the vision of the gods;
that great-minded Nārada himself is possessed of great splendor."
Tormented for a thousand divine years,
the Blessed One remained without breath, mindful of the gravity of Tumburu’s offense.
Then that great mass of asceticism performed supreme and most terrible penance;
at that time, the great sage Nārada heard [a voice] in the intermediate space.
“O tiger among sages, for what purpose do you perform this difficult austerity, accompanied by a divine, loud, wonderful, and bodiless voice?”
Go and see Ulūka, if your mind is devoted to singing;
on Mount Mānasottara, he is known as Gānabandhu.
"Go quickly and behold him; you shall become a master of song.
Thus addressed, Nārada, the best among those skilled in speech, was filled with wonder.
On Mount Mānasottara, he indeed went to the abode of Gāna,
where Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and hosts of Apsarases resided.
Then, sitting all around Gānabandhu here and there,
they mastered the science of song and were instructed by that bird.
There, seated together with voices sweet and resonant,
Gānabandhu, upon seeing Nārada, spoke;
having prostrated according to custom, he honored him with a welcome.
For what purpose, O Mahāmati, have you come here, Blessed One?
"O Brahmin, what task must be performed by me? Tell me, what shall I do for you?
Nārada said:
"O highly wise Lord of Owls, listen to everything exactly as it is."
O learned one, I shall relate my own most wonderful past history, which occurred in a bygone age when I was in the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Having shaken me off and summoned Tumburu with great joy,
Viṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī, listened to that supreme song.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were displaced from their positions and driven away;
meanwhile, those beginning with Kauśika sat down and indeed sang to Hari by means of the yoga of song.
Having thus propitiated him, they attained the status of leaders of the Gaṇas at their pleasure;
therefore, afflicted by extreme suffering, I have come here to perform penance.
Whatever has been given by me, whatever has been offered in sacrifice, whatever has been heard, and whatever has been studied— all this does not equal even a sixteenth part [of the merit of that].
O twice-born one, having reflected upon the yoga of song associated with the majesty of Viṣṇu, I then performed severe penance for that purpose.
O bird, for a thousand divine years thereafter, I again heard a voice arising from the sky addressed to you.
"O divine sage, go to Ulūka, the kinsman of Gāna, if you have the inclination;
O Brahmin, if he is still alive, you shall find him there after some time."
Thus impelled by him, I have come here into your presence;
what shall I do as your disciple? Protect me, O Imperishable One! (LiP 2.3.22)
Gānabandhu said:
Listen, O high-minded Nārada, to what occurred in the past concerning me—
a most wonderful, auspicious account that removes all sins.
In ancient times, there was a righteous king renowned as Bhuvaneśa;
he performed thousands of horse sacrifices and ten thousand Vājapeya sacrifices.
Likewise, he gave ten million and one hundred million cows,
as well as garments, chariots, elephants, maidens, and horses.
Having given the earth to the brahmins and protecting it, that king,
while residing in his own kingdom, would propitiate Keśava through the practice of singing.
Or if he should sing another [hymn] by means of a song, he would deserve to be killed with all his soul; therefore, the Supreme Person is to be praised by the Vedas.
By means of musical performance, let women everywhere sing constantly;
and let the assemblies of Sūtas and Māgadhas indeed cause you to hear songs.
Having thus received this command, the one of great splendor protected the kingdom.
In the vicinity of that king’s city, there was one known as Harimitra.
A Brahmin devoted to Viṣṇu, free from all dualities,
having reached the sandy bank of a river and [found] an auspicious image of Hari, [should proceed].
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, and having offered abundant milk-rice with plenty of ghee and curd, as well as sweetmeats and cakes, one should present them to Hari.
Having prostrated according to the prescribed rule, with his mind fixed upon Him,
he sang there of Hari in accordance with the proper tempo, rhythm, and cadence.
Filled with excessive affection and with his inner self absorbed in her,
the spies then arrived there by the command of the king.
Having thoroughly searched everywhere for that entire act of worship and so forth,
they seized that brahmin and reported the matter correctly to the king.
Then the evil-minded king, having rebuked the best of the twice-born and seized all his wealth and other possessions, banished him from the kingdom.
The Mlecchas then seized the image of Hari and departed;
subsequently, after a long period of time, he met his end according to the law of time.
That king, though being honored from all sides throughout all the worlds, was afflicted by hunger and likewise exhausted; being deeply distressed, he spoke to Yama.
"Hunger and thirst persist constantly for me, O Lord, even though I have gone to heaven.
What sin have I committed, or what indeed shall I do, O Yama? (LiP 2.3.38)
Yama said:
"Indeed, a very great sin was committed by you out of ignorance and delusion toward Harimitra,
who at that time was solely devoted to Vāsudeva."
O King, because you committed a sin against Harimitra while engaged in the worship of Vāsudeva and other rites,
you have been afflicted by this chronic digestive ailment ever since.
O lord of men, all your acts of charity, sacrifices, and the like have perished,
along with that great-minded one who was singing accompanied by vocal and instrumental music.
Having summoned Harimitra, you seized that wealth—
the entire offering and so forth— in the presence of Vāsudeva.
O best of kings, at that time, by your command, your servants committed sins,
and they did nothing else except to suppress the fame of Hari, even as Brahmā looked on.
"You should not have sung while engaged in the *geya* [chanting]; therefore, sin has been committed by you.
Today you have been abandoned by all the worlds; go now to the hollow of a mountain cave."
Constantly hacking away at and devouring that very body he had previously cast off,
he remained in that corner, perpetually hungry and consuming this present body as well.
"You shall remain situated in the Great Hell for as long as a manvantara lasts;
then, when that manvantara has passed, you will appear upon the earth."
"Then, in the course of time, having attained human birth, you shall understand [this]. Having spoken thus, the wise Yama vanished on the spot. Gānabandhu said: [Thus it was told]. LiP_2,3.47.
The illustrious Harimitra, being praised by the leaders of the Gaṇas,
departed for the world of Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot, taking his kinsmen with him.
Indeed, King Bhuvaneśa dwells here within this mountain cave,
constantly devouring corpses and afflicted by hunger and thirst.
I saw that king there and told him all of this;
having observed him and recognized him, I approached Harimitra.
Surrounded by immortals, I travel in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun;
indeed, through the grace of Indradyumna, I have attained this supreme lifespan.
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, I beheld Harimitra;
by the power of his sovereignty, my mind was completely captivated.
O Sage, at that time I sat down with the Kinnaras regarding the science of song; for sixty thousand years, I applied myself to the practice of singing.
Once my tongue was purified and made articulate, I then taught her singing;
thereafter, in exactly twice that time, she became like this for me.
Ten manvantaras passed while I was thus engaged in the practice of singing;
there, the Gandharvas and others assembled, and I became their master of song.
"These hosts of Kinnaras have indeed come to me, their teacher;
O one whose wealth is austerity, the science of song cannot be mastered through asceticism alone."
"Therefore, endowed with sacred learning, receive the Gāna from me.
Having been addressed thus, the sage then bowed to him and sang it.
"Listen to that, O best of sages, after bowing down to Vāsudeva.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Having been addressed thus by the owl, Nārada, the most excellent of sages," [proceeded].
Engaged in the sequence of training, he taught him singing there;
then Gānabandhu, casting aside all shame, said this to him: "You have now become [proficient]. (LiP 2.3.59)
Ulūka said:
"In matters of sexual union, as well as in song, gambling, the assembly for exposition, legal proceedings, eating, and the acquisition of wealth; [these are the times when one should remain silent]."
He should always be free from shame regarding income and expenditure;
he should never wear garments that are wrinkled, concealed, or constantly worn out.
Indeed, one should never sing by means of the movement of the hands, nor with the mouth wide open, nor through the application of protruding the tongue.
One should not sing with arms raised, nor with eyes cast upward in any way; likewise, one should not look at one's own limbs while singing, nor gaze at another person.
In the case of a collision or rising up, the placement of the hands on the waist is not recommended;
likewise, laughter, anger, trembling, or elsewhere, mindfulness [is required] once again.
"O Great-minded One, O Sage, these forms of instruments are not suitable for the practice of singing; it is impossible to strike a rhythmic beat with only one hand. (LiP 2.3.65)
One who is afflicted by hunger, afflicted by fear, or likewise afflicted by thirst should never engage in the practice of singing, nor ever in darkness.
And other such things as these should not be performed by one who sings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed by those characteristics of the prescribed rules spoken by him, that Blessed One—
In that manner, he taught him divine song for a thousand years.

Then, he became accomplished in all [arts], including the expansion of songs and so forth; he was proficient in the lute and other instruments, and was a knower of the distinctions between all musical notes.
And thirty-six million, eight thousand, and one hundred—
the best of sages understood these through the application of the divisions of vowels.
Then the hosts of Gandharvas and likewise those of Kinnaras,
united with the Sage, become filled with joy.
Having attained unsurpassed song, the sage said to Gānabandhu:
"Having approached you, he has indeed become an expert in singing."
"O enemy of the crow, O one of great wisdom, what may I do for you, O Teacher?
Gānabandhu replied:
"O Brahmin, in a single day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus."
Then, O great sage, the dissolution of the three worlds will occur; for that long shall my life-span endure, and for that long shall my supreme auspiciousness remain.
"O best of sages, let my sacrificial fee be placed upon my mind.
Nārada said:
"In the conjunction of a past kalpa, you shall become Garuḍa."
"May it be well with you, O one of great wisdom; I shall depart, be gracious to me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Nārada then went to Janārdana.
On Śvetadvīpa, he caused Hṛṣīkeśa to sing songs;
having heard them there, the Blessed Mādhava spoke to Nārada.
"O Nārada, you are not yet superior to Tumburu in songs even today;
I shall tell you the time when you will become superior."
Having approached Gānabandhu, you have become a knower of the meaning of song;
I [am he] in the twenty-eighth yuga of Vaivasvata Manu.
O high-minded one, in the Dvāpara age I shall be born into the family of the Yadu lineage as Kṛṣṇa by name, the son of Vasudeva and Devakī.
Then, having approached me, you should remind me of [the events] exactly as they occurred;
there, I shall make you, who are perfected in song, a performer of the great vow (mahāvrata).
And likewise for one who is equal to Tumburu or even endowed with his excellence,
they remain for that duration of time, as appropriate, within the wombs of gods and gandharvas.
Having said, "Instruct me according to what is right," he vanished;
then the sage, having bowed to him who was endowed with such excellence, [departed].
The celestial sage, resembling a god and adorned with all ornaments,
was an ultimate treasury of asceticism and devoted solely to Vāsudeva.
Having mounted the lute Vipañcī upon his shoulder, he wandered through all the worlds—
the realms of Varuṇa, Yama, Agni, Indra, and Kubera.
Having reached the assembly in the northwestern and northeastern directions, the knower of dharma,
skilled in playing the lute, properly sang praises of Hari.
Being honored here and there by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
he eventually reached the world of Brahmā after the lapse of some period of time.
And the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, experts in song and instrumental music,
are the divine and eternal singers of Brahmā, the most excellent of Gandharvas.
There, having approached those two while singing praises to Lord Hari,
that best of sages, possessed of great splendor, was honored by Brahmā as well.
Having bowed down to that great-souled one, the grandfather of all the worlds,
Nārada wandered at will through all the worlds.
Then, after a long time, having reached the house of Tumburu and taking up his lute, the great sage remained there and sang.

The seven notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, which reside there and are considered equivalent to the heavenly realms, were perceived by the Blessed One as he played; and having seen them, he departed with great haste.
There, the high-minded Nārada, the great sage, was repeatedly instructed in various matters by Śikhaṇḍin, who was himself engaged in the practice of ascetic toil.
Beholding the seven notes as his wives, he was an expert in the science of song;
yet, when joined with the lute, those strings did not reach [the same pitch].
Then, having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa at Ravaityaka, the great sage reported in its entirety everything that had previously occurred in Śvetadvīpa.
Having heard that unsurpassed method of singing taught by Nārāyaṇa,
Kṛṣṇa laughed and joyfully spoke to Jāmbavatī.
"O blessed lady, instruct this best of sages in the proper manner regarding the combination of lute and song. Having said "So be it" to Hari, she [did so].
Laughing as was appropriate, she instructed that sage;
then, when a full year had passed, she returned once more to Mādhava.
Having prostrated, he stood before him; then Keśava spoke again:
"Satya, come near and instruct me according to the prescribed rule."
Having said "So be it," the sage prostrated before Satyabhāmā;
instructed by her, the learned one returned after a full year had passed.
Directed by Vāsudeva, that best of sages went to the residence of Rukmiṇī; there he was met by those women who were her handmaidens.
"O sage, although you were singing thus, you did not indeed know the musical note;
therefore, through great exertion for a period of three years," LiP 2.3.101.
Then, having been instructed by Queen Rukmiṇī, the sage sang;
thereafter, the celestial nymphs attained the mastery of stringed instruments from the great sage.
Having summoned the great sage himself, the immeasurable Lord Kṛṣṇa personally instructed him in the unsurpassed art of vocal music.
Then, having attained excellence over Tuṃbaru, that best of sages,
the divine seer, bowed down to Janārdana and danced.
And Hṛṣīkeśa said: "O great sage, you are omniscient;
smiling, sing in my presence by means of the yoga of song."
"This which you have requested has been obtained by you in my world;
therefore, sing eternally together with Tuṃburu according to the truth."
Thus addressed, the sage proceeded there according to what was appropriate,
while Kṛṣṇa worshipped Rudra, the lord of the world.
Then, at the command of Hari, the great sage indeed went to Śaṅkara along with Rukmiṇī, Satyā, and Jāmbavatī.
And by Kṛṣṇa, O best of kings, this sequence of songs of the sage was proclaimed for you, O tigers among sages, he who is an expert in the Vedas and the musical scales.
O King, a Brāhmaṇa who sings the name of Vāsudeva with great devotion attains the same world as Hari; one who sings the praises of Rudra shall become even more exalted.
Otherwise, one who sings of another deity would surely go to hell;
however, one who is devoted solely to Vāsudeva through action, mind, and speech shall not.
By singing and by listening, one attains it; therefore, they know that it is to be sung as the supreme.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vaiṣṇava Song," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"Those who are called Vaiṣṇavas are those who are solely devoted to Vāsudeva."
O you of great intelligence, tell us what their signs truly are.
Or what does this Blessed One, the creator of all beings, do for them?
O Sūta, you who know the meaning of all things, explain all of this to me.
Sūta said:
"The sage Mārkaṇḍeya was indeed questioned by Ambarīṣa in former times;
that which has been spoken by you today, I shall relate exactly as it happened."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to that which you ask me according to the proper method:
wherever there is a devotee of Viṣṇu, there Nārāyaṇa is present.
For those for whom Viṣṇu alone is remembered as the deity everywhere,
there arises a horripilation whenever Hari is being glorified.
Trembling, perspiration, and drops of water are seen on their limbs—
those who are endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu and who promote the practices prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
He who becomes joyful upon seeing [the Lord] is proclaimed a Vaiṣṇava;
such a Vaiṣṇava does not wear any other garment in the world than that of the Lord.

Furthermore, whoever, upon seeing a devotee of Viṣṇu approaching, stands facing him and performs prostrations and other marks of respect toward him just as they would toward Vāsudeva himself; ||| LiP_2,4.8 |||
He indeed should be known as a devotee; he shall be victorious throughout the three worlds, even while hearing harsh words or being addressed in such a manner by a follower of the Bhāgavata.
He who indeed speaks with patience preceded by a prostration is truly a Vaiṣṇava;
for he who carries all things, such as perfumes and flowers, upon his head [is likewise one].
Thinking thus that "everything belongs to Hari," he is indeed remembered as a Vaiṣṇava;
filled with affection, he performs only auspicious deeds in the sacred field of Viṣṇu.
One who is self-restrained should constantly worship the image of Hari;
he is to be known as a devotee of Viṣṇu by virtue of his actions, mind, and speech.
For he is a great devotee of the Lord who is eternally devoted to Nārāyaṇa and performs every service for his sustenance according to his ability.
And it is said that for one who is devoted to Viṣṇu, according to the proper rule,
the wise man who is intent upon Nārāyaṇa eats with a joyful mind.
There is no doubt that the food which has reached the mouth of Hari is as good as eaten;
Mādhava, the soul of the universe, becomes pleased even by one's own worship.
Having seen that great devotee in the Mahābhāgavata, he who is affectionate toward his devotees beheld him as one devoted to Vāsudeva, a Vaiṣṇava whose sins were burnt away.
Even the gods, being afraid, go to him and bow down, returning as they came;
hear indeed the ancient account of the majesty of a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Upon seeing his devotee, the Vaiṣṇava whose sins had been burnt away, Yama too rose up,
joined his palms in reverence, and bowed down to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Therefore, a person should worship Vaiṣṇavas with devotion just as they would Viṣṇu;
he attains proximity to Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt to be made.
A devotee of Viṣṇu excels over thousands of other devotees;
a devotee of Rudra excels over thousands of devotees of Viṣṇu.
There is nothing in this world superior to a devotee of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should worship with every effort a Vaiṣṇava or even a devotee of Rudra for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotees of Viṣṇu," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"Aṃbarīṣa, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, was indeed devoted solely to Vāsudeva."
He protected the earth, following the command of Viṣṇu.
O one of great intelligence, this has been heard; you ought to explain all of that, as well as how the discus of that Hari is eternally [protective] against fear from enemies, diseases, and so forth.
"It is heard in the world that the deeds of the righteous and high-souled Ambarīṣa destroy [all sins]. O best of beings, tell me all of that."
O Sūta, we wish to hear correctly about his majesty, his spiritual power, and the unsurpassed yoga of devotion; you ought to speak of them.
Sūta said:
O tigers among sages, listen to the life-story of that wise Ambarīṣa,
his supreme majesty which removes all sins.
She was the beloved wife of Triśaṅku, adorned with all auspicious marks;
she was the mother of Ambarīṣa and was ever endowed with purity.
He beheld the high-souled Nārāyaṇa, who had ascended into yogic sleep, reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch, and from whom the lotus of the cosmic egg had arisen.
Through *tamas* he is known as Kālarudra; through *rajas*, he is the one born from the golden egg;
and through *sattva*, he is Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one who is saluted by all the gods.
He constantly worshipped [him] with the actions of speech, mind, and body;
he himself performed everything, such as the offering of garlands and other rites.
Likewise, the preparation of perfumes and other such items, as well as incense materials and the like; the smearing of the ground and so forth, and the cooking of sacrificial oblations (havir).
Filled with that curiosity, the auspicious Padmāvatī herself constantly uttered the words "Nārāyaṇa" aloud.
Speaking only the word "Ananta" constantly for ten thousand years with her inner self focused on him, that devoted wife remained steadfast.
Pure, he worshipped Govinda with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
as well as the highly fortunate devotees of Viṣṇu who were free from all sins.
She constantly gratified him with gifts, honors, worship, wealth, and jewels;
then, on one occasion, that goddess, having observed a fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), [spoke].
The highly fortunate lady slept there with her husband at the front of Hari;
there, the god Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, spoke to her.
"What boon do you desire from me, O blessed lady? Speak, O beautiful one.
Having seen him, she chose a boon: "May my son indeed be a devotee of Viṣṇu."
The universal monarch, of great splendor, devoted to his own duty and pure,
said "So be it" and gave her a single fruit, O Janārdana.
Having woken up and seen the fruit, she reported everything to her husband;
with her mind fixed upon it, she joyfully ate the fruit.
Then, in the course of time, that queen gave birth to a son who increased the glory of his lineage,
who was of virtuous conduct, and devoted to Vāsudeva.
Seeing that his son had been born endowed with auspicious marks and hair marked by the sign of the wheel, the father indeed performed all the necessary rites.
The illustrious and great sage became known in the world as Ambarīṣa; when his father had passed away, he was consecrated as king.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he performed severe austerity for a thousand years, chanting the name of the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus, within the middle of a solar disc,
he has four arms and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Resembling pure gold, whose nature consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
the Lord is adorned with all ornaments and wears yellow garments.
Then, having mounted Garuḍa, the god who bears the Śrīvatsa on his chest— the Puruṣa, the Supreme Person— was praised by all the gods.
That Soul of All, honored by all the worlds, arrived, having indeed made Garuḍa appear as inconceivable as Airāvata; thus did Hari come.
Seated there like Śakra himself, he said to that best of kings:
"I am Indra; blessings be upon you! What boon shall I grant you?"
"I, the Lord of all the worlds, have come here to protect you.
Ambarīṣa said:
"I did not undertake this ascetic practice here with the intention of deceiving you."
"I shall take back what was given by you; go, Śakra, as you please.
Nārāyaṇa is my lord; I bow to him, the Lord of the World."
"Do not go there; do not cause the destruction of my intellect.
Then the Blessed One, laughing, assumed his own supreme form.
Holding the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace in his hands, with a sword in his grasp, Janārdana—
the soul of all— sat upon Garuḍa like another blue mountain.
Being praised on all sides by hosts of gods and gandharvas,
he bowed down and, being well-pleased, offered hymns of praise to the one whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Be gracious, O Lord of the lords of the worlds, my protector Janārdana;
O Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Lord of the universe, you who are saluted by all the worlds.
You are the beginning, you are without beginning, you are the infinite Puruṣa, the Lord;
you are the immeasurable, all-pervading Viṣṇu, Govinda, the lotus-eyed one.
Born from the body of Maheśvara, you are Puṣkara in the center, the sky-goer, and the bird;
you are Kavyavāha, Kapālī, Havyavāha, and Prabhañjana.

The primordial god, the bliss of action, the Supreme Self abiding within the self—I have taken refuge in you, O Govinda; victory to you, O son of Devakī! Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World; protect me, O lotus-eyed one!
"There is no other destination for me but you; you alone are my refuge.
Sūta said:
The Blessed Viṣṇu said to him, "What is it that you desire to do in your heart?"
"I shall give all that to you, for you are my devotee, O observer of noble vows;
I am always fond of devotion, and therefore I have come here to grant it."
Ambarīṣa said: O Lord of the World, O Supreme Bliss, my mind is constantly fixed upon Vāsudeva through speech, thought, and the actions of my body.
O God, Janārdana, just as I am yours, O Viṣṇu, so too am I yours, O Deva, as you are to Bhava, the God of gods and the Supreme Self.
I shall protect the earth, having indeed made the world Vaiṣṇava;
and by means of sacrifices, oblations, and worship, I shall satisfy the best of the gods.
"I shall protect the Vaiṣṇavas and I shall slay my enemies; my mind is resolved thus because I am afraid of the terror that afflicts the world. (LiP 2.5.42)
The Blessed Lord said: "So be it; let this Sudarśana discus go as you wish.
Indeed, in the past, by the grace of Rudra, this which is difficult to obtain was acquired by me."
"Having said, 'I shall eternally destroy for you the suffering arising from the curses of sages and the like, as well as that from enemies, diseases, and so forth,' he vanished."
Sūta said:
Then, having bowed down to the Lord Nārāyaṇa with joy,
the king entered the beautiful city of Ayodhyā and ruled over it.
He assigned the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes to their respective duties,
[establishing] those stainless devotees of Viṣṇu who were eternally devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
With a joyful heart, the lord of men protected [the earth] with particular distinction;
having performed a hundred horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
He protected this earth, bounded by the oceans;
Hari was present in every house, and the sound of the Vedas resounded in every home.
While that tiger among kings was ruling the kingdom, there arose the sound of the name of Hari as well as the sound of sacrifices.
The earth was not without grain nor without grass, nor was it afflicted by famine and the like;
the subjects were eternally free from passion and devoid of all calamities.
The greatly resplendent Ambarīṣa protected the earth;
while he was ruling in this manner, a lotus-eyed daughter was born to him.
She was renowned by the name Śrīmatī, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Having arrived at the time for the gift, she was as beautiful as divine illusion.
At that time, the illustrious sage Nārada indeed arrived,
as did the high-minded Parvata, before King Ambarīṣa.
Seeing that both had arrived, the immensely radiant Ambarīṣa prostrated according to the prescribed rite and honored those two sages.
Seeing that maiden sporting amidst the clouds like a flash of lightning, the blessed Nārada then spoke to her with a smile.
"O King, who is this highly fortunate maiden, resembling the daughter of a god?
Tell me, O best among the upholders of dharma, for she is adorned with every auspicious mark."
The king said:
"O Lord, this daughter of mine, auspicious by name and known as Śrīmatī,
has reached the time for her giving in marriage and seeks a bridegroom."
O twice-born ones, having been addressed thus, Nārada, that tiger among sages, desired her;
and Parvata, too, O best of sages, truly fell in love with her.
Having taken leave of the king, Nārada spoke these words:
"O righteous one, call me aside in private and give this daughter of mine to me."
For Parvata, the powerful lord, spoke thus to the king in private;
then both of them, afflicted by fear, prostrated themselves before that righteous-souled one.
"Since both of you are seeking my daughter, O highly wise one, how shall I act? Listen, Nārada, to my words."
And you, Parvata, listen to my words, O Lord, which I shall speak:
if this auspicious maiden chooses one of you two as her husband, [then all will be well].
"I shall give my daughter to him; otherwise, I have no power [to do so].
Having said, "So be it," they then added, "We shall go tomorrow."
Having spoken thus, those two tigers among sages, both supreme among the knowers of wisdom and eternally devoted to Vāsudeva, departed with joyful minds.
Then, having gone to the world of Viṣṇu, Nārada, the best of sages,
prostrated before Hṛṣīkeśa and spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, O Protector, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, there is something that must be heard; I shall speak to you in secret. Homage to you, O Lord of the World! (LiP 2.5.66)
Then Govinda, the soul of the universe, having laughed and dismissed all those others, said to that sage, "Speak," and the sage spoke to Keśava.
Your illustrious king, the lord of the earth Ambarīṣa,
has a daughter of large eyes named Śrīmatī by name.
Listen to my words: I went there intending to marry her;
this glorious mountain sage is your servant and a treasure-house of asceticism.
"O Blessed One, that lord of men, the highly resplendent Ambarīṣa, also desired her and said to us both: 'This maiden is for you two as a bridegroom.'"
"If he should choose one endowed with beauty, I shall give her to him"—thus the king spoke there to us; having said "So be it," I have come here.
"O King, I shall come to your home tomorrow at dawn;
I have now arrived, O Lord of the World, and you ought to do what is pleasing to me. (LiP 2.5.72)
O Lord of the World, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, act in such a way that the face of this mountain shines like the face of a monkey.
Having said, "So be it," Govinda Madhusūdana spoke to Prahasta:
"I shall do as you have said; go, gentle one, back the way you came."
Having spoken thus, the sage, delighted, prostrated before Janārdana;
considering himself to have attained his goal, he then departed for Ayodhyā.
When that best of sages had departed, the great sage Parvata also,
having bowed to Mādhava with joy, spoke this secret to him in private.
Having reported his conduct before Nārada, the Lord of the World, [he said:
"Act in such a way that his face shines like the face of a golangūla monkey."
Having heard that, Lord Viṣṇu said, "I shall indeed do as you have requested;
go quickly to Ayodhyā, but do not let Nārada know."
Having said to me, "So be it," he departed from there after making an agreement with you;
then the king, having learned that the two excellent sages had arrived, [acted accordingly].
He adorned the entire city of Ayodhyā, which was garlanded with banners, with various auspicious flowers and parched grain on every side.
The doors of the houses were sprinkled with water, as were the marketplaces and the great highways;
the city was endowed with divine fragrances and essences, and perfumed with celestial incenses.
Having constructed the city, the king adorned that assembly hall with divine perfumes, incenses, and various kinds of jewels.
It was adorned with pillars of jewels, beautified by various garlands,
and furnished with divine, excellent thrones provided with the most precious coverings.
Having performed these rites, the king took that maiden,
who was adorned with every ornament and possessed long, beautiful eyes like the goddess Śrī, and entered [the city].
At that time, she was seen surrounded by women— divine, illustrious, and radiant— with a waist equal in measure to her palms, possessing the five qualities of smoothness, and a beautiful countenance.
And that assembly hall of the lord of kings was prosperous, variegated with the finest jewels and excellent gems;
it was well-constructed, adorned with garlands, and provided with seats; and the hosts of those royal men arrived at it.

Then another son of Brahmā, the illustrious and high-souled Nārada, a great sage who had mastered the three Vedas, was the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman; accompanied by Parvata, he arrived there.
Then, perceiving that they had arrived, the king, with a mind full of agitation,
took up a divine seat and honored them both.
Both were celestial sages and perfected beings, both the best among those who possess knowledge;
those two high-souled and most excellent of munis sat together for the sake of the maiden.
Having prostrated before them both, the king spoke to that illustrious and auspicious maiden, his daughter, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who was endowed with great fame.
"O blessed lady, whichever of these two you desire in your heart as the better,
bow down according to the prescribed rite and give this garland to him."
Thus addressed by the women,
that fair-eyed maiden, surrounded by them, then took up a divine golden garland.
Where those two great-souled ones were seated, she then approached and stood there,
gazing upon the two best of sages, Nārada and Parvata.
I do not see Nārada, the best of sages, nor Parvata;
yet between these two is one who is less than sixteen years of age.
With her mind bewildered there like a plantain tree in a gale, that great king stood still and said to her: "O Vatsā, what will you do?"
"O auspicious one, give this garland to whichever one of these two you intend," she said to her father in fear; "these two are that man and the monkey. (LiP 2.5.96)
I do not see Nārada, the best of sages, nor Parvata;
however, between these two is one who is slightly less than sixteen years of age.
Adorned with all ornaments, resembling the atasi flower,
long-armed, large-eyed, and possessing an excellent, prominent chest.
His hips and neck were marked with lines, his long eyes had reddish corners,
and he was adorned by a pair of eyebrows capable of mimicking a bent bow.
His beautiful belly was clearly marked with three distinct folds at the navel;
he was clothed in golden garments, his auspicious nails were high and jeweled,
and he possessed hands shaped like lotuses, a face like a lotus, and eyes like lotuses.
He has beautiful nostrils, a heart like a lotus, a navel like a lotus, and is encompassed by splendor;
his rows of teeth are exceedingly like jasmine buds.
Beholding me laughing and stretching out my right hand,
I saw him standing there with beautiful hair.
To her, who stood there with a bewildered mind, trembling like a plantain tree, that king said: "O child, what will you do?"
When this was said, the sage Nārada, having fallen into doubt, spoke:
"O daughter, tell me truly, how many arms does he have? (LiP 2.5.104)
"And I see two arms," said the maiden of pure smiles.
Thereupon Parvata spoke to her regarding his auspicious chest.
"What do you see? Tell me, or what do you see in his hand?
The maiden said to him, "I see indeed a garland of five unsurpassed forms."
"I see upon his chest, and in his hand, the bow and arrows.
When they had spoken thus to one another, those two most excellent sages were unsurpassed.
Reflecting in their minds, they thought: "This must be some kind of illusion;
surely this Janārdana himself is a deceptive thief."
"Having arrived here, how could I not act? Yet, what will become of this face of mine?
Nārada reflected thus for a month, thinking, "I have become a monkey."
Parvata also, in accordance with propriety, fell into such reflection in his mind as to how he had attained the state of a monkey.
Then the king, having bowed down to both Nārada and Parvata, said:
"What was this that you two did there, born of a delusion of the intellect?"
"May you both remain in good health, intent upon the matter of the maiden.
Thus addressed, the two eminent and formidable sages spoke to the king.
"You alone are causing this delusion; I do not at all approve of it here. Of us two, let her choose only one of you without delay."
Then that maiden, having again prostrated before her chosen deity,
assumed an illusory form and stood composedly between the two of them.
Adorned with all ornaments, resembling the *matasī* flower,
with long arms, well-nourished limbs, and eyes reaching as far as his ears.
Having seen the man as before, she indeed gave him a garland;
immediately thereafter, that maiden was no longer seen by men.
Then a sound arose, and they were filled with wonder, asking, "What is this?
Taking her with him, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, went to his own abode.
In former times, having performed penance incessantly for that purpose, that illustrious and beautiful woman was born; and she likewise went to Hari.
Then those two tigers among sages, deeply distressed by their reproach,
went to the abode of Hari, Vāsudeva.
Seeing that the two had arrived, the Blessed Lord Hari said to Śrīmatī:
"The two best of sages have come; indeed, conceal yourself here."
Having said "So be it," that goddess smiled and acted accordingly;
then Nārada, having prostrated before him, spoke to Hari, Dāmodara.
"Indeed, you have done me a kindness today, O Parvata;
for it was surely you, Govinda, who carried off that maiden."
"Having deluded us and deceived us by your own intelligence, O best of gods,"—
when thus addressed, the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, covering his ears with both hands, said: "What has been uttered by you two?"
"Alas, this disposition of yours possesses desire, even though you follow the conduct of a sage!
When he was addressed thus, that sage Nārada spoke to Vāsudeva.
"How did you get a monkey's face at my ear?
he asked him at his ear, and he replied, "I made you into a monkey."
"O learned one, that face of yours resembling a monkey was fashioned by me there for your sake, O Parvata; it was done for your pleasure, and not otherwise."
Parvata spoke likewise, and he (Dāmodara) replied to him in the same way;
while both were listening there, Dāmodara uttered these words.
"I have done what was pleasing to you both; by truth I swear this.
Thus spoke the righteous-souled Nārada, who stood between the two of them.
"Who was that archer who reportedly abducted her from here and went away?
Hearing this, Vāsudeva spoke to those two best of sages.
There are many great-souled masters of illusion who are most excellent;
among them, that illustrious lady surely did not see those two best of sages.
"I am Cakrapāṇi, eternally established as four-armed;
indeed, I did not desire it to be otherwise, for that is known to you both."
When they were addressed thus, they prostrated before him and spoke with joyful minds:
"O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, O Master of the World, what fault is there here on your part?"
"This is indeed the wickedness of that king; he has truly practiced deception," having said this, the two sages, Nārada and Parvata, departed from there. (LiP 2.5.133)
Having approached Ambarīṣa, Nārada and Parvata likewise afflicted him with a curse, saying: "Since we two have come here [uninvited]..."
"After having summoned [him], you subsequently gave the maiden to another through the application of illusion; therefore, darkness shall indeed overcome you."
"And by that, you shall know yourself exceedingly well as it truly is.
When the curse had been thus pronounced, a mass of darkness then arose.
Then, in an instant, Viṣṇu’s discus appeared before the king;
terrified by that terrible discus, those two fled toward him.
Then, with all their limbs trembling in terror, the two great sages ran away,
looking back at that unassailable mass of darkness following behind them.
"Aha! We have attained the success of obtaining the maiden," they cried, rushing with great speed toward the edge of the Lokāloka mountain, driven incessantly by fear.
Crying out "Save us! Save us! while tormented by fear, they then went to the world of Viṣṇu, saying, "O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World! (LiP 2.5.140).
O Vāsudeva, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Janārdana!
Protect us both, O lotus-eyed one; you are our lord, O Supreme Person.
Then the glorious Nārāyaṇa, marked with the Śrīvatsa, having reflected,
desiring to show favor to his devotees, restrained both the discus and the darkness.
Ambarīṣa is my devotee, as are these two best of sages;
therefore, I must now act for the benefit of both him and them.
Having summoned that darkness, the glorious Lord Hari, the Blessed Viṣṇu, gladdening it with his speech, said: "Listen to these words of mine."
The sage’s curse did not occur otherwise, nor was my boon granted to the king for his protection altered; there is no changing that once given.
The son of Ambarīṣa’s grandson,
a highly illustrious and glorious king named Daśaratha, will be a righteous ruler.
I shall be his eldest son, named Rāma;
and there, my right arm shall indeed become Bharata by name.
The one on the left is named Śatrughna, and that remaining one is known as Lakṣmaṇa;
come there to me now, for you shall no longer go to the king.
And Mādhava said to him, "Leaving aside the two best of sages,
you [are he]," and as soon as this was spoken, that darkness indeed vanished instantly.
The discus of Hari was repelled and remained as it was before;
the two best of sages, freed from fear, prostrated themselves before Janārdana.
Having departed, tormented by grief, the two of them said to one another:
"From this day forward until the end of our lives, we shall not take a daughter as a wife."
Having said, "We shall not do so," and having made that vow, those two sages remained as before, pure and devoted to yoga and meditation.
And that King Ambarīṣa, having protected the earth along with his servants and kinsmen, indeed went to the world of Viṣṇu.

Those who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas, dedicated to their daily rites,

Where both husband and wife are mutually antagonistic.
"Accompanied by your wife, you may enter his house free from fear;

Enter there, O Blessed One, free from fear, where you are beyond reproach;

For those men, there is no recitation of mantras, fire oblations, and so forth; there is no sacred ash in their homes;

Those who are devoid of the name of Viṣṇu and are associated with evil-minded people— [for them, there is no refuge] except for the salutation to Kṛṣṇa, Śarva, Śiva, and Parameṣṭhin.
And those foolish, evil-minded men, the Brahmins, do not speak [the truth] there;
O child, you must always enter that very place together with your wife.
"Enter that place where there is no sound of the Vedas, nor any worship of gurus and the like, and which is devoid of ancestral rites— even with your wife."
"Enter, free from fear, this house night after night, where mutual quarrels constantly occur with her."

O Viśa, enter without fear that very place where there is no worship of the *liṅga*, where there is no recitation (*japa*) and so forth, where there is devotion to Rudra, and where there is slander [of him].
Whether it be a guest learned in the Vedas, a preceptor, or even a Vaiṣṇava,
if there are no cows in one's house, you should enter that home together with your wife.
Where, while children were looking on, you ate edible foods without giving any away— enter there with your wife, filled with joy.
Without having worshipped Mahādeva or Vāsudeva, and without having offered oblations according to the prescribed rule, you have always entered into that place. 2,6.43.
Enter that house or that region where fools, delighting in evil deeds and devoid of compassion, dwell together with one another.
One who destroys walls and houses is not to be honored as a housewife;
rather, having entered that home, dwell there always with a joyful mind.
Where there are thorny trees, where there is the niṣpāva creeper,
and where the brahmavṛkṣa tree is located— enter that place together with your wife.
Or indeed, Agastya, Arka, and others, as well as Bandhujīva in the houses;
especially Karavīra, or even Nandyāvarta.
Or enter the house of those who have jasmine, or where you may find a wife;
or where there is a maiden, or a creeping vine, or a hostile man with matted hair in the house. (LiP 2.6.48)
Where there are many plantains, you, together with your wife, should enter;
as well as the *tāla*, *tamāla*, *bhallāta*, and the grove of *tittiḍī* trees.
"O you who are accompanied by your wife, enter either a kadamba or a khadira tree,

"Enter, together with your wife, either an udumbara or a panasa tree,
or that [man] in whose neem grove, garden, or even house there is a crow's nest."
Whether you are a staff-bearer or a shaven-headed ascetic, enter together with your wife into that house where there is one female slave, three oxen, and five buffaloes.
Enter, together with your wife, that [palace] which has six horses and seven elephants,
wherein the goddess Kālī resides in the form of a *preta* and a *ḍākinī*.
Or enter that place where a guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) resides together with his wife,

Or, having approached a Buddhist image, enter fully into it there;
whether at times of lying down or sitting, or during the activities of eating and walking.
That house where their speech always speaks of the names of Hari is declared to be the dwelling place for you and your wife to reside in.
Devoted to the practices of heretics, excluded from the Śrauta and Smārta rites, they were devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu and were revilers of Mahādeva.
Enter that assembly along with your wife, where there are atheists and rogues who do not acknowledge the supremacy of the wielder of the Pināka bow over all.
Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, and Śakra, the lord of all the gods, remember him as common [to them all]; therefore, enter into him along with your wife.
Those evil-minded ones do not say that [the gods] are born from the grace of Rudra;

Foolish people of deluded minds call a firefly the sun;
such is the state always found in their house, field, or dwelling.
Enter their house and eat there, O you whose mind is focused on none other,

And enter the homes of those who are devoid of auspicious bathing rites—
those women who have fallen away from purity and are bereft of bodily refinement.
Always delighting in eating all things, enter into her presence;

Enter the houses of those householders whose teeth are stained with food-remnants,

"Enter the homes of those who do not listen during the twilight prayers;

Enter their houses, those who are deluded by the practice of gambling and dice,
those who steal the property of Brahmins, and those who perform sacrifices for the unworthy.
Or enter the house of those who eat the food of Śūdras—
those sinful ones who are addicted to drinking liquor and intent on eating meat.
Enter the house of those mortals who take pleasure in the wives of others,
who fail to perform worship on sacred festival days, or who indulge in sexual intercourse during the daytime.
Enter the houses of those who engage in sexual intercourse at twilight,
or those whose intercourse is from behind, like that of dogs or deer.
Or if he should engage in sexual intercourse in water, you, together with your wife, enter him; or if that lowest of men should approach a woman in her menses or a Caṇḍālī woman.
Enter their house, or that of a maiden, or even a cow-pen; what is the use of much talk? They are excluded from their daily obligatory rites.
"Enter the house of those who are devoid of devotion to Rudra;

"Enter this, along with your wife; from it, you shall cause [the enemy] to flee in terror.

"Do not enter their house with offerings of food, flowers, and incense";

moreover, inauspiciousness constantly dwells in villages and on the outskirts of mountains.

Śrī Viṣṇu said:
Those who [worship] the sinless Rudra, Śarva, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita, as well as Ambā Haimavatī, the mother of the worlds; LiP_2,6.85.
Those who here revile my devotees—their wealth indeed belongs to you alone;

For those foolish and unfortunate ones, though they are my devotees, their wealth belongs to you;

Having spoken thus, Janārdana abandoned that Alakṣmī along with Lakṣmī.

O twice-born ones, there is no doubt that women should always be honored with every effort and at all times by those devoted to Viṣṇu, even with various offerings, provided they possess strength.
Whoever should read, or even hear, or cause the best of the twice-born to hear this,

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Account of Alakṣmī," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: By reciting what mantra is a living being liberated from fear of all the worlds and other such afflictions?
