"Or rather, having utterly abandoned misfortune through the recitation of mantras, that mortal shall indeed become an abode of fortune; O Sūta, you ought to speak of this here."
Sūta said:
In former times, this was told by the Grandfather (Brahmā) to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
I shall now recount it all in brief for the benefit of all the worlds.
Let everyone listen to these words after prostrating before Janārdana—
the god of gods, the unborn Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, the infallible and the imperishable.
He who is wise and performs meritorious deeds through mind, action, and speech— [he attains] that which removes all sins, is pure, bestows liberation, and proclaims Brahman.
Having prostrated before Puruṣottama, one should constantly recite the name of Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, while sleeping one should think of the god Nārāyaṇa, and while walking, one should likewise think of Nārāyaṇa.
O brahmins, while eating, standing, waking,
opening the eyes, or even closing them, one should indeed say, "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa."
Having consecrated food to be chewed, drunk, and licked by reciting "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," and partaking of it while touching it, he goes to the supreme goal.
Freed from all sins, he attains the destination of the virtuous;
and I have also described Alakṣmī, who was the wife of Duḥsaha.
Having heard the word "Nārāyaṇa," one goes there indeed, without a doubt;
she who is the Lakṣmī of Hari Kṛṣṇa, the God of gods, his beloved.
O you of excellent vows, having churned all the scriptures and reflected upon them again and again, [it is clear that] he dwells within the house, the field, the dwelling, and the body.
When this one [deity] is perfectly accomplished, Nārāyaṇa is always the object of meditation;
what need has he for many mantras, and what need has he for many vows?
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all purposes;
therefore, at all times, one should recite "Namo Nārāyaṇa."
O best of Brahmins, he who chants thus goes to the world of Viṣṇu along with his kinsmen.
Furthermore, O most excellent sages, listen to [the power] of the God of gods.
In the past, I mastered this mantra which accomplishes the purpose of all the Vedas;
it is composed of twelve syllables, is the ancient twelve-fold self, and is endowed with the essence of the twelve [suns].
I shall now describe its greatness here to you in brief: once, a certain highly wise brahmin, having performed austerities in some manner...
Having begotten a single son by her and having performed the sacramental rites for him in due order, he further performed his initiation at the appropriate time.
Then he taught him, yet the latter said nothing;
his tongue did not move, and that best of the twice-born became distressed.
"Aitareya certainly calls him Vāsudeva;
and his father, having likewise married another wife according to the prescribed rite," (LiP 2.7.19).
In that same manner, he procreated sons according to the prescribed rites;
having mastered the Vedas, they became accomplished and honored by all.
His mother, distressed and fainting with grief, said to Aitareya:
"My sons have been accomplished; they have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."
Being honored by the brahmins, they indeed bring joy to their mother;
yet you were born as a deformed son to me, who am devoid of fortune.
"In this matter, death is better for me than life by any means whatsoever.
Having spoken thus, he departed and went indeed to the sacrificial enclosure.
When he had departed, the mantras no longer took root among the twice-born;
while Aitareya remained there, the brahmins were then bewildered.
Then, O brahmins, a voice arose from the chanting of "Vāsudeva"; having prostrated themselves, those [disciples] of Aitareya spoke to him exactly as it was.
Then they performed worship to the sacrifice that had arrived of its own accord;
thereafter, having completed that sacrifice, Aitareya [honored him] with wealth and other gifts.
Composed in mind, all the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches spoke to him;
likewise, the Brahmins and the twice-born, beginning with Brahmā, offered hymns of praise.
The sky-dwelling Siddhas and Cāraṇas showered rains of flowers;
having thus completed the sacrifice, O best of the twice-born, Aitareya [departed].
Having honored his mother, he indeed went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus has the entire majesty of the twelve-syllable mantra been told.
It constantly destroys the great sins of those who read it or hear it; that person who constantly recites the imperishable twelve-syllabled mantra, [attains the highest goal]. (LiP 2.7.30)
He goes to that incomparable, divine, supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
even if he has been a practitioner of evil deeds— provided he is devoted to the twelve-syllable mantra.
He attains the supreme state; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
How much more so those who abide in their own duty and are devoted to Vāsudeva?
Those of great soul who observe excellent vows attain the divine abode.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Praise of the Twelve-Syllable [Mantra]," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The son said:
"O best of the twice-born, the eight-syllable [mantra] is 'namo nārāyaṇa'."
And the twelve-syllable mantra is the supreme [mantra] of the Supreme Self.
O Brahmins, the six-syllabled mantra is the collection of the meaning of all the Vedas;
and the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya" is the accomplisher of all aims.
Likewise, "to the most auspicious one" (śivatarāya) is the divine and auspicious five-syllabled mantra;
and likewise, "to the bestower of joy" (mayaskarāya), and "salutation to you, O Śaṅkara."
This seven-syllabled mantra belongs indeed to Rudra, the Pradhānapuruṣa;
it is Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, and all the gods together with Indra.
O best of the twice-born, by means of these mantras, the sages worship that Śaṅkara, the god of gods, the creator of bliss, who is born from the Unborn.
They call him Śiva, Śaṅkara, Rudra, the God of gods, and the Lord of Umā;
they say "Obeisance to Śiva" and "Salutations to you, O Śaṅkara."
By reciting [the mantra] for Rudra, the maker of bliss, and likewise for Śivatarā,
a Brahmin shall indeed be liberated in an instant from the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such offenses.
Formerly, O Lord, during the third Tretā-yuga of the Manu-period, there was a certain powerful brahmin known as Dhundhumūka.
Indeed, in the kalpa named Meghavāhana, Brahmā, the Supreme Self,
having become a cloud, [approached] Mahādeva, the Lord clad in an elephant hide.
Out of great reverence for Rudra, Janārdana, the God of gods,
became exhausted by the excessive weight of Rudra and ceased both his exhalations and inhalations.
Having made his request to Śitikaṇṭha, the lotus-eyed one performed austerities;
through that austerity, he attained supreme sovereignty as well as wonderful power.
He received [this] from Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord and the Supreme Self;
therefore, that kalpa was then known by the name Meghavāhana.
In that kalpa, through the sage’s curse, there arose Dhundhumūka;
from him was born his son, and thus he became that evil-minded one.
In former times, Dhundhumūka was infatuated with his wife; deluded by passion, he conceived a child in her through a mind attached to desire.
On the very day of the new moon, during the hour presided over by Rudra, his wife became pregnant; she was then released by him to go as she pleased.
And she, named Viśalyā, gave birth to a son with great effort during the Rudra-muhūrta, while Mandya was the aspecting planet, O best of sages.
O brahmins, the two sages then spoke thus to one another concerning Dhundhumūka: "He has brought about misfortune for his mother, his father, and likewise for himself."
"O Mitra and Varuṇa, this is a bad son," Vasiṣṭha said to the two most excellent ones, even though he himself was base, through the power of Bṛhaspati.
"Even though he is evil-minded, this son of yours shall be liberated from his sin;
that Dhundhumūka, though suffering, will see his son standing [safe]. (LiP 2.8.19)
Having performed the birth rites and other ceremonies himself according to the rules,
O best of the twice-born, he also instructed him in the sacred knowledge according to the prescribed ritual.
Having performed his marriage according to the prescribed rule, O sages of firm vows, he then went to live under the authority of Dhaundhumūka, devoted to the service of his preceptor.
O best of sages, by this very Dhaundhumūka, out of excessive pride,
having enjoyed another low-caste woman and seeing her, he reviled his own wife day and night.
That lowest of the twice-born, dull-witted and mute as a beast, shared his bed and seat with others;
thus did he of evil intellect conduct himself, having abandoned the supreme path of Dharma.
O best of the twice-born, for some reason whatsoever, he drank honey-wine with her in order to increase his passion directed toward her.
And that ill-omened Vṛṣalī was slain by the sinner;
then, at that time, her father was killed by his brothers.
The mother of that evil-minded Dhaundhumūka was beautiful, as was his wife; and those brothers-in-law of that evil-minded man were also observers of excellent vows.
In an instant, O King, the lineage of both her and him was destroyed;
and he went to Dhaindhumūka with ease, by whatever means possible.
Having seen that best of sages, who was devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-mantra,
he had indeed previously obtained that Pāśupata [weapon] from the god Maheśvara.
Having obtained both the five-syllabled and the unsurpassed six-syllabled mantra,
one should again recite each of the five-syllabled mantras separately one hundred thousand times.
Having performed the divine twelve-month vow according to the prescribed rite,
he passed away at the end of the kalpa and was indeed honored by Yama.
Likewise, his mother was delivered, as were his father and his brothers-in-law of virtuous vows;
and his wife became fortunate, possessing a beautiful smile and devoted to her husband.
Having ascended those celestial chariots and being praised by the gods including Indra,
he attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas and became beloved of Rudra.
Therefore, from this eight-syllable mantra as well as the twelve-syllable one, there shall arise merit a hundred million times greater; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Therefore, one should constantly recite the *dhī* mantra according to the previously mentioned procedure, conjoined with the seed-syllable of Śakti; such a person attains the supreme goal.
All this, the supreme essence of all narratives, has been told to you;
whoever reads it, hears it, or causes the best of the twice-born to hear it, [attains the highest merit].
He indeed goes to the world of Brahmā by means of this unsurpassed recitation of the Rudra-mantra.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"In ancient times, the gods performed the auspicious and divine Pāśupata vow."
And it was composed by Brahmā himself, O Sūta, and by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds.
And how did the outcaste brahmin Dhaindhumūka attain his destination by performing and reciting the Pāśupata vow? LiP_2,9.2 //
How did the god Paśupati, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord [attain his state]? You ought to tell us this, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Sūta said:
Long ago, the highly illustrious son of Brahmā, having been released from a curse,
came here from the Maru country to the presence of Rudra, the God of gods.
Having cast off his camel body through the grace of Rudra by the command of the Goddess,
he approached the son of Śilāda and paid him homage according to the prescribed rites.
O best of sages, having heard the unsurpassed Dharma concerning Maheśvara on the summit of Meru,
that most excellent of munis questioned him again and again.
"Having prostrated before this Nandin, how did the Lord Paśupati speak?
You should tell us all of that," and he (Nandin) then related it all.
The lord Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana heard all of that;
having heard it from him, I shall indeed relate it to you.
Having heard these words and paid homage to Maheśvara,
Sanatkumāra said:
"How is the god Paśupati [defined], and who are proclaimed to be the *paśus*?"
"By which nooses are they bound, and how are they liberated?
Śailādi said: "O Sanatkumāra, I shall explain all of this to you exactly as it is."
For you, who are devoted to Rudra, peaceful, and pure-minded,
[there are] the beings from Brahmā down to the immovable, belonging to the wise God of gods.
Those subject to the power of saṃsāra are proclaimed as "beasts" (paśu); because he is their lord, the Blessed Lord Rudra is remembered as Paśupati.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the imperishable sustainer who is without beginning or end,
binds living beings like cattle with the noose of Māyā, O Supreme Lord.
He alone, when served through the yoga of knowledge, is their liberator;
for those bound by the noose of ignorance, no other liberator is recognized.
Apart from that Supreme Self, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord,
the twenty-four principles are indeed the bonds of Parameṣṭhin.
Worshipped by living beings, Śiva alone liberates them with those nooses;
yet he alone binds the bound souls (paśus) with twenty-four nooses.
That very Lord Rudra, when served, liberates one even from the fetters consisting of the ten senses that arise from the internal organ.
The Lord releases the bound souls from the fetters of the elements and the subtle essences;
having bound the sense-objects with the fetters consisting of the objects of the senses, the Lord [releases them].
In this way, through service to the Supreme Lord, devotees indeed become swift;
for this verbal root *bhaj* is proclaimed to mean "service. (LiP 2.9.19)
Therefore, service is declared by the wise to be more frequently expressed by the word "devotion" (bhakti).
Having bound all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, Maheśvara [remains the Lord].
He himself causes [the soul] to perform its duties through the three bonds consisting of the qualities (guṇas),
while being worshipped by the bound souls (paśus) with firm yoga of devotion.
Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, immediately liberates them;
devotion is said to be service performed through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
Because he is the cause of all effects, he is most capable of severing the bonds;
"He is the Truth, he is omnipresent," and so forth—this is the contemplation of the qualities of Śiva.
The wise know that mental devotion consists in reflection upon the material substratum of form,
while they know verbal devotion to consist in the recitation of the *praṇava* and other such mantras.
Devotion to the body through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth by the virtuous is said to be this bondage of embodied beings by the snares consisting of dharma and adharma.
The liberator is Śiva alone, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord;
the twenty-four principles consist of Māyā, Karma, and the Guṇas.
Objects of sense are called "nooses" because they bind the individual soul;
all embodied beings bound by them are liberated only through devotion to Śiva.
Śaṅkara binds the individual souls with nooses consisting of the five afflictions;
yet he alone is their liberator when properly worshipped with devotion.
The best of bipeds declare that ignorance, egoism, passion, hatred,
and clinging are the afflictions that have come to function as fetters.
The wise declare that ignorance exists in five forms: as *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and what they call *andhatāmisra*.
The illustrious Śiva liberates all those living beings from ignorance, O tigers among sages; there is no other liberator whatsoever.
Those wise ones devoted to yoga say that ignorance is darkness (*tamas*), egoism is delusion (*moha*),
and passion is great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
The wise call hatred *tāmisra* and also *andhatāmisra*,
as well as dogmatic attachment and false knowledge.
The divisions of *tamas* are said to be eightfold, and *moha* is likewise remembered as being eightfold;
furthermore, the subdivisions of *mahāmoha* have been considered by the wise to be ten.
The wise have declared that *tāmisra* is of eighteen kinds,
and likewise, the varieties of *andhatāmisra* are recorded as being eighteenfold.
There would be no past or future connection of this god Śambhu, who dwells in the body, with ignorance or with passion.
In the three times, there can be no connection with hatred for that Lord,
the omnipresent Sthāṇu Paśupati, who has transcended all illusion.
In that very same way, there is never any connection with attachment to Śaṅkara, the refuge, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
For Śambhu, who has transcended ignorance, there can be no connection whatsoever with wholesome or unwholesome actions throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, there can be no association with the ripening of karmas for anyone who is at all times auspicious and the bestower of auspiciousness.
Untouched by pleasures and pains occurring throughout the three periods of time, Śambhu— the supreme one whose essence is consciousness and bliss— remains unaffected by those transitory states.
Untouched by the mental dispositions that range within the three periods of time,
this Lord of intellects, who is his own source, is Mahādeva, the Great Lord.
The Blessed One, the destroyer of Death himself, is untouched by the impressions of karma existing throughout the three periods of time, and likewise by the impressions of experience.
The Lord, the Blessed One, the Supreme Sovereign, is the supreme among all beings;
he transcends the entire manifold universe composed of both sentient and insentient entities.
In the world, knowledge and sovereignty are observed to possess degrees of excellence;
however, the wise call that which possesses excellence beyond all else "Śiva."
At the beginning of each secondary creation, he alone is the instructor of the extensive scriptures to the Brahmins born therein, who exist within the constraints of time.
He is the Guru even of those gurus who are bound by the limitations of time;
he is the Lord of all, himself devoid of the limitations of time.
This supreme connection between consciousness and excellence is beginningless;
for all things thus established, it is pure by their very nature.
Indeed, in the absence of any personal motive, the Supreme Lord has only the favoring of others as the purpose for all his actions.
The *praṇava* is the designator of that Śiva, the Supreme Self;
even among words such as "Śiva" and "Rudra," the *praṇava* is remembered as the highest.

Through the contemplation of Śambhu, who is denoted by the syllable Om (praṇava), as well as through its recitation, that perfection which is unattainable for oneself or others certainly comes to pass; of this there is no doubt.
The supreme Pāśupata yoga, which is the reality of knowledge,
has been taught with effort by the God of gods out of compassion for all beings.

Yājñavalkya said: "O Gārgī, that which yogis declare to be the Imperishable (akṣara)—which is neither gross nor infinite, yet is a great wonder; which is neither long nor red, neither head nor mouth, neither hand nor foot; which is without measure, without sound, without touch, without form, without decay, without taste, without smell, without eye, without ear, without speech, without mind, without vigor, without breath, without mouth, without measure, without pleasure or pain, without name or lineage, immortal, undecaying, free from disease, deathless, beyond the syllable *oṃ*, soundless, deathless, unenclosed, without before or after, without end, and without exterior."
Then he eats nothing at all; he does not eat anything at all.
Having understood that this is the expenditure of time, one whose purpose is indeed the supreme goal in this Pāśupata yoga should know the Lord Pāśupati.

Having made the syllable *oṃ* your lamp, seek the subtle Householder who dwells at the beginning and the end; having restrained the gatekeeper—the exceedingly swift wind—and the leader of the senses, for what reason do you boast with webs of words?
Indeed, no fear is seen at all; behold Śambhu residing within the body! Why do you wander among others in the darkness of the snare of weapons?
Having thus correctly understood this, as taught by the sages and by Śiva,
one should divide the *asamarasa* into five parts and unite them with the self.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Tell me once more of the majesty of the Lord of Umā."
O devotee of Bhava, O highly wise one, O Blessed Nandikeśvara!
Śailādi said: O Sanatkumāra, I shall describe to you in brief and in its entirety the majesty of Maheśa, Bhava, the Supreme Lord.
He had no bondage to the material nature (prakṛti), nor any bondage of the intellect (buddhi);
he had no bondage of the ego (ahaṃkāra), and no bondage of the mind (manas).
He had no binding of the mind, nor was there any binding of the ears;
never indeed did a binding of the skin or of the eyes arise for him.
O observer of noble vows, he had no binding of the tongue, nor any binding of the nose; there was no binding of the feet, no binding of the hands, and no binding of speech.
The organ of generation and the bondage of the elements and subtle essences [are transcended];
by virtue of its eternally pure nature, it is eternally awakened by its very essence.
"He is declared by the sages who know reality to be eternally liberated;
[this is the nature] of Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who is without beginning, middle, or end."
By the impulse of the Puruṣa, Prakṛti produces the intellect (buddhi);
by the impulse of that [intellect], it produces the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) for him.
By his command, the ten senses, the one [mind], and the subtle elements belong to the Self-born One, who is renowned as the Inner Controller within bodies. (LiP 2.10.9)
Ego (ahaṅkāra) brings forth the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) by the command of Śiva, the Supreme Lord; they are produced from him, O Master.
The wise Mahādeva [created] the great elements in their entirety,
as well as the connection with bodies for all embodied beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
By the command of Śiva, all the great elements (mahābhūtas) without exception bring them into being;
by the command of that All-pervading Lord, the intellect determines all objects.
The sovereignty of the Self-born One, who is renowned as the Inner Controller within bodies, is established by his own nature; from that very nature come all prosperities.
By his command, the ego (ahaṅkāra) conceives of all objects;
the mind (citta) perceives, and the intellect (manas) also forms volitions.
The ear hears by its own power, as do sound, touch, and the rest,
solely through the force of the command of Śambhu, the supreme lord Bhava.
By the command of that god, he never at any time issues a word or speech for all bodies without exception, such as the taking up [of breath] and so forth.
The hand performs the act of grasping, and never the acts of going and so forth;
this is by the very decree of the Creator for all living beings alike.
His foot makes its dwelling [there], never abandoning it or departing,
by the very command of Śiva, for the sake of the entire multitude of embodied beings.
By the command of the Supreme Lord, the anus performs the excretion of all living beings that are born; it should never speak.
By the command of the Lord, and by the instruction of the Sovereign himself, the organ of procreation constantly brings forth joy for all living beings.
Space always provides room for all beings without exception,
solely by the command of that Supreme One.
Through its own divisions, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and others, the Wind, by means of the various manifestations of Śiva himself,
sustains the bodies of all living beings.
By the instruction of the God of gods, the Wind, abiding within the seven layers,
carries out the course of the world through its own divisions, beginning with Āvaha.
The wind, by the command of the supreme deity, operates within bodies through fivefold divisions beginning with the *nāga*.

By the command of Śaṅkara alone, the Fire-god carries the oblation (havya) to the gods and the ancestral offering (kavya) to the consumers of such offerings (kavyāśins), and he also performs the act of cooking.
Likewise, by the command of the Lord of the Universe, the fire residing within the stomach always digests whatever food has been consumed by embodied beings.
By his command, the waters sustain all beings without exception;
for the supreme command of that Great One is indeed inviolable by all.
By his command alone, all beings, both moving and unmoving, are sustained;
by the command of that God, Purandara, the god of gods, [is empowered].
The Sustainer of the Universe constantly afflicts those who live with diseases and those who are dead with hundreds of torments— afflictions that cannot be transgressed by any people at all.
Protecting the gods and slaying the demons, he stands over the entire triple world;
by the command of Śiva, he brings about the destruction of those who are unrighteous.
By his command, Varuṇa sustains the worlds with the waters;
by his decree, he submerges them and binds the asuras with his nooses.
In accordance with their merit, he bestows wealth upon all living beings;
by the command of that supreme-lipped Lord, the Master of Wealth [Kubera] grants riches.
By his command, the sun performs the rising and setting,
thereby effecting time for that eternal, true Supreme Self.
By the command of the Ordainer of Time, the moon— the possessor of nectar, the bearer of its digits— causes the flowers born of medicinal herbs to bloom and gladdens all living beings.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts,
as well as all other deities, were created by his command.
The Gandharvas, the Devasaṃvas, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, and the Cāraṇas,
as well as the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas, abide within the scriptures of the Creator.
The planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as sacrifices, the Vedas, and ascetic penances—
all the hosts of sages abide under his command.
The hosts of those who consume the offerings to the ancestors, the seven oceans, the mountain rivers,
the forests, and the lakes all abide within his dominion.
The divisions of time— kalās, kāṣṭhās, nimeṣas, muhūrtas, days, nights,
seasons, years, fortnights, and months— are established by his command.
By the command of this Śambhu, yugas, manvantaras,
as well as other divisions of time such as parārdhas and aparārdhas, endure.
The eight classes of gods and the five classes of animals,
as well as human beings, proceed from the wise God of gods.
The multitudes of beings born within the fourteen classes of existence, dwelling throughout all the worlds, remain so by his very command.
The subjects born and residing in the fourteen worlds are subject to the command of that very Lord, the Sovereign of All.
By his command, all the netherworlds, the worlds,
and the remaining cosmic eggs, along with their coverings, [were established].
By his command, all the existing universes,
together with all living beings and other entities, proceed everywhere.
By his command, even the countless Brahmāṇḍas of the past proceeded forth on all sides, accompanied by floods of material objects.
The cosmic eggs, together with their constituent elements and along with all their coverings, shall come into being and carry out the command of Śiva.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, describe to me the manifestations (vibhūtis) of Śiva and Śivā."
O best among those who know the higher and the lower, O you who are permeated by the Supreme Lord!
Nandikeśvara said: "Ah, O Sanatkumāra, lord of yogins and best of the sons of Brahmā, I shall indeed recount to you the manifold powers (vibhūtis) of Śiva and Śivā."
The Supreme Self is declared to be Śiva, and Śivā is proclaimed as his consort;
the wise say that the Lord is indeed Śiva, and they know Māyā to be Gaurī.
The twice-born declare the Puruṣa to be Śaṅkara and Gaurī to be Prakṛti;
Śambhu is Artha and Śivā is Vāṇī; the day is Aja and Śivā is the night.
The seven-threaded [sacrifice] is Mahādeva; Rudrāṇī is remembered as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Ākāśa is the god Śaṅkara, and the Earth is the beloved of Śaṅkara.
The Blessed One Rudra is the ocean; the Daughter of the Lord of Mountains is the shore;
the trident-armed God is the tree; and the beloved of the Trident-bearer is the creeper.
Brahmā and Hara, Sāvitrī who shares half the body of Śaṅkara,
Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, Lakṣmī and the supreme goddess Bhavānī.
Vajrapāṇi is Mahādeva; Śacī is the daughter of the Lord of Mountains;
Jātavedas is Rudra himself; and Svāhā is the one whose body is half of Śarva.
The god Yama has the three-eyed one as his deity, and his beloved is Girikanyakā;
the lord Varuṇa has Rudra as his deity, and Gaurī is the bestower of all goals.
The wind is the crescent moon on the peak; Śivā is the one who is delightful to Śiva.
The lord of the yakṣas has the half-moon upon his crest; Ṛddhi herself is remembered as Śivā.
The moon-crested one is Candra; Rohiṇī is the beloved of Rudra;
the seven-horsed sun is Śiva; his consort is Umā-devī; and Suvarcalā is [his] wife.
The six-faced one, the destroyer of Tripura, Deva, Senā, Harapriyā, Umā, and Prasūti are to be known as the goddesses; Dakṣa is the god Maheśvara.
The Manu named Puruṣa was Śambhu, and Śatarūpā was the beloved of Śiva;
they knew Ākūti as Bhavānī and Ruci as the Supreme Lord.
Bhṛgu is the god who destroyed Bhaga’s eyes; Khyāti is dear to the Three-eyed One.
Marīci is the lord Rudra, and Saṃbhūti is the beloved of the All-pervading Lord.
You know Bhavānī as Rucirā and the Supreme Lord as Kavi;
she is to be known through the speech of Gaṅgādhara, and Smṛti is remembered as Umā herself.
Pulastya is the moon-crested one; Prīti is the beloved of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Pulaha is the destroyer of Tripura; Dayā is the beloved of the enemy of Time (Śiva).
The wise have declared that Kratu was Dakṣa, Saṃnati the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Dāyitā the consort of the Lord, Trinetra was Atri, and Umā herself was known as Anasūyā.
They say that Ūrjā is Umā, Vṛddhā is Vasiṣṭha, and Maheśvara is Śaṅkara;
all males are Puruṣas, and all females are Maheśvarī.
Those which are denoted by masculine words are proclaimed to be forms of Rudra;
those which are denoted by feminine words are all manifestations of Gaurī.
All women and men are said to be the manifestations (vibhūti) of those two alone;
whatever powers of entities there may be, the wise know them as Gaurī.
She is the Goddess Viśveśvarī, and he is the universal Maheśvara;
whatever objects possess power, all that is the universal Maheśvara.
The eight primary forms (prakṛtis) of the Goddess are proclaimed to be her very embodiments;
likewise, her transformations (vikṛtis) are her manifestations bound within bodies.
Just as sparks are known to emanate in many ways from a fire,
so too do all individual souls (jīvas) emerge from Śarva, having entered into the state of dualistic existence.
All bodies of embodied beings are forms of Gaurī,
and likewise all embodied beings are established as portions of Śaṅkara.
The entire form of Umā is that which is to be heard, and the Lord Maheśvara is the hearer;
the omnipresent one assumes the state of being the subject, while Umā consists of the objects of perception.
The beloved of Śaṅkara sustains the multitude of created things,
while he alone— the creator who is the soul of the universe and whose crest is adorned with the crescent of the young moon— is the progenitor.
The Sovereign of the World bears the visible object in the form of the subjects;
the Seer is the Lord of the Universe, the God whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon.
The entire range of flavors is the form of Umā, and all that is to be smelled is likewise her form;
Śambhu is the god who tastes, and the Lord of the World is the one who smells.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī assumes the state of being the object of meditation;
the meditator himself is that very Universal Self, Mahādeva Maheśvara.
The beloved of worldly existence assumes the form of the object to be known;
that very Lord, the Blessed One whose crest is the young moon, is the knower.
The goddess Umā is in the form of a pedestal (pīṭha), and Śaṅkara is in the form of a liṅga;
having installed them with great effort, the gods and asuras worship them.
Whichever objects are marked with the male organ (liṅga) are the manifestations of Śarva;
whichever objects are marked with the female organ (bhaga) are the manifestations of Gaurī.
The eightfold covering of the cosmic egg, extending from heaven to the netherworlds, is to be known as entirely the form of Umā; the Knower is the Lord Maheśvara.
The Goddess, beloved of the Destroyer of Tripura, maintains the state of the field (kṣetra),
while the Blessed Lord, the Slayer of Andhaka, assumes the state of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
He who abandons the Śiva-liṅga and worships other deities shall go,
along with his kingdom, to the Raurava hell.
A king who is not a devotee of Śiva, but one who is devoted to other gods,
is like a young woman who, having abandoned her own husband, takes pleasure with paramours.
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, kings of great supernatural power,
as well as human beings and sages— all of them worship the Liṅga.
Having slain Rāvaṇa along with his army— the son of Brahmā— Viṣṇu duly installed a liṅga with devotion on the bank of the lord of rivers.
Having committed thousands of sins and likewise having killed a hundred Brahmins, one who takes refuge in Rudra with true devotion is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
All worlds consist of the *liṅga*; all are established upon the *liṅga*.
Therefore, one should worship the *liṅga* if one desires the eternal state.
These two auspicious forms in all their aspects, which bring welfare, should always be worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon by men seeking their own highest good.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Tell me of the eight forms of the high-souled Śaṅkara."
O high-minded Lord of the Gaṇas, [this is the hymn] of the god Viśvarūpa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O you who were born from the lotus-born [Brahmā], I shall indeed tell you of the majesty of the Lord of Umā, the god whose form is the universe."
Earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sun, the consecrated one,
and the moon are declared to be the forms of Bhava, Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
Space, the self, the moon, fire, the sun, water, the earth, and wind—
these are declared to be the eight forms of that wise God of gods.
When the Agnihotra is offered into that great Self, whose nature is the Sun,
all the gods who bestow all things are likewise perpetually satisfied by that manifestation.
Just as the branches and twigs of a tree flourish by the watering of its root,
so too do the gods and their manifestations prosper through the worship of him.
The form of that Lord, consisting of the Sun, is divided twelvefold;
it is the embodiment of all the gods, and the preeminent sages worship it as the object of sacrifice.
The digit of that entire sun-formed being is called Amṛtā;
it is the life-restoring activity that is constantly drunk by the world in this universe.
The rays called "moon" from that Dhūrjaṭi, who is of the nature of the sun,
spread forth a shower of snow for the sake of increasing the medicinal herbs.
The white rays known as Śuklā, belonging to that Śambhu who has taken the form of the sun,
spread righteousness in the world and are the cause of the ripening of crops and other such things.
Of that Supreme Lord, whose essence is the sun, there is a hand named Harikeśa,
which is renowned as the nourisher of the stars.
The ray of that god Sarveśvara, who takes the form of the seven-horsed sun, is named Viśvakarman, the nourisher of Budha.
The ray of that wielder of the trident, who is of the nature of the sun, is known as Viśvavyacas; it is recognized as being in the state of nourishing the semen.
He who is known as Saṃyadvasu is the ray of the trident-bearing one whose nature is that of the thousand-rayed sun; he nourishes the red-bodied planet Mars.
The ray of that wielder of the Pināka bow is known as Arvāvasu;
it always nourishes Bṛhaspati by means of its heating nature.
Known as Svarāṭ, he is a partial incarnation (aṃśu) of Śiva;
he nourishes Śanaiścara, who is of the nature of Haridaśva, day and night.
The ray known as Suṣumṇā, belonging to the Sun-natured God, the source of the universe and Lord of Umā, always nourishes the cool-rayed Moon.
The form of Śaṅkara, the teacher of the world, which is called Soma, has attained the state of being the primordial nature of the gentle ones born from the Vasus.
The lunar form of that god,
the ruler of the Destroyer, exists as semen within all embodied beings.
Within the minds of all embodied beings without exception resides the body of Śambhu, the teacher of the entire world, which is composed of the essence of the moon.
The supreme form known as Soma, which consists of the sixteenfold divided portions of nectar residing within the bodies of all beings, belongs to Śambhu.
The form of that ruler of the gods of gods, known as Soma, constantly nourishes the gods and the ancestors with nectar and ambrosia.
The body called Soma nourishes the various plants for the purification of embodied beings; one should designate that as Bhavānī.
This form of Umāpati, consisting of the syllable *mum*, is indeed well-known as the lord of sacrifices, of living beings, and of austerities.
The body of that blessed Lord Śambhu is renowned for being the lord of waters and herbs; it is composed of the essence of Soma.
The god is golden and pure, distinct from one another,
the formless essence of all the instruments and of all the deities.
While that Lord Śiva, whose nature is the Moon, remains as the principle of life-force (jīvatva),
Madhurā, the sole protector of all the worlds, attains dissolution.
The Śiva-form, which is invoked by the sacrificer, nourishes all the deities with sacrificial offerings day and night, as well as the hosts of ancestors with ancestral oblations.
That body which is called the sacrificer and is born from the oblation,
through that rain it clearly nourishes everything, both the transcendent and the immanent.
The water situated within and without the cosmic eggs,
and that which resides within the bodies of living beings— this is the most venerable form of Śambhu.
The Lord of Umā is the manifest nectar of rivers, always the [nectar] of streams as well,
and he is omnipresent throughout all oceans.
She is the reviver of all living beings and their purifier;
she is Ambikā, who abides in the vital breaths, whose supreme form consists of water.
Abiding both within and without the cosmic eggs, the fire of the worlds,
and residing within the bodies of sacrifices, he is the most venerable form of Śambhu.
And the sovereign form of Śambhu, which resides within the bodies of all beings and is established in the fire, is the most auspicious form, highly honored by all.
Forty-nine varieties have been proclaimed by those who know the Vedas;
it is the body of Śambhu, whose nature is sacrifice, that carries the oblation to the gods.
The *kavya* offered by the twice-born to the hosts of ancestors is the body of Śambhu, which consists of all the gods, is most excellent, and has fire as its essence.
Those learned in the Vedas and Śāstras declare that he performs sacrifices according to the prescribed rules;
he is the wind situated within the cosmic eggs of the universe and also existing outside them.
And residing within the bodies of living beings is the most potent form of Śiva:
the vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, those beginning with nāga and kūrma, and the winds beginning with āvaha.
All the various manifestations are proclaimed to be of the one form of Īśāna;
the universe of cosmic eggs resides within him, while the all-pervading Lord exists outside it as well.
Residing within the bodies of all beings is the most venerable form of Śambhu;
the Earth is the form of Śambhu, the presiding deity of all Brahman.
She is considered the support for all beings, both moving and unmoving;
the wise know the bodies of moving and unmoving beings to be her.
O best of sages, the five elements, the moon, the sun, and the self have in every way been derived from these five forms.
They say there are eight forms of the wise Śiva, the God of gods;
his eighth form is the supreme one, called the sacrificer (yajamāna).
Then, the lords of sages declared that the Self resides within all bodies, both moving and unmoving, and that it is the initiated Brahmin who is that very Self.
The form known as Yajamāna is the embodiment of Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness;
these eight forms of Śiva should be diligently saluted.
Those who seek their own welfare should always [revere] these, for they are the sole causes of all that is auspicious.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Nandin, tell me once more the majesty of the Lord of Umā."
Of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), who possesses eight forms; LiP_2,13.1 //
Nandikeśvara said: I shall describe to you the majesty of Maheśa, the Lord of Umā,
the Supreme Being who exists pervading the universe as one whose form is eightfold.
The god who is the sustainer of all beings, both moving and unmoving, and whose nature is the supporter of the universe,
is called Śarva by those who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures.
The wife of that Viśvambhara, the supreme lord of all, is said to be Vikeśī, and his son is remembered as Aṅgāraka.
The Lord, the Blessed One, is called *Bhava* by those who expound the Vedas; he is the supreme self (*paramātman*) of existence (*bhava*), the source of life for all worlds.
The goddess Umā has been celebrated by the wise, as well as her son Śukra;
he pervades the seven cosmic eggs and is the sole protector of all the worlds.
The Lord God Paśupati is remembered by the wise as having fire as his essence;
Svāhā is declared to be the beloved wife of that Paśupati, existing in the form of his consort.
The six-faced Lord is declared by the wise to be the Son;
he pervades all worlds and is the sustainer of all embodied beings.
O God, he whose nature is wind is proclaimed by the wise as Īśāna;
[this is the praise] of the god Īśāna, the creator of the world, whose nature is wind.
The goddess Śivā has been described by the wise as his daughter, and his son is Manojava,
who grants all desires to all beings, both moving and stationary.
The Lord God, whose self is the sky, is called Bhīma by the wise; such is the deity Bhīma of great majesty, whose nature is the firmament.
The ten directions are remembered as goddesses, and their son is the creation, according to the wise;
the divine Lord, whose self is the sun, is the bestower of prosperity upon all.
The Lord is called Rudra by the gods, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation;
he is the Sun-souled Rudra who grants devotion to his devotees.
The goddess Suvarcalā is remembered as his wife, and his son is Śanaiścara;
he is renowned for being the primordial source of all gentle substances.
The wise remember the god who consists of Soma as Mahādeva;
[this is] the god Mahādeva, who consists of Soma, according to the learned.
Rohiṇī was declared his beloved, and Budha was born from his body;
at that time, he established the order of sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral rites (kavya) for those who consume such offerings.
The Lord Mahādeva, who is identical with the sacrificer,
is called "Ugra" by the wise, and "Īśāna" by others among the virtuous.
The wise have declared that for the Lord known as Ugra, whose nature is that of the sacrificer,
Dīkṣā is the wife and the son is named Saṃtāna.
Those desiring to know the reality of Śarva should understand that the earthly body among the bodies of embodied beings is as hard as Koṅkaṇa and the like. LiP 2.13.19.
But within every body, O Lord of Gods, resides that imperishable essence of the embodied beings,
which consists of the substance of reality, belonging to Bhava, the Supreme Self.
And this should indeed be known by those who know reality and have reached the further shore of the meaning of all the Vedas:
that which is the fiery transformation within the bodies of embodied beings.
That which is the transformation of wind within the bodies of embodied beings is to be known as Paśupati, the embodiment [of the deity], by those who desire to know the ultimate reality.
The wise should know that the Lord (Īśa) is his body, of this there is no doubt;
for he is the cavity situated within the bodies of all embodied beings.
That body of Bhīma should be known by those desiring the realization of reality as the splendor residing in the eyes and other senses of embodied beings that is situated within their bodies.
Those desiring to know the ultimate truth should understand that the body of Rudra is that which,
within the bodies of all beings, consists of the mind and the nature of the moon.
That form of Mahādeva is to be understood by those who contemplate reality as the Self known as the sacrificer, which dwells within the bodies of all beings.
That form of the Fierce One is to be known by those desiring to know the Supreme Self as the source of all beings born within the fourteen classes of origins.
The supreme seers declare that there is no difference between [the Lord] and his eightfold form;
they say that the limbs of embodied beings consist of the seven forms of the Lord.
The Self (ātman) is his eighth form, residing within the bodies of all beings.
One should worship this Lord, the pervasive one who consists of all worlds and possesses eight forms.
Devote yourself with your whole being if you desire to attain the highest good;
for even if a favor is done toward any living being whatsoever, it brings merit.
Whether one has performed worship of Maheśvara, who possesses eight forms,
or whether one has inflicted punishment upon any embodied being in the world, [the same result follows].
That very same [penance] would be ordained for Maheśvara, who possesses eight forms,
if disrespect were shown toward any embodied being whatsoever in the world.
That [gesture] which grants freedom from fear to any living being whatsoever is ordained as the Mahāśa (Great Peace) of the Lord who possesses eight forms.
Therefore, there is no doubt that the propitiation of the Eight-formed Lord has been performed;
it consists of acting for the benefit of all and the granting of fearlessness.
The propitiation of the God who possesses eight forms is, without doubt,
the performance of every service and indeed the bestowing of grace upon all.
The lords of sages have declared that worship of you, who possess eight forms, is supreme;
furthermore, you must bestow grace upon other embodied beings.
And the granting of safety to all [beings] by one who desires the propitiation of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: "O Nandin, best of the Gaṇas, tell me about the five Brahmans."
These purifiers bring about the highest good for embodied beings.
Nandikeśvara said: O best of sons, I shall describe to you, born from the lotus, the five forms of Śiva himself known as the Brahmās, according to their true nature.
The sole destroyer of all worlds, the sole protector of all worlds,
the sole creator of all worlds, Śambhu is the essence of the five Brahmās.
They say that Śiva is remembered as fivefold: he is the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) and the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa) of all the worlds.
The five renowned forms, called the five Brahmans, are the supreme manifestations of Śiva,
the Supreme Self, who is the refuge of all worlds.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the first form of Śiva, the Supreme Lord;
he is designated as Īśāna, the enjoyer of the category of Prakṛti which is the object of enjoyment.
And the second form of Sthāṇu is called Tatpuruṣa;
for that should be known as Prakṛti, whose nature is the cave of the Supreme Self.
The third form of Śambhu is called Aghora, the most venerable;
it is said that this form is the intellect (buddhi), endowed with the eight limbs beginning with dharma.
The fourth form of Śambhu, known as Vāmadeva, is the most exalted;
it abides pervading everything by means of its nature as the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
The fifth form of Śambhu is said to be named Sadyojāta;
it exists within all embodied beings as the essence of the principle of the mind (manas).
Īśāna is the supreme deity, the eternal Parameṣṭhin;
he abides within all beings as the essence of the sense of hearing.
The divine Tatpuruṣa resides within the bodies of embodied beings;
he is described by those who know the principles as being of the nature of the sense-organ of touch.
Although Mahādeva is Aghora, he is proclaimed by the wise as the eye-soul,
established within the bodies of all living beings.
Vāmadeva is also renowned as being of the nature of the faculty of taste;
he is established within the limbs of all beings who possess limbs.
Sadyojāta is remembered by the wise as being of the nature of the olfactory faculty;
he is established within the bodies of all living beings.
Established within the bodies of all living beings as the essence of the organ of speech, he is called Īśāna by the wise.
Among those who assume all forms, that person is said by the wise to exist as the very essence of the sense-organ of touch within all bodies.
For even Aghora is established within the bodies of all embodied beings;
he is proclaimed by the knowers of reality as being of the nature of the organ of the feet.
Vāmadeva is established as being of the nature of the organ of excretion;
he is remembered by the sages as residing within the bodies of all classes of living beings.
The Lord Sadyojāta, abiding as the self present in the body,
is recognized by those learned in the Vedas and scriptures as the sustainer of the vital breaths within the bodies of living beings.
The hosts of sages and the progeny of the gods declare the Lord of living beings to be the deity whose form consists of the subtle element of sound, and who is the generator of space.
The lords of sages have declared that divine Being to be the *tatpuruṣa*, whose essence consists of the subtle element of touch; they declare the Blessed One to be the progenitor of wind.
Those foremost among the knowers of the Vedas declare that the god Aghora, though himself terrible, consists of the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra) and is the progenitor of Jātavedas (Fire).
Because it consists of the subtle element of taste,
those who know the principles declare Vāmadeva to be established as the progenitor of the waters.
Those who know the true meaning of all principles praise Sadyojāta Mahādeva, who has the form of the subtle element of smell and is the very self of the earth.
O lords of sages, they declare that Īśāna, the primordial deity whose self is space,
is a marvel born of supreme greatness.
The wise know the Lord, the divine Tatpuruṣa, who is the wind and whose nature is wind, celebrated as such because he pervades all the worlds.
Then those who know the meaning of the Vedic statements declare that Aghora, who is of the nature of fire, is the Great Self, renowned for being worthy of worship.
O sages, you know that Mahādeva, who is Vāmadeva, the delightful one, consists of water; he is described as the very life-force of the world.
The best of poets know the Lord to be the very essence of the earth, Sadyojāta, the teacher of the world, the sole sustainer of all that is moving and unmoving, and the Supreme.
The sages who perceive the truth declare that the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the five Brahmās and is the bliss of Śiva.
That which appears in the phenomenal world as consisting of the twenty-five principles is Śiva himself, existing as the essence of the five Brahmās; he has not become something other than that.
Śiva, whose self consists of the twenty-five principles and who is composed of the five Brahmās,
should therefore be constantly meditated upon with effort by those seeking the highest good.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Five Brahmas," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O high-minded one, please recount once more the majesty of Śiva.
For you are omniscient, O Great Virtuous One, the supreme lord of all beings.
Śailādi said: O sage, listen with one-pointed attention as I shall describe to you the majesty of Śiva,
which has been celebrated in many ways by the most excellent of sages using numerous words.
Some sages and wise scholars proclaim him to be Śiva, saying that he is both existent and non-existent in form, and also the Lord of the existent and the non-existent.
It is called the second through its transformation into the state of being manifest;
because it is devoid of that manifestation, it is also called the unmanifest and the non-existent.
For both of these are indeed of the nature of Śiva; nothing other than Śiva exists.
And because he is the lord of those two, Śiva is called the Lord of the existent and the non-existent.
Some sages who contemplate the principles declare Śiva, the Great Lord, to consist of both the perishable and the imperishable, and likewise to be beyond the perishable and the imperishable.
The imperishable is said to be unmanifest, while the perishable is declared to be manifest;
these two forms belong to Śaṅkara alone, and therefore nothing higher than him is spoken of.
Beyond those two is Śiva, the peaceful one, who is beyond the perishable and the imperishable; he is called Mahādeva Maheśvara by the wise according to the ultimate truth.
But by then remembering that form which is both the aggregate and the individual, he is liberated—
that form which is both the aggregate and the individual, and the cause of both the aggregate and the individual.
Some teachers declare Śiva to be the supreme cause;
the lords of sages know the unmanifest to be the collective totality (samaṣṭi) and the manifest to be the individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi).
When those two forms of Śambhu are described, there is no other possible existence of substance;
for through the absence of agency in those two, Śiva is indeed the Supreme Lord.

It is said by those learned in the Yoga-śāstras that Śiva is the cause of both the collective and the individual; and by some, he is declared to be the embodiment of both the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
The Supreme Self, the supreme light, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ruler,
is the cause of the twenty-four principles both collectively and individually.
They say that the enjoyer, the Puruṣa, is designated by the term "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña);
these two, the field and the knower of the field, are the two forms of that Self-existent One.
The wise have declared that there is nothing other than Śiva;
he is Śiva, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, yet who takes the form of the Lower Brahman.
Some say that Mahādeva is the Lord who is without beginning or end,
whose nature consists of the elements, the senses, the internal organs, primordial matter (pradhāna), and the objects of the senses.
The lower Brahman has been pointed out, and the higher Brahman consists of consciousness;
these are the two Brahmans of this Maheśvara, Śiva, the self-existent.
For Śaṅkara, who is the Supreme, nothing exists apart from Śiva;
yet some declare that Śaṅkara is the very embodiment of both knowledge and ignorance.
The Ordainer, the Disposer, the primordial god, the Great Lord—
him alone the lords of sages call both "Vidyā" and "Avidyā."
The entire multitude of conceptual proliferations within the nature of the Self-existent One is delusion; knowledge and the supreme [state] are the unsurpassed form of Śiva.
Some sages, through yoga and by knowing the traditional scriptures, attained knowledge regarding objects of manifold forms; that [knowledge] is called delusion. LiP_2.15.21.
Cognition in the form of the Self is proclaimed by the wise as *vidyā*;
that reality which is free from conceptual construction is designated as the Supreme (*param*).
The third form of the Lord is nothing other than [the totality] everywhere;
Śiva is described by some as having the nature of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower.
The Supreme Lord is the ordainer and the sustainer of all worlds;
the wise call the twenty-three principles by the term "manifest" (vyakta).
They speak of primordial nature (prakṛti) by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta), and likewise they describe the person (puruṣa), who experiences through the qualities, by the word "knower" (jña).
In that [state], this triad is the form of Śaṅkara; there is nothing else whatsoever that is not Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O one of great intelligence, I desire to hear once again the truth in its true nature.
They have been designated by the lords of sages through many words in manifold ways.
Śailādi said: O sage, I shall describe to you again and again the forms of Śiva,
which have been designated by the lords of sages through many words in manifold ways.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), primordial nature (prakṛti), the manifest (vyakta), and the self as time (kālātman)— thus they are called by certain lords of sages, teachers who have reached the further shore of the ocean of scripture.
The wise call the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) the Puruṣa, and they call Pradhāna the Prakṛti;
likewise, they call the entire collection of transformations arising from Prakṛti the Manifest (vyakta).
Time is the sole cause of transformation for both Pradhāna and Vyakta;
indeed, that quartet is the fourfold form of the Lord.
Some teachers describe the Supreme Lord Śiva as Hiraṇyagarbha, the Puruṣa, the Pradhāna, and the one whose form is manifest.
Hiraṇyagarbha is the creator and the enjoyer of this universe, the Puruṣa;
the collection of transformations known as the manifest is Pradhāna, the supreme cause.
The fourfold nature of those [powers] is declared to be the fourfold form of Śiva, which is the intellect (buddhi); other than Śaṅkara, there exists no entity whatsoever.
However, some describe the Lord as having the nature of the "lump" (piṇḍa);
indeed, all bodies, both moving and unmoving, are designated as "lumps. (LiP 2.16.9)
All generalities, as well as the Great Generality itself,
are designated by the term "jāti" (genus) as the forms belonging to the Wise One.
Virāṭ, whose essence is Hiraṇyagarbha, is declared by some to be the Lord;
Hiraṇyagarbha is the cause of the worlds, and Virāṭ is the soul of the worlds.
Some proclaim that form to be the unmanifest Śiva;
for that form of the Supreme Lord is indeed the unmanifest Pradhāna.
That by which the worlds abide, like clusters of jewels upon a thread—
know that to be the Thread (sūtra), whose form possesses wondrous prowess.
By some he is proclaimed as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), by others as the Supreme Lord (Para-Īśa);
he is the self-luminous, self-known Śiva, Śambhu, and Maheśvara.
Śiva is remembered as the inner controller (antaryāmī) of all beings;
because he is superior to all beings, he is called the Supreme (para).
The Supreme Self is Śiva, Śambhu, Śaṅkara, and Parameśvara;
they know his three forms to be named Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva.
That very [reality] consists of the three states—deep sleep, dreaming, and waking;
it is designated as Virāj, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the state called the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta).
Of this Śiva, who is the Fourth and who traverses the three states,
[the forms] Hiraṇyagarbha, Puruṣa, and Kāla are thus proclaimed.
The three states of the Lord, known as Bhava, Viṣṇu, and Viriñca, are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world.
Having propitiated [Him] with devotion, embodied beings attain liberation;
for the wise declare that there is the agent, the action, the object, and the instrument.
Four forms of Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, are proclaimed:
the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and likewise the resulting cognition.
These four forms belong to Śiva alone, without a doubt;
they consist of Īśvara, the Unmanifest (avyākṛta), Prāṇa, and Virāṭ, which are the nature of the elements and the senses.
This world is a modification of Śiva alone, just as waves are of the ocean;
they call the Lord the efficient cause and likewise the material cause of the worlds.
For that Pradhāna is declared by the proponents of the Vedas to be indeterminate;
it is remembered as Hiraṇyagarbha, known as Prāṇa, and as Virāṭ, whose nature consists of the worlds.
The great elements, the beings, the effects, and the sense organs—
these, O best of sages, are declared to be the forms of Śiva.
The wise know that there is no Supreme Self other than Śiva;
the twenty-five principles have been produced from Śiva by the sages.
These have been described as not distinct from that [reality], like a multitude of waves from the water;
they know the Śiva-tattva to be superior to the twenty-five categories.
Therefore, those principles— Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and the rest— are non-different from the Śiva-principle, just as bracelets and other ornaments are non-different from gold.
Those born are not other than that; the substance of clay is like the breaking of a jar. Māyā is the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) and the power of action (kriyā-śakti), which consists of action.
Born from Śiva, there is no doubt, like rays from the sun;
[they arise] from the divine Śiva, who is the self of all and the ordainer of the refuge of all.
Devote yourself with your whole being if you desire to attain the highest good.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O best among the hosts of gods, listen further to the supreme majesty of Śiva.
As I listen to the drinking of the nectar of your words, there is no satiety for me.
How is the Blessed One embodied? Why is Rudra so majestic? How is Śambhu the soul of all, and what is the Pāśupata vow?
"How was Śaṅkara heard of and seen by the chief gods?
Śailādi said: "From the Unmanifest arose Sthāṇu, Śiva, the supreme cause."
That seer, endowed with all causal powers, the omniscient lord,
[beheld] the first god among the gods being born from his lotus-like mouth.
And he saw Brahmā before him and gazed at him by his command;
having been seen by Rudra, that Lord of Gods emitted the entire universe.
The Virāj indeed established the system of the social classes and stages of life;
he created Soma for the sake of sacrifice, and from Soma this world was born.
Caru, Vahni, Yajña, Vajrapāṇi, Śacīpati,
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and the glorious Śrī— all this world consists of Soma.
With the Rudrādhyāya, the gods praised Rudra, the Lord;
the Master stood in the midst of the gods with a serene countenance.
And having withdrawn their consciousness, Maheśvara—the gods indeed questioned that god Śaṅkara—asked, "Who are you? LiP 2.17.9.
The Blessed Lord Rudra said: "I alone am the ancient one;
O best of gods, I was the very first, and I exist [now]."
And I shall exist in this world; there is nothing whatsoever other than me from any source, O best of gods. There is nothing distinct from me, nor is there anything else at all.
I am eternal and non-eternal, O sinless one; I am Brahmā, I am the Lord of Brahman;
I am the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, and I am both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
I am the Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Anuṣṭubh meters; I am Śiva, who consists of them.
I am Truth, all-pervading, and peaceful; I am the three sacred fires, weightiness, and the Guru.
I am the bull, I am the cave, and I am eternally dwelling in the depths;
I am the eldest of all principles, I am the most excellent, and I am the lord of the waters.
I am Āpa, O Blessed One; I am Īśa; I am Tejas; I am also the Vedi;
I am the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda, O Self-born One.
I am the Atharvaveda, I am the mantra, and likewise the best of the Aṅgirasas;
I am the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, I am the ritual manual (kalpa), and I am even the creative imagination (kalpanā).
I am the imperishable and the perishable; I am patience, peace, and forbearance.
I am the secret in all the Vedas, I am the most excellent, and I am the unborn.
I am the lotus, the purifier, and that which is beyond the center; likewise, I am the exterior and the interior, and I am the imperishable one who exists before all.
I am light and I am darkness; I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
I am the intellect, the ego, the subtle elements, and the senses.
O best of gods, he who knows me as all this— indeed,
he alone is the knower of all, the All, the Self of all, and the Supreme Lord.
O best of gods, [I swear] by the cows with the cows, by all the Brahmins with devotion to the Veda, by the sacrificial oblations,
by life with life, and likewise by truth with truth.
"I satisfy all things with dharma through dharma by means of my own splendor";
having spoken thus at the beginning, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Then those gods did not see the god Rudra, the supreme cause;
they meditated upon Rudra, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self.
The gods, together with Nārāyaṇa and Indra, as well as the sages,
likewise raised their arms upward and praised Rudra-Saṃkara.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The gods said:
"He who is the Lord Rudra is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara."
And likewise Skanda, as well as Caidya, the fourteen worlds,
the two Aśvins, the planets, the lunar mansions, the stars, the sky, and the directions.
Likewise, the elements, the sun, the moon, and the eight planets;
as well as Prāṇa, Kāla, Yama, Mṛtyu, Amṛta, and the Supreme Lord.
To Maheśvara, who is the past, the present, and the future, the entire universe,

In the beginning you were likewise such, as were Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;
at the end you are the universal form, for you are the head of the world.

you are peace, as well as nourishment, contentment, the unoffered oblation, and the offered oblation.

the God who is both created and uncreated; the supreme and the inferior, the eternal;
the ultimate refuge of both the virtuous and the wicked—Śaṅkara.
We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal; we have reached the light, we have found the gods.
What can hostility now do to us? And what, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do?
This is the divine, imperishable, subtle, and immutable benefit for the world.
The Prājāpatya, the Pavitra, the Saumya, the Agrāhya, and the Avyaya;
or the Agrāhya may be taken up by means of the Agrāhya, and the Vāyavya by means of the Samīraṇa.
He swallows the gentle with his own gentle power, effortlessly by means of his own splendor;
homage to him, the withdrawer, the great devourer who wields the trident.
All deities reside in the heart; they are established in the vital breath within the heart.
You are eternally present in the heart, but he who transcends the three measures (mātrās) is beyond that.
The head is indeed in the north and the feet likewise in the south;
that which is truly in the north is the eternal Oṃkāra itself.
That which is the syllable *oṃ* is indeed the *praṇava* that stands here pervading all;
it is infinite, the savior, subtle, white, and like lightning.
He is the Supreme Brahman, he is Īśāna, and he alone is Ekarudra;
you are Bhava, Maheśvara, and Mahādeva in person—of this there is no doubt.
Because it causes [the breath] to rise upward, it is proclaimed as Oṃkāra;
because it protects the vital breaths (prāṇa), it is therefore celebrated as Praṇava.
Because he pervades everything, he is the eternal one who pervades all;
even Brahmā, Hari, and the Blessed Lord have not found his beginning or end.
Likewise, others say that from him [comes] the infinite Rudra, the supreme cause;
he who delivers one from saṃsāra is designated as "Tāra."
Becoming subtle, he indeed presides over all bodies at all times;
therefore, O Blessed One, the Lord Nīlalohita is called "Subtle" (sūkṣma).
It is both blue and red due to its connection with the primary matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa);
for from this [connection] his semen is emitted, and likewise the semen departs.
Because he illuminates, he is therefore celebrated as Vaidyuta;
and because of his vastness and his power to nourish, he is called Bṛhat, encompassing both the higher and the lower.
Therefore, because it expands (bṛṃhati), it is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman;
moreover, the Lord is the non-dual Fourth (turīya), the Supreme Sovereign.
The wise Indra-sages always [worship] the Lord of all, the Ruler of this world, the Eye of those who behold the heavens. LiP 2.18.22.
He who is called Īśāna is the lord of all sciences;
and whatever the Blessed One beholds as that which is to be observed, he does so by his own command.
Mahādeva himself imparts the knowledge of the Self and Yoga;
the Lord is called the God, the God of gods, Maheśvara.
This Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, who seizes all the worlds in due order,
emits them and causes them to dwell [within himself] as well, by his mere sport.
For this God pervades all directions; he was born first, and he is within the womb.
He alone is born, he is yet to be born; facing every direction, he stands with faces on all sides.
This imperishable reality must be diligently worshipped by the virtuous,
for it is that from which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it.
The very non-grasping of that [object] which speech here speaks with effort—
whether it be the lower or the higher— is itself the supreme goal (parāyaṇa).
They speak these words: "Śaṅkara is omniscient, blue-and-red;
he is all this. Homage to him! He is the tawny Puruṣa, Śiva. (LiP 2.18.29)
He is this very Mahārudra, the universe, that which has been and that which will be— the world born in many ways, produced here and there.
The Lord with golden arms, the Master of gold, the Sovereign,
the Lord of Ambikā, the Ruler, whose seed is gold, and who has the bull as his banner.
Umāpati, Virūpākṣa, Viśvasṛj, and Viśvavāhana—
he who appointed the eternal Brahmā as his son in the beginning.
He abandoned that very knowledge which illuminates the self—
that one Puruṣa, Rudra, who is invoked by many and praised by many.
In the center of the heart, [resides] Viśvadeva, the size of a grain of rice, in the form of fire, most excellent;
those wise ones who perceive him as abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others.
He who is greater than the great and subtler than the subtle, the imperishable Self,
the Great Lord, is hidden within the cave of this living being.
He himself is the abode of this entire universe, seated within the lotus;
he resides in that deep and impenetrable abyss, and stands at its very summit.
Therein also, within that small space, is the syllable Om, the Supreme Lord;
in its center is the Truth, the ultimate cause, the size of the tip of a hair.
Truth is Brahman, Mahādeva, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose delight is in the upward path, the sovereign Lord, the three-eyed one, unborn and self-born.
He who presides over the womb, the one Lord of speech,
by whom the fivefold body is sustained— that ancient Īśāna.
They say that within the vital breaths (prāṇas) is the mark of the mind, in which reside anger, thirst, and forbearance.
Having cut through thirst—the root of the web of causes—and having established the inconceivable in Rudra by means of the intellect, [one attains liberation].
They call him the one, indeed, the eternal Rudra, the Supreme Lord;
he who is even higher than the highest, the constant one who is higher than the highest.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva as the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Vāyu,
one should purify the limbs with fire, cleansing each part individually.
Having restrained the five elements according to the sequence of qualities and the rules for the measures (mātrā),
there follow the five measures, the four measures, and thereafter the three measures and so forth.
Indeed, that which consists of a single measure and is without measure is established at the end of the twelve;
having remained there, having become established, and having become immortal, one should practice the Pāśupata vow.
"I shall practice this Pāśupata vow in brief:
having established the sacred fire according to the rules, with [mantras] derived from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas."
Having fasted, being pure, bathed, and personally wearing white garments,
he should likewise wear a white sacred thread and be adorned with white garlands and unguents.
The wise one, free from passion, should offer oblations; he shall become free from passion.
"May the five winds, speech, mind, conduct, and the rest, be purified. (LiP 2.18.47)
Then the ear, the tongue, and thereafter the breath; likewise the intellect, as well as the head, the hands, the sides, and immediately after that the back and the belly.
The calves, the thighs, the generative organ, the anus, and likewise the penis;
as well as the skin, flesh, blood, fat, and bones.
May sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell,
as well as the elements and the bodily humors such as phlegm and the rest, be purified.

"May food, vital breath, mind, and knowledge be purified by the will of Śiva," [reciting this] while offering oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel sticks, and cooked rice (caru) in due order.
Having extinguished the Rudra-fire and carefully collected the ashes,
the wise practitioner should rub his limbs while reciting "Agniriti" and the subsequent mantras.
This divine Pāśupata vow, which liberates one from bonds,
has been proclaimed as beneficial for Brāhmaṇas and likewise for Kṣatriyas.
It is likewise appropriate for worthy Vaiśyas, especially for ascetics (yatīs),
for those in the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprastha), and even for virtuous householders.
Liberation for those practicing celibacy is indeed seen through this procedure:
having taken the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice with the mantra beginning with "Agni," etc. (LiP 2.18.55).
That Pāśupata Brahmin, having wiped his limbs, should touch them while covered in ashes;
thus the learned twice-born is freed from the consequences of great sins.
One is instantly liberated from evil and is released without a doubt;
for the ash is the potency of fire, and thus one who possesses the ash becomes possessed of power.
A Brahmin who delights in bathing with ashes, who sleeps upon ashes, and has conquered his senses,
being liberated from all sins, shall attain union with Śiva.
Therefore, with every effort, a wise person should worship the limb of prosperity;
one should not utter the sound "re-re" nor likewise the sound "tuṃ-tuṃ."
"O fair-faced one, neither the Lord of Gods, nor Brahmā, nor even Keśava can endure this, that my son Gaṇeśa should be a wearer of ashes."
He who avoids that which is contrary to those [rules], even if he be a householder devoid of Vedic knowledge, goes to the ocean of hell if he does not apply the *tripuṇḍra*.
For such a person, acts of worship, ritual performance, giving, and likewise bathing—
all become fruitless, just like an oblation poured into ashes.
"Therefore, in all rites, a wise man should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Having spoken thus, the Lord Brahmā, the sovereign, praised [him] together with the gods.
O lord of the people, covered by ashes himself, he ceased [speaking];
then the Lord, the Master of Creatures, for the sake of winning their favor, [acted].
The Lord made his appearance together with Ambā;
then they praised Rudra, the preeminent among the gods, who was thus present.
Having looked upon the gods with compassion, even the god whose banner is the bull— the Lord of all, the God of gods, and the husband of Umā— [spoke] by means of the Rudrādhyāya.
"I am pleased," said the slayer of the enemies of the gods, in order to grant a boon to the deities.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa. Śailādi said:
Having prostrated before that Lord, the bull-bannered one, whose mind was filled with joy—
The sages and gods, their skin bristling with joy, questioned him.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, by what path is the Lord to be worshipped by the twice-born?
In what place, or in what form? O Śaṅkara, you should tell us."
"O Lord, who has the authority for worship? How is it for a Brāhmaṇa, O Master?
And how, O God, Bull-bannered One, is it for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas?"
You ought to tell us everything for the benefit of the entire world— how it may be for women, Śūdras, or even for those such as the Kuṇḍas and Golakas.
Sūta said:
Having observed the disposition of those sages, Sadāśiva, Nīlalohita,
seated within the circle, spoke with a profound voice.
And in the mandala, he beheld before him the God of gods together with Umā,
as well as all the gods and sages, possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
The god has eight arms, four faces, twelve eyes, and mighty limbs;
he is the Lord who is half-woman, wearing a crown of matted hair.
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing red garlands and unguents,
clad in red garments, he is the agent of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
His eastern face is yellow and serene, having the nature of Puruṣa;
his southern face is Aghora, resembling a mass of black collyrium.
In the north is [the face] extremely fierce, with fangs that are formidable, surrounded by garlands of flames,
possessing red whiskers and matted locks, and having the luster of coral.
His western face, known as Vāmadeva, is gracious, bestows boons, possesses a universal form, and is auspiciously white like cow’s milk.

One should meditate upon the divine face of the Sun, the enemy of Smara, which is adorned with necklaces made of pearls, radiant with a forehead mark (tilaka), and possesses a freshly manifested countenance.
Beholding Āditya before him as before, with four faces;
and the god Bhāskara before him, likewise with four faces as previously described.
He saw the god Bhānu to the south and the four-faced one as before; he saw Ravi to the north, likewise with four faces as before.
Vistārā is situated at the eastern part of the mandala of Prajāpati, Uttarā in the south,
and Bodhanī in the western portion of the mandala.
And in the north is Adhyāyanī; all these Śaktis, possessing one face and four arms, are adorned with every ornament and are esteemed by all.
One should place Brahmā on the right side and Viṣṇu, the subduer of men, on the left;
thus, through the path of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, one worships Śiva as consisting of these three forms.
The Lord Īśāna, the boon-granting god, the sovereign Supreme Lord, seated upon the Brahma-throne, bestowing boons atop the seat of dharma and knowledge.
In that which is endowed with dispassion and sovereignty, abundant and likewise stainless,
one should worship the Lord who is the essence, the Sovereign of All, the supreme bliss.
Situated in the center of a white lotus and surrounded by Dīptā and the others—
Dīptā herself being subtle, auspicious, possessing the brilliance of lightning, and having the form of a blazing flame.
One should meditate on Jayā, who has the form of a flame of fire; on Prabhā, who has the luster of gold; on Vibhūti, who resembles coral; and on Vimalā, who is like a lotus.
