One should meditate upon the Goddess who is unfailing, shaped like a pericarp, possessing the colors of lightning and all hues,
four-faced, four-colored, and indeed facing in every direction.
Soma, the god Aṅgāraka, Budha— the best among the intelligent—
Bṛhaspati of vast intellect, and Bhārgava, the treasury of splendors.
Śiva, the Lord of the World, always moves slowly and with gentle gait all around him; Soma is there in person, and Umā herself is present.
Having beheld the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, all the sages saw that the five elements, the remainder, and all that is moving and unmoving are composed of him.
With palms joined in reverence, all the sages and likewise the deities addressed the boon-granting Nīlalohita with their cherished words: "May it be so!"
The sages said: Homage to Śiva, to Rudra, to Kadrudra, to the wise one, to the most bountiful, to the All-pervading, to Śipiviṣṭa, and to the Swift One.
Upon the abundant, stainless, essential, supreme, and blissful foundation,
one should meditate on the Lord, the Sun, who resides within a lotus, enveloped by the nine powers.
Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, the god Divākara;
likewise Umā, Prabhā, Prajñā, Sandhyā, and Sāvitrī.
I bow to the goddess Vistārā, the northern one, and to Bodanī;
to Āpyāyanī, Varadā, Brahmā, Keśava, and Hara.
Having worshipped the assembly beginning with Soma in due order according to the prescribed sequence of mantras,
I remember the god Śaṅkara, the primordial deity Sadāśiva, who resides within the solar orb.

I likewise meditate upon Indra and the other gods, as well as the Īśvaras, Nārāyaṇa, and the primordial god born from the lotus; and in due order, from the east to the beginning and down to the nadir, I meditate upon the vajra and the others, ending with the lotus.
To you who are the color of vermilion, who possess a mandala, who are adorned with golden vajras,
whose eyes have the luster of lotuses, who hold a lotus, and who are the cause of Brahmā, Indra, and Nārāyaṇa.

I remember the chariot with its seven horses and the hero Anūru, as well as the sevenfold host in their proper order; I remember the Vālakhilyas through the flow of the seasons, and the destruction of the Mandeha hosts.
Having offered various oblations such as sesame seeds into the fire, and having likewise completed everything,
I meditate upon your form, O God of gods, which resides within the lotus of my heart after you have been dismissed.

I remember her images in their proper sequence: those with lotus-pure eyes, red in hue, holding a lotus in the right hand and the gesture of granting boons (varada) in the left, likewise adorned with ornaments.
I remember your divine face, formidable with tusks, radiant as lightning, and the destroyer of the Daityas; it is intent on protecting the twice-born and terrifying the hosts of Mandeha Rākṣasas.
One should visualize Soma as white, Bhūmija (Mars) as having the luster of fire, Budha (Mercury), the son of the Moon,
as golden-hued, Bṛhaspati as resembling gold, Śukra (Venus) as white, and Mandaga (Saturn) as very black.

I remember Mahādeva Bhāskara, whose right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness and whose left hand rests upon his thigh, bestowing boons, and who extends to the very edge of the Mandara mountain.
Having prepared a sturdy copper vessel filled with auspicious water and a handful of flowers the color of the full moon, I shall offer you the arghya; O Blessed One, be gracious!
Salutations to the auspicious god, to the Lord with matted hair;
to you, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, who are the embodiment of the Sun.
Sūta said:
He who, having thus worshipped the divine Lord Śiva in the maṇḍala with a concentrated mind, recites this unsurpassed hymn in the morning, at midday, and in the evening; LiP_2,19.42 //
In this way, one attains union with Śiva; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Thereafter, Rudra Mahādeva, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), remained within the maṇḍala.
He is indeed worthy of worship by the Brāhmaṇas and especially by the Kṣatriyas.
There is no entitlement for Vaiśyas or Śūdras, nor for one who performs service, nor for women to perform worship and other such rites; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, through worship [of this], women and Śūdras shall obtain that same fruit;
and for the benefit of kings, it is especially so for Brāhmaṇas and others.
"In this manner, the Brahmins and others should indeed always worship Sadāśiva.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra himself vanished on the spot.
All those gods and sages, those great-souled ones, being overwhelmed by meditation upon Rudra, bowed down to Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara.
The gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity departed as they had come;
therefore, one should always worship the Sun, who is the very form of Śiva.
"For the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation, [we pray] through mind, deed, and speech.
The sages said:
"O Romaharṣaṇa, O omniscient one, best among all upholders of the scriptures!"
O illustrious disciple of Vyāsa, son of Vahni, speak now of that which was [taught] by Śiva,
the God of gods, out of a desire for the welfare of his devotees.

Having extracted [the essence] from the Veda with its six limbs and from Sāṃkhya and Yoga in their entirety, and having performed extensive austerities difficult for even gods and dānavas to practice; LiP_2,20.9.

It is endowed with meaning, place, and so forth; it is profound, free from ignorance, and unblemished; in some respects it is contrary to the duties (dharma) performed by those of the various castes and stages of life, yet in others it is identical to them.

The scripture spoken by Śiva, consisting of one hundred crores of verses, is for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation; therein, O Lord, how is the worship of the All-pervading One performed?
"Indeed, we have a great curiosity to hear about the methods for ritual bathing and other such practices.
Sūta said:
"In ancient times, on the beautiful summit of Mount Meru, Sanatkumāra [expounded this]."
The god Nandīśvara, the son of Śilāda who is esteemed by Śiva, was questioned;
having been thus questioned from all sides by the foremost of sages, he prostrated himself and spoke.
O best of sages, listen to that knowledge of Śiva which was told by Nandin, the delighter of his lineage, to Sanatkumāra.
The Śaiva [system], which is a summary of what is declared in the Vedas and expounded by Śiva,
is free from praise and blame and produces immediate conviction.
Sanatkumāra said: "O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Nandīśvara, Maheśvara! [This is] divine, born of the grace of the Guru, and bestowing liberation without effort."
O Son of the Mountain, you should explain to me, who have approached with humility, how worship and other rites lead to the attainment of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation for Śambhu.
Sūta said:
Having observed [the situation] and having heard those words once more, the blessed Nandin,
the best among speakers, spoke again to Kālavelādhikāra.
Śailādi said:
"Based on both the teacher and the scripture, I declare this qualification;
it is out of respect alone that he is designated as a Śivācārya, and not otherwise."
He who practices [right conduct] himself and also establishes others in that conduct,
and who gathers the meanings of the scriptures, is therefore called an Ācārya.
Therefore, a devoted disciple should seek out a Guru who knows the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas, who lies upon ashes, who is fortunate, and who is pleasing to behold.
He brings joy to people, follows the path of the Śruti and Smṛti,
bestows fearlessness through knowledge, and is free from greed and fickleness.
Having seen that wise teacher who guards right conduct and is firmly established in the observances, one should worship him with one's whole being as if he were Śiva himself.
With his own person and with wealth, according to the extent of his faith and possessions,
the disciple should propitiate him in such a way that he becomes pleased.
When the illustrious one is perfectly propitiated, the destruction of bonds occurs immediately;
the Guru is to be honored, the Guru is to be worshipped, for the Guru alone is Sadāśiva.
Or else, he should examine his brahmin disciples for three years by means of entrusting them with his life-force and possessions, and by sending them on various errands.
One who is superior should be employed among the inferior, and one who is lowly among superior things;
for those who do not fall into despondency even when dragged about or beaten.
They are worthy, firmly established in the dharma of Śiva, devoted to the dharma of Śiva, self-controlled, endowed with righteousness, and followers of the path of the Śruti and Smṛti.
Enduring all dualities, steadfast, with minds always alert and diligent,
they are devoted to helping others and intent upon serving their gurus.
They are upright, gentle, self-composed, agreeable, and pleasant-spoken;
they are free from pride, wise, devoid of rivalry, and free from longing.
Endowed with the virtues of purity and right conduct, free from hypocrisy and envy,
all such twice-born ones are indeed worthy, being solely devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Those endowed with such conduct through the actions of speech, mind, and body,
and being purified in this manner, are indeed fit for the purification of the principles (tattvas).
A disciple who is pure, endowed with discipline, free from falsehood and harshness, and who obeys the commands of the guru, is worthy of favor.

The Guru is traditionally described as one who knows the scriptures, is wise, ascetic, and affectionate toward people; he is devoted to worldly conduct and, being a knower of reality, is the bestower of liberation.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, proficient in all scriptures,
and knowing the application of all means, [he is nevertheless] fruitless for one who is devoid of reality.
For one who has no certainty regarding the supreme reality that is self-cognizable within oneself, there is no benefit for oneself;
how then can there be benefit for another?
But that twice-born man who is awakened is pure and accomplishes [his goal] as well.
For how can there be awakening in one devoid of reality? And how indeed can there be the grasping of a self?
All those who are free from possessiveness are declared to be non-animals (paśu); however, all those who are impelled by animals are remembered as being animals themselves.
Therefore, those who know reality are liberated and they liberate others as well; reality is that which generates consciousness and gives rise to supreme bliss.
But he by whom reality is known is alone the one who reveals bliss;
not, however, he who is devoid of true realization and possesses only the name.
One cannot possibly rescue another; how could one stone ever rescue another stone?
For those whose liberation occurs by the mere mention of a name, that liberation is indeed merely nominal.
Furthermore, through the sight, touch, or even speech of yogins,
the Command (ājñā) that brings about the destruction of the fetters is immediately produced.
Alternatively, having entered the body of the disciple by means of the path of yoga,
one should awaken him through yoga after purifying all the principles (tattvas).
The purification of the six and a half [limbs] has been prescribed for yogins through the yoga of knowledge,
after having examined a disciple who knows the Dharma, is righteous, and has mastered the Vedas.

Having perceived through knowledge the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya who is free from many faults, and having realized the object of knowledge— [this knowledge] having come from ear to ear— one [should initiate them].
Just as one lamp may be lit from another, so too does the teacher proceed through the stages of the ritual (vidhipada);
likewise, there is the stage of the worlds (bhauvana), the stage called the phonemes (varṇa), and the supreme stage of the measures (mātra).
O highly fortunate one, there is also the great sacrifice of time (kālādhvara), which is known as the principles (tattva) and is accepted by all.
By whose mere command, through his power, everything is split asunder on all sides.
His accomplishment and liberation arise from the compassion of the Guru;
furthermore, the elements such as earth enter into him within the earthly realm.
Sound, touch, as well as form, taste, and smell— these,
O Brahmin, are the objects known as words and letters, which constitute the conceptualization of the sense organs of cognition.
The organs of action are indeed merely the measure; beyond that are the mind and the intellect, then the ego, and the unmanifest—this is remembered as the sacrificial path of time.
From Puruṣa up to Viriñci, the state beyond the mind (unmanatva) is said to be higher than the highest;
likewise, it is called the state of Īśvara, which awakens one to the meaning of all the principles (tattvas).
One who is not a yogin does not know the purity of reality, which is of the nature of Śiva.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having examined the ground according to the rules by means of its smell, color, taste, and other qualities, [he should proceed].
Having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments, [one should prepare] a place capable of receiving the invocation of the Lord.
One should fashion a mandala measuring one cubit;
in its center, one should draw a lotus adorned with five jewels.
With powders, one should draw a circular eight-petalled lotus, either white or red,
provided with a surrounding border and endowed with great beauty.
Having invoked Śiva, the supreme cause, into the pericarp,
one should worship him with all effort, according to the extent of one's available wealth.
O great sage, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are said to be on the petals,
while in the pericarp (karṇikā) is the delightful stalk of dispassion and knowledge, with the root of Dharma.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Vikaraṇī,
Balavikaraṇī, and Balapramathinī follow in sequence.
The powers that subdue all beings reside in the filaments,
while Manonmanī and Mahāmāyā reside upon the seat of Śiva in the pericarp.
One should install [the deities] together with Vāmadeva and the others according to the rule of pairs; then, one should place Mahādeva Manonmana in the center with Manonmanī.
Due to its connection with the sun, moon, and fire, one should place upon the eastern petal the Person named Praṇava, whose nature is Śiva and who possesses the radiance of the sun.
Aghora is in the southern vessel, resembling a mass of blue collyrium;
Vāmadeva is in the northern [vessel], similar in appearance to a hibiscus flower.
One should place Sadyojāta on the western petal, white as cow’s milk;
and Īśāna in the pericarp, resembling pure crystal.
With the mantra "to the heart," one [places] that which resembles the lunar disc;
in the south-eastern direction, the region of Rudra, [one places] "to the head" of smoky luster.
One should place "And salutation to Śikhā" on the petal in the southwest (Nairṛta), which has a reddish luster;
and "To Kavaca, who has the luster of collyrium," one should assign to the petal in the northwest (Vāyu).

One should assign [the mantra] "to the weapon, which has the luster of flames of fire" to the cardinal directions; and with "to the eyes," one should assign it to the northeast, [saying] "to the tawny ones."
One should meditate upon the auspicious Śiva, the ever-auspicious God Maheśvara, who is beyond this,
as well as Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Viriñca, according to the principle of emanation.
Salutation to Śiva, who has the form of Rudra; to Śambhu, who transcends peace;
to the peaceful one, the bestower of peace upon the Daityas, and likewise to the Moon.
To the one to be known, to the bearer of knowledge, to the fire, to the one with the luster of fire;
to Time, to the foundation, to the savior, and to the end-maker.
With these mantras— nivṛttyai, dhanadevāya, dhārāyai, and dhāraṇāya— one should worship Sadāśiva, whose body consists of the great elements.
The God whose crown is Īśāna, whose face is Puruṣa, the Ancient One;
whose heart is Aghora, the joyful Maheśvara whose secret part is Vāma.
One should meditate upon the god Sadyomūrti, the cause of the manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent,
who has five faces, ten arms, and consists of the thirty-eight kalās.
Having divided the Lord, who consists of the *kalās*, into eight types including *sadyojāta*, and having divided the pervasive Vāmadeva into thirteen kinds; ||| LiP_2,21.21 |||
Having divided Aghora into eight parts, he abides in the form of the *kalās*;
and having likewise divided Puruṣa, who consists of the *kalās*, into four parts.
Having divided Īśāna into five parts, established in the form of the five mūrtis,
and endowed with devotion to Śiva by means of the mantra "haṃsa haṃsa," [one should worship].
The syllable Oṃ alone, the letter A, which is of uniform form, as well as Ā,
Ī, Ū, E, and likewise Aṃ, are in their sequence the very forms of the Self.
The God who is accompanied by Pradhāna, who is devoid of dissolution and origination, who is subtler than the subtle, unborn, and greater than the great; LiP_2,21.25.
To the one whose vital energy flows upward, the Sovereign Lord, the three-eyed one, the husband of Umā,
the thousand-headed god, the thousand-eyed, eternal one.
The Lord has a thousand hands and feet, is neither ending nor consisting of sound;
his form is like a firefly, and his appearance is shaped like the crescent moon.
The god Śiva, who is one's own bliss and nectar, is situated in sequence at the end of the twelve, between the eyebrows, in the middle of the palate, in the throat, and in the region of the heart.
Resembling a circle of lightning, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
it is dark blue and red in form, having the three powers (śakti) as its seat.
One should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva, who is endowed with the three principles (tattvas),
and one should worship the god, whose form consists of Vidyā, according to the proper sequence.
Likewise, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) individually, starting from the east, with their respective weapons;
and having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the rules, one should offer it to Śiva.
Having given half to Śiva, one should perform the oblation with the remaining half using the Aghora mantra; then, one should cause the disciple to eat the excellent [remnant].
Having touched water and become pure, one should worship Puruṣa according to the prescribed rite;
then, having consumed the five products of the cow consecrated with the Īśāna mantra.
With the Vāmadeva mantra, one whose limbs are smeared with ashes should dust oneself with ashes in due order;
and at the two ears, one should mutter the goddess Gāyatrī, whose presiding deity is Rudra.
Together with its thread and its cover, it was wrapped in a pair of garments;
that golden vessel had previously been perfumed with a multitude of gold and jewels.
Then, one should place five water-pots with five Brahmins;
and one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial porridge (caru), according to the extent of one's means.
And he should cause the devoted disciple to dwell on the right side of the mandala,
reclining upon a bed of darbha grass and intent upon meditation on Śiva.
Having again offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Aghora mantra according to the rule, one should purify the impurity of bad dreams at dawn.
And thus, having fasted, the disciple— having bathed, his body adorned,
wearing a new upper garment and a turban, and having performed the auspicious rites— [should be initiated].
Having bound the eyes with a cloth such as dukūla, one should cause [the disciple] to enter,
accompanied by golden flowers and according to the extent of one's available wealth.
One should offer a handful of flowers to the Lord with the Īśāna mantra,
or alternatively, having performed three circumambulations while reciting the Rudrādhyāya.
Then, solely by means of the syllable *praṇava*, being intent on the meditation upon Śiva,
one should meditate upon the Lord of the gods of gods and personally dissolve [the universe] into Īśāna.
Whichever mantra the flower falls upon, that mantra is mastered by him;
having touched [the disciple] with the water of Śiva and with the ashes of Avoraka.
Having placed [the hand] upon the head of the disciple, one should worship the disciple with perfumes and other offerings;
for the western door is the most excellent and supreme for all castes.
The western gate is specifically prescribed for Kṣatriyas;
having removed the veil from their eyes, one should then show them the maṇḍala.
Having established Kuśāsena and taken his stand before Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
he should then perform the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) according to the fivefold method of the principles.
O son born from the essence of the womb, by means of *nivṛtti* [kalā] one reaches as far as Rudra;
and by means of *pratiṣṭhā*, one goes beyond that up to the sphere of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
O observer of noble vows, knowledge indeed extends only as far as Viśveśvara by a mere fraction;
having purified the path beyond that through devotion to Śiva, one should lead [the soul] to Śiva.
For the sake of worshipping that reality, which is indeed the Lord of Enjoyment (Bhogeśvara),
[one should perform it] by means of the threefold division of reality, or likewise with four.
One should perform the oblation with the limb-mantras for Sadāśiva, who transcends the Śānti level;
and with the four [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Vāmadeva, one should offer separately for each Kalā up to the Śānti level.
O best of sages, one should perform the directional fire-oblation (diśā-homa) one hundred and eight times for each direction, either with the Śāntyatīta mantra or with the Īśāna mantra.
In the northeast, the fifth lord is proclaimed as the principal deity;
one should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
The seven substances are to be offered with the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end;
O Brahmin, the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for these is prescribed by means of the mantra of Īśāna.
O observer of noble vows, atonement is prescribed with the *sahasra* [mantra], according to rule, preceded by the *praṇava*,
and with the *aghora* mantra.
One should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in sequence, beginning with Jaya and ending with Sviṣṭakṛt,
joining it with the primary [mantra] according to the manner of the qualities and their number.

Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna) by means of mantras dedicated to the elements, or even by means of seeds and so forth, or else by means of the primary principle alone, the silent sage [should proceed].
With the sixth [syllable], one should dissolve the Kula and Akula, ending with the Praṇava of the Self,
having mutually withdrawn Brahmā, Keśava, and Hara.
One should meditate upon Rudra within Rudra, the Lord Īśāna, the auspicious god Maheśvara;
therefore, by means of this method of emanation, one should contemplate the destroyer of worldly existence.
Having established this living soul (jīva), one should perform its striking, the showing of the door,
the kindling, the grasping, and the binding, together with worship.
And one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) according to the prescribed rule:
[the mantra] ending in the sixth [case], joined with Sadyojāta, and endowed with the third [person].
The withdrawal is said to end with *phaṭ* and proceed according to the five elements;
it is accompanied by the six mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, ending with the crest (*śikhā*), and concluding with *phaṭ*.
Striking is said to be the gateway even for yogins to the principles;
having encapsulated the primary principle with the third, there is illumination.
Enveloping [the mantra] with the first [syllable], it is taught that the principal [mantra] is grasped;
having enveloped the principal [mantra] with the very first [syllable] as before.
Bondage is fulfilled by [the element] plāvana and by amṛta;
beyond that is śānti, and then the stainless kalā called vidyā.
Establishment, cessation, and the transition of the *kalās* are recorded;
these are joined with the principles (*tattvas*), phonemes (*varṇas*), and *kalās*, along with the worlds (*bhuvanas*), in their proper order.
Having purified [the area] according to the rule, one should perform the hymn of praise with the mantras as the feet,
having first fashioned [the seat] with the seed-syllable of the womb (yonibīja) as before.
Know that worship, sprinkling, striking, and likewise seizing; the conjunction of what has been gathered, as well as dispersal, in due order;
and similarly, worship, the holding of the embryo, and then birth again.
The sun shall have authority, and dissolution especially so.
O observer of noble vows, O great sage, the first syllable [of the mantra] combined with the final one— the seed-syllable of the womb— is used for lifting up, sprinkling, and striking.
With the Aghora mantra ending in *phaṭ*, there is the emanation [of the universe], of this there is no doubt;
for this is the sequence for each principle (*tattva*) by way of the path of yoga, O observer of good vows.
One should lead [the breath] gradually by means of the fist for as long as it takes;
then, by means of the equinox yoga (viṣuva-yoga), one proceeds from the stage of cessation (nivṛtti) up to Śiva.
In one place it attains equality, but not otherwise as something separate;
for yogins, [it is] at the tip of the nose with the *dvādaśānta* and the back.
"O best of brahmins, 'It must be forgiven'— this is the command of the God of gods,
[to be fulfilled] with gold, silver, copper, and so forth, prepared according to the prescribed rite."
O observer of noble vows, [the vessel] should be filled with water from a sacred ford, containing gems within, and wrapped with a thread together with a water-pot and a cloth.
Then, with water consecrated by the *saṃhitā* and the hymns of the *Rudrādhyāya*,
he should sprinkle the disciple, who is a devotee of Śiva and righteous.

That disciple, too, should respectfully undergo initiation in the presence of Śiva, in the presence of the preceptor, and before the fire; and having been initiated, he should conduct himself accordingly.
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head than to eat without having first worshipped the Blessed One, Sadāśiva.
In this manner, the initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed, as well as the worship according to the proper sequence;
one should worship the Supreme Lord either three times a day or once a day.
The Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, the Vedas, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees—
none of these are equal to even a sixteenth part of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
One who worships Śiva even once is always performing sacrifice with ritual offerings, always bestowing gifts, and always subsisting on air alone.
Those who worship Mahādeva once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or constantly at all times—they are Rudras; of this there is no doubt.
One who is not Rudra should not touch Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra;
one who is not Rudra should not chant the name of Rudra; and one who is not Rudra shall not attain Rudra.
Thus, in brief, has been declared the sequence of rules for those qualified [to perform worship],
which serves the purpose of worshipping Śiva and bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Śailādi said: Having indeed performed the rites of bathing, sacrifice, and so forth for the Sun-god...
Then one should perform the ritual bath for Śiva, the ash-bath, and the worship of Śiva.
Having taken earth with the sixth [mantra], he should cast the earth upon the ground with devotion;
likewise, having sprinkled it with the second, he should purify it with the third.
One should divide the impurity with the fourth [part] and purify with one;
having bathed with the sixth, one should again take the remaining clay held in the hand.
Having divided everything into three parts, one should again divide the middle portion into four;
with the sixth [mantra] and the root [mantra], one should touch the left side seven times.
Furthermore, touching ten times with the sixth [mantra] is proclaimed as the binding of the directions.
Having applied the sacred clay to the bathing site with the left hand and to the body with the right,
one should bathe while remembering the Sun and perform the ritual ablution with all [the waters].
With a horn, with leaf-cups made of *parṇa*, or with a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree,
and with various other auspicious substances dedicated to the Sun that grant all accomplishments.
O observer of excellent vows, I shall also proclaim the Sārauṇi and the Bāṣkala and other such [texts],
which among all the gods are the limbs that are the essence in every respect.
Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam, oṃ ṛtam, oṃ brahmā.
This nine-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the Bāṣkala.
It is called the imperishable *ṛta* because it does not perish within the worlds.
It has been stated that the true syllable is imperishable, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ. Oṃ, obeisance to Sūrya, obeisance to Khakholka. LiP 2.22.9.
This nine-syllable root mantra of the great-souled Bhāskara, with its radiant face, has been proclaimed as the root mantra for Bhāskara.
I shall now describe the mantras for the worship of Indra in their proper sequence:
the first is with the Vedas and so forth, and the middle one is with the *praṇava*.
Oṃ bhūḥ, to the heart of Brahmā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, to the head of Viṣṇu; Oṃ svaḥ, to the crest of Rudra; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, to the flame-garlanded crest; Oṃ mahaḥ, to Maheśvara as the armor;
Oṃ janaḥ, to Śiva as the eyes;
Oṃ tapaḥ, to the burner as the weapon, phaṭ. Thus have the various solar mantras been declared.
With these vessels, such as those made of horn and so forth, one should cause oneself to be sprinkled.
A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or indeed a Vaiśya, being composed, [should perform the rite] with a copper jar containing water,
along with kuśa grass and flowers, while reciting all the mantras.

Clad in red garments, the best of the twice-born should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rules, reciting "The Sun is the light by day" and "Fire is the light by night."
The waters shall purify [the practitioner] at midday; this is called the sipping of water with mantras (mantrācamana).
Having performed purification with the sixth [mantra], one should then recite the foremost and unsurpassed [mantra].
Likewise, one should place the unsurpassed nine-syllable root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* upon the fingers,
the thumb, and the middle and ring fingers.
And one should place the index finger and thumb as parts of the fists;
having thus formed a body consisting of nine syllables, it is further purified by the limbs.
Having contemplated, "I am the Sun," with these mantras in their proper order,
[he should perform the rite] with water held in the left hand, mixed with perfumes and white mustard seeds.
Having sprinkled [the water] with a bunch of *kuśa* grass, its roots and tips arranged eightfold,
and having recited the hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should indeed smell the remainder of the water.
One should contemplate Śiva within the body through the left nostril alone;
and having taken the *arghya* water, one should [offer it] to that which resides in the body through the right nostril.
One should visualize [the deity] as being of black color, situated externally upon the stone;
one should then offer libations to all the gods, and especially to the sages.
One should cause the arghya offering to be given according to the rule to the beings and to the ancestors;
and one should properly perform the worship of the all-pervading, supreme moonlight of the twilight.
One should present the *arghya* offering in the morning, at midday, and in the evening;
and one should prepare a mandala measuring one cubit with water mixed with red sandalwood.
O best of the twice-born, one should prepare a well-rounded surface on the ground and,
facing eastward, request [the recipient] for a copper vessel filled with a *prastha* measure and scented with fragrances.
One should fill [the vessel] with scented water and red sandalwood,
along with red flowers, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains of rice.

Having filled [the vessel] with dūrvā grass, apāmārga, and cow-products, or with pure ghee alone, and having honored the God of gods while kneeling upon the earth, using the root mantra consisting of nine syllables; // LiP_2,22.26 //
Having placed that vessel upon his head, he should offer the *arghya* with the root mantra;
the fruit of which is proclaimed to be equal to performing ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having offered the universally esteemed water-offering (arghya) to the Sun, one obtains that fruit;
having indeed offered the arghya, one should worship with devotion the God of gods, the Three-eyed One (Tryambaka).
Alternatively, having worshipped the Sun, one should perform the Āgneya bath;
the Śiva-bath is performed as before, distinguished only by the mantra.
Having first performed the cleaning of the teeth, one should bathe and worship the Sun, Śiva,
Vighneśa, Varuṇa, the Guru, and the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having assumed the lotus posture at the sacred site, one should likewise worship the sacred site;
having gathered the sacred water according to the rule, one should enter the place of worship.
Having stepped upon the sandals with the path [of the mantra] and the *arghya*-purifier,
one should perform the placement of the hands and the placement on the body as before;
then, having taken up the sacred water (*tīrtha*) according to the rule, one should enter the place of worship.
The ritual offering of the *arghya* has thus been briefly described;
having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the yogi should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having gathered red flowers such as lotuses and the like, one should consecrate them;
placing them to one's right and a water vessel to one's left.
For the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, one should take up copper vessels dedicated to the Sun,
and having received the vessel for the *arghya* offering, wash it according to the prescribed rule.
Together with the previously mentioned water, likewise in the water-vessel,
one should prepare the arghya offering along with the weapon-water and the arghya ingredients.
Having joined the mantra with the *saṃhitā* and worshipped it with the first [syllable],
and having veiled it with the fourth, one should place it around oneself.
One should place the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), together with fragrance and flowers,
in a vessel purified with water, setting them apart as before; then,
having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the *Saṃhitā* mantras and having veiled [the offerings] with the *Kavaca* mantra.
Having sprinkled the materials, especially the water for the *arghya* offering, with that water,
one should recite the mantra to the god Āditya, who is saluted by all the gods.
Having paid homage with the words, "The Sun indeed bestows splendor, vigor, strength, fame, and vitality," and so forth, one should prepare a seat for the Lord.

One should place the heart-mantra in the center, ending with the intermediate directions, within the corners starting from the southeast— abundant, stainless, essential, worshipful, and supremely blissful.
One should likewise assign the limbs, as well as the seed and the sprout;
[the stalk] should be provided with a hollow interior and joined with thread and thorns.
The petals and the tips of the petals are very white, golden-hued, and red;
it is endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and surrounded by the Śaktis beginning with Dīptā.
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā,
Aghorā, and Vikṛtā— these are the eight powers (śaktis) beginning with Dīptā, in their respective order.
All of them have faces radiant like the sun, are auspicious with palms joined in reverence,
or else they hold lotuses in their hands, adorned with every ornament.
One should install the goddess Varadā, who faces in all directions, in the center;
then one should invoke the goddess Bhāskara, the Supreme Lord.
By means of this nine-syllable mantra spoken by Bāṣkala, the invocation and the presence of the Sun-god are prescribed.
And the mudrā of the great-souled Bhāskara is called the Padmamudrā;
one should then offer arghya at the base, followed by pādya and ācamana separately.
Furthermore, by offering the *arghya* according to the prescribed rule with the *bāṣkala* mantra,
one should offer red lotuses, flowers, and red sandalwood.
Lamps, incense, food offerings, mouth-perfumes, and the like,
as well as betel, wicks, lamps, and so forth, are prescribed by Bāṣkala.
In the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest,
as well as in the east and the west, the sixfold arrangement is prescribed.
Having worshipped the corners of the eyes according to the prescribed rule with the syllable Om at the beginning and "Namaḥ" at the end,
and having assigned them to the pericarp, one should perform the meditation on the form (rūpakadhyāna).
All those with the brilliance of lightning were pacified; this is proclaimed as the Raudra weapon, which has a face made terrifying by fangs, possesses eight forms, and is fearsome.
Their right hands grant boons and their left hands are adorned with lotuses;
they are endowed with all ornaments and are decorated with red garlands and unguents.
All his forms are arrayed wearing red garments;
the Great God, together with his mandala, has a body as crimson as vermilion.
The Lord has a lotus in his hand and nectar in his mouth; he possesses two hands and two eyes, is adorned with red ornaments, and is decked with red garlands and unguents.
One should meditate upon Bhāskara, the Lord of the World, wearing such a form;
and here, outside the lotus, there are auspicious mandalas on all sides.
[Soma], Maṅgala, Budha—the best among the intelligent—Bṛhaspati of great intellect, and Bhārgava, the son of Rudra; || 2.22.58 ||
Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu are proclaimed to be smoky in appearance;
all of them have two eyes and two arms, and Rāhu holds his body upright.
With his mouth wide open, having joined his palms in *añjali*, his eyes crooked with a frown,
Śanaiścara has fangs for a face and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands.
They should be worshipped with diligent effort, using their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha.
One should worship the seven groups of seven outside the deity:
the sages, the gods, the gandharvas, the serpents, and the hosts of apsarases.
O leaders, the Yātudhānas, and likewise the Yakṣas as the foremost,
should first worship the seven horses of the Lord, which consist of the seven Vedic meters.
One should also honor the host of Vālakhilyas and the taking up of the Lord's remains;
one should worship the seat of the Sun and likewise worship the deity.
Then, having bowed down, one should cause the *arghya* offering to be given to them individually according to the rule—
at the invocation, at the end of the worship, and likewise at their dismissal.
One should first recite the Bāṣkala hymn one thousand times, or half of that, or one hundred and eight times; and then one should perform the ritual application with a tenth part of that number.
And one should construct a pit in the west, circular and with a rim,
measuring four finger-breadths in both height and width.
In both daily and occasional rites,
having fashioned the pit in the shape of an *aśvattha* leaf with a measurement of one cubit, the navel should be ten finger-breadths deep.
Half of that measure is prescribed for the front part, which is shaped like the lip of an elephant;
the neck is one *aṅgula* wide, and the remainder is twice as broad.
Having abandoned [the area] by that same measurement, one should carefully construct the girdle (mekhalā) for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
only after having thus prepared it with effort should one subsequently perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
With the sixth [mantra], one should perform the marking (ullekhana) and sprinkle [the site] again with water;
then, being composed, one should arrange the seat in the center using the first [mantra].
Then one should install the power (śakti) Prabhāvatī with the very first [syllable],
having worshipped her in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the Bāṣkala [tradition].
One should perform the ritual separately for each [deity] with the Bāṣkala mantra according to the prescribed rule;
afterwards, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered with the root mantra.
In this manner, by following the sequence of the ritual procedure, the fire of the sun shall be generated;
one should then place the previously mentioned lotus according to the previously stated ritual method.
Having worshipped the Lord Bhāskara above the mouth as before,
O great sage, ten oblations should be offered with the *bāṣkala* mantra.
Likewise, each of the ancillary rites (aṅga) should be performed separately according to the Saṃhitās,
beginning with the Jaya-homas and ending with the Sviṣṭakṛt, as well as the throwing of the fuel-sticks (idhma).
Having offered all the worship, oblations, and so forth, as well as the water for honor (arghya) and circumambulation;
having worshipped with the [five] limbs, having performed the abbreviated rite, having dismissed [the deity] into the heart, and having paid obeisance— LiP 2.22.78.
Then one should perform the worship of Śiva for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha.
Thus has the sacrifice to Bhāskara been briefly described;
he is endowed with all sovereign powers and is incomparable in splendor.
Whoever worships even once the God, the God of gods, the Teacher of the world,
the Sun, the Supreme Self, attains the supreme goal.
He is completely liberated from all sins, entirely devoid of all evil,
endowed with every form of sovereignty, and peerless in his splendor.
Surrounded on all sides by sons, grandsons, friends, and kinsmen,
he shall indeed enjoy abundant pleasures in this very world, possessing wealth and grain.
Endowed with vehicles and carriages, as well as various ornaments,
even after death he rejoices for eternal time with the Sun.
Returning again from there to this world, he becomes a righteous king;
or else, he is born here as a Brāhmaṇa, perfected in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Furthermore, through the connection with former impressions, one who is righteous and has mastered the Vedas may,
by worshipping the Sun alone, attain union with the Sun.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Śailādi said: Now I shall fully describe to you the unsurpassed worship of Śiva.
One should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire-ritual according to one's ability.
Having first performed the ritual bath for Śiva and the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) as before,
he should then enter the place of worship with flowers in hand and a concentrated mind.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) and the acts of burning and bathing, with hands perfumed by scents and other substances, one should properly apply the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
Having diligently formed a body from consciousness for the fire of Brahman,
[he forms] a body produced from the unmanifest, intellect, ego, and the subtle elements.
Purified by the nectar of Śiva and according to the true nature of Śiva,
it remains one span below the anus and above the navel.
One should know that heart to be the great abode of the universe;
for within the pericarp of the heart-lotus resides the Lord Sadāśiva himself.
He has five faces and ten arms, adorned with all ornaments;
each face has three eyes, and he bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), one should first meditate upon the upward-facing face, which resembles pure crystal, and then the eastern face, which resembles saffron.
The southern face of the Supreme Lord is blue in luster, the northern is deep red,
and the divine western face is as white as cow's milk.
In his right hands he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and a spear;
in his left hands he holds a noose, a goad, a bell, a serpent, and an excellent iron arrow.
Or else, he may have his hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; the rest is exactly as before—Śiva is adorned with all ornaments and wears variegated garments.
One should worship with one's whole being the Lord who has the limbs of Brahmā as his body, the most excellent among all gods, the Master of Brahmā by means of the limbs of Brahmā.
The five Brahmans have been described; now hear from me, O observer of good vows, the limbs of Śiva, as well as the heart and the others, which constitute his powers (śakti).
Oṃ, to Īśāna, the lord of all sciences, to the heart, the seed-syllable of power, obeisance. Oṃ, to Īśvara, the lord of all beings, to the nectar, to the head, obeisance. (LiP 2.23.14)
Oṃ, homage to the crown-lock (śikhā) of Kālāgni, the sovereign lord of Brahmā.
Oṃ, homage to the armor (kavaca) of Kālacaṇḍamāruta, the sovereign lord of Brahmā. LiP 2.23.15.
Oṃ, homage to Brahmā, the nourisher, the embodiment of knowledge, the eye;
Oṃ, homage to Śiva, the ever-auspicious, the wielder of the Pāśupata weapon, the unimpeded—phaṭ phaṭ!
Oṃ, salutations to Sadyojāta, who exists in being, non-being, and beyond being; to the source of existence, whose form is Śiva, I bow.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, the most auspicious one, who is the swan-crested, whose body is knowledge, whose nature is the Self, and who is both transcendent and immanent. LiP 2.23.17.
The limbs of Śiva and his Mūrti-vidyā have indeed been described;
likewise, in the teaching of Śiva, the Brahmāṅga is taught together with the Mūrti and the Vidyāṅgas.
O observer of noble vows, I shall also proclaim the Saura texts, beginning with the Bāṣkala,
which are the limbs of all the Vedas and constitute their very essence, O observer of noble vows.
Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam, oṃ ṛtam. This nine-syllabled mantra of Brahmā is proclaimed as the Bāṣkala.
Because it does not perish in this world, it is therefore called "akṣara" (the imperishable).
It is said that the "akṣara" is the Truth (Satya), beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with "namaḥ."
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects.
Homage to Sūrya, the sky-weaponed one; homage! LiP 2.23.21.
This is declared to be the root mantra of the great-souled Bhāskara;
with this nine-syllabled root mantra beginning with "Dīpta," one should worship Bhāskara.
One should worship the limb-mantras; I shall describe them in brief:
the first is with the Vedas and so forth, while the middle one is with the *praṇava*.
Oṃ bhūḥ, salutation to Brahmā, the heart. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the head.
Oṃ svaḥ, salutation to Rudra, the tuft of hair. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, salutation to the deity Jvālāmālinī. Oṃ mahaḥ, salutation to Maheśvara, the armor.
Oṃ Añjanaḥ, for the welfare of the eyes; Namaḥ! Oṃ Tapas-tāpanāya, for the weapon (astra); Namaḥ!
Thus, in this context, the mantras dedicated to the Sun have indeed been declared here.
And the Śaiva [mantras], O observer of good vows, should be applied in brief by means of the yoga of placement (nyāsa).
In this manner, one should worship the deity consisting of mantra within the lotus of the heart;
then, having generated [the fire], the oblation (homa) should be performed in the navel according to the prescribed sequence.
In one's mind, one should [perform] all rites for the divine Lord Īśvara in the fire of Śiva— Śiva,
who is Sadāśiva, the embodiment of Śiva, arising from the five Brahmās as his limbs.

O observer of good vows, having carefully performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa [the infusion of the deity's limbs] for [the image] seated upon a red lotus throne, one should do so with the root mantra, the mūrti-mantra, and the Brahma-aṅga mantras.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter,
one should mentally recollect the full stream that has arisen from the lunar orb, from the station of the moon.
According to the procedure for the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the teaching of Śiva,
the knower should meditate upon Śiva as having entered the mouth, consisting solely of the radiant energy of Śaṅkara.
One should again meditate upon the Lord of the gods of gods on the forehead or between the eyebrows,
having completed the entire detailed ritual procedure within the heart-lotus.
One should meditate on the destroyer of worldly existence, who has the form of a pure lamp-flame;
one should always worship the god Sadāśiva either in a linga or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa. Śailādi said:
I shall now briefly proclaim the explanation of the procedure for the offering of worship.
This was told of old by Śiva, according to the path taught in the Śiva-śāstra.

Then, having made an añjali with both hands smeared with sandalwood paste while reciting the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having recited the *mūrti-vidyā*, *Śiva*, and so forth, one should assign [the mantras] from the thumb to the little finger for Īśāna and the others; from the little finger to the middle finger for the Heart and the others up to the third; the fourth with the thumb;
the fifth with the ring finger; the sixth with the two palms joined in the manner of the *nārāca* weapon; and again the root mantra.
Having recited [the mantra] and veiled [the disciple] with the fourth [vessel], it is called the "Hand of Śiva."
With that hand, one should perform the worship of Śiva.
Having established the self as having attained reality, one should perform the purification of reality as before.

Having established [the elements] ending with earth, water, fire, air, and space—namely, the five, four, and the end of the ten million pure [units]—along with their respective streams, one should first perform the purification of those [elements].
The purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi) is performed with the sixth mantra, *sadyojāta*; the purification of the earth (dharāśuddhi) is performed with the third mantra, ending with *phaṭ*.
The purification of the principle of water (*vāritattva*) is performed with the third *sadyojāta* mantra, accompanied by the sixth [seed-syllable] and ending with *phaṭ*.
The purification of fire is performed with the third verse addressed to Agni, beginning with "phaṭ."
The purification of the wind is performed with the fourth mantra of the Vāyavya group, joined with the sixth and ending in *phaṭ*.
The purification of space is performed with the sixth mantra, which consists of six syllables, the third mantra ending in *phaṭ*.

Having thus withdrawn [the elements], one should perform the striking (*tāḍana*) with the third root mantra ending in *phaṭ* and the sixth [mantra]; the seizing (*grahaṇa*) is by enclosing [the object] with the third [mantra]; the binding (*bandhana*) is by enclosing it with the root mantra itself and the womb-seed (*yonibīja*). Having performed this, as before, from the cessation of the past, future, and present states, one should meditate upon the three principles (*tattva*) with the *praṇava*. One should contemplate oneself, in the form of a lamp-flame, accompanied by the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), as transcending the triad, [and through] the agitation of power (*śakti-kṣobha*), [pour down] a stream of nectar into the *suṣumṇā*.
Having meditated.

Having performed the Brahma-nyāsa—which consists of the sequence from Śāntyatītā down to Nivṛtti; from the internal *nāda*, *bindu*, *a*, *u*, and *m*; from Śiva, Sadāśiva, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā; and the nectarification (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of the emanations—and having assigned the fifteen eyes upon the five faces, one should bind the Mahāmudrā with the root mantra from the feet to the tips of the hair, meditate "I am Śiva," and [assign] Śakti and the others.

Having placed [the seed-syllable] in the heart, and immediately after the sprout of the Śakti-bīja, one should meditate upon the channels, the thread, the thorns, the petals, and the filaments as the attributes of dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya; and upon the sun, moon, and fire; and upon Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī on the filaments; and also Manonmanī in the pericarp.

Having thus prepared the seat along with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and having made the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) ready through external yogic practice, one should prepare the seat as before within the fire-pit (*vahnikuṇḍa*) at the navel and meditate upon Sadāśiva. Then, having visualized a stream of nectar falling from the *bindu* into the *śivamaṇḍala*, and having meditated upon Maheśvara in the form of a lamp-flame at the forehead, the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*) is thus accomplished; [so too are] the *prāṇa* and *apāna*.

Having restrained the breath and established it within the *suṣumṇā*, having performed the *tālumudrā* with the sixth [syllable], and having performed the *digbandha* (binding of the directions) with the sixth, one should perform the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*). Having consecrated the garments and other items, as well as the *arghya* vessel and so forth, with the *praṇava*, and having projected the three principles (*tattvatraya*) therein, one should meditate upon the *bindu* above them. Having filled [the vessels] and prepared the ritual substances, and having performed the immersion in nectar (*amṛtaplāvana*), [one does so] in the *pādya* vessel and others.
Having prepared a seat for them as if for the *arghya* offering, having consecrated it with the *saṃhitā*, worshipped with the first [mantra], rendered it nectar (*amṛta*) with the second,
purified it with the third, veiled it with the fourth, gazed upon it with the fifth, and performed protection with the sixth,
he should sprinkle himself and the ritual substances again with *arghya* water using a bundle of *kuśa* grass and the fourth [mantra], and [finally] with flowers.
One should purify all the ritual substances individually.
With the *sadyojāta* mantra one offers perfume, with the *vāmadeva* mantra clothing, with the *aghora* mantra ornaments, and with the *puruṣa* mantra the food offering;
with the *īśāna* mantra one offers flowers; then one should consecrate them with mantras.
One should sprinkle the remainder with the Śivagāyatrī mantra.
One should consecrate the five nectars, the five products of the cow, and so forth, with the Brahmāṅga mantras, the Mūla mantra, and others.

Having offered water for honor (arghya), incense, and water for sipping (ācamanīya) to each [deity] individually with their respective root mantras, and having also shown them the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā), veiled them with the armor-mantra (kavaca), and performed protection with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should perform the purification of the ritual substances.

First, taking the water for the *arghya* offering with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and purifying it with the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the rites beginning with worship and ending with protection; having thus performed the purification of the materials, maintaining silence until the conclusion of the presentation of the offerings, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should recite all the mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*,
and then cast away the handful of flowers— this is the purification of the mantras.

First, having filled the general *arghya* vessel with milk, consecrated it with the *saṃhitā* [mantras] using perfumes, flowers, and so forth, displayed the *dhenamudrā*, veiled it with the *kavaca* [mantra], and protected it with the *astra* [mantra];

then, having worshipped the stale offering with the *gāyatrī*, offered the general *arghya*, and presented perfumes, flowers, incense, and water for sipping— either ending with *svadhā* or *namaḥ*— one should offer individual handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the *brahma* mantras, and [finally] with the *astra* mantra ending in *phaṭ*.

Having removed the withered flowers and worshipped Caṇḍa in the northeast, as well as the seat and the image of Caṇḍa, one should purify the pedestal of the liṅga and Śiva with the general weapon-mantra (sāmānyāstra) and the Pāśupata weapon-mantra respectively; then, placing a flower upon the head [of the liṅga], one should worship it—this is the purification of the liṅga.

One should prepare the seat by arranging the seed-sprout upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), and upon that, the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā). Within the hollow of the stalk of Ananta, one should conceptually arrange the thread, petals, thorns, pericarp, filaments, and the powers of dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, aiśvarya, as well as the sun, moon, fire, and the filament-power (śakti) of Manonmanī within the pericarp.

Having thus briefly prepared the seat with the mantra "to the infinite seat of Manonmanī," one should meditate upon Sadāśiva above it—consisting of the kalās such as Nivṛtti and the rest, accompanied by the sixfold [limbs], and possessing a body composed of the limbs of the kalā of action (karma-kalā).

With both hands holding flowers, pressing the flower with the thumb and using the *āpāhana* mudrā, one should slowly raise it from the heart up to the head; then, having uttered the root mantra along with the *hṛdaya* [mantra] as a *pluta* vowel, one should invoke and establish [the deity], who is more extensive than the station of the *bindu*, shaped like a lamp-flame, with hands facing all directions, and who is both the pervaded and the pervader, by means of the *sadyojāta* [mantra].

The instruction is as follows: one should perform the act of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*) and the act of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the *pūrvahṛd* mantra through the union of Śiva and Śakti; the invocation (*āvāhana*) by means of the *sadyojāta* mantra together with the root-mantra (*mūla*) starting from the heart; the confinement (*sannirodha*) upon the root-mantra by means of the *aghora* mantra together with the heart-mantra; the presence (*sānnidhya*) upon the root-mantra by means of the *puruṣa* mantra together with the heart-mantra; and one should worship by means of the *īśāna* mantra together with the root-mantra and the heart-mantra.
Just as the creation of one's own body was previously performed together with the five mantras, so too is the instruction for the deity and likewise for the fire.

Having performed the visualization of the form (*rūpakadhyāna*) and having concluded with the root mantra ending in *namas*, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) ending in *svadhā* or entirely ending in *namas*;

the water for honor (*arghya*) ending in *svāhā*; a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; and everything else ending in *namas*. One should worship [the deity] either with the Heart-mantra, or with the Īśāna-mantra, or with the Rudra-gāyatrī, or with the root mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*. // LiP_2.24.25 //

Having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), [he offers] incense and water for sipping (ācamanīya) again; with the sixth [mantra], he performs the scattering of flowers and the dismissal (visarjana); having bathed [the deity] with the root mantra and consecrated water (mantrodaka), he performs the sprinkling with all substances (sarvadravyābhiṣeka) using the Īśāna mantra; offering eight flowers for each substance, as well as the arghya, scent, flowers, incense, and water for sipping, he performs the removal of the worship with the Astra mantra ending in "phaṭ" and bathes [the deity] with pure water using the root mantra.
With ground amalaka and other such substances.

Having purified the form of the *liṅga* together with its pedestal using warm water mixed with turmeric and other substances, one should bathe it while reciting the *Rudrādhyāya*, using perfumed water, golden water, and water consecrated with mantras, accompanied by the *Nīlarudra*, *Tvaritarudra*, *Pañcabrahma*, and other hymns, ending with the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
Having thus placed a flower upon the head [of the deity], one should not leave the top of the *liṅga* empty; regarding this, there is a verse: LiP_2,24.28 //
In whose kingdom the top of the *liṅga* bears the mark of emptiness,
for that [kingdom] there shall be misfortune, great disease, famine, and the destruction of vehicles.
Therefore, for the sake of dharma, pleasure, and liberation, a king should avoid [such places];
for if a king himself visits a deserted linga, both he and his kingdom will perish.

Having thus bathed [the deity] and offered the *arghya*, and having wiped [the image] with a cloth, one should offer perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, and so forth, while reciting the root mantra.
It is stated that the worship of incense, water for sipping, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, using the primary root mantra, constitutes the purification of the upper [deities]. // LiP_2,24.32 //

One should display the lamps for the removal of obstacles (*ārārti*) and so forth, which are marked with the *dhenu-mudrā*, enveloped by the *kavaca-mantra*, and protected by the sixth [mantra]. These should be shown at the *liṅga*, below the *liṅga*, and in the common area.

Having made a request with the root mantra and a prostration, one should worship according to the path of the enjoyment of the limbs of Brahmā, accompanied by the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*stāpana*), confinement (*sannirodha*), presence (*āniddhya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers, incense, food offerings (*naivedya*), further water for sipping, the waving of lights (*hastasvadhauta*), and mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*). || 23.34 ||
The meditation on the manifest form is the recollection of the unmanifest; the meditation on the higher and lower is the muttering of the root mantra.

The offering of the muttering of the Brahma-aṅgas constitutes one-tenth [of the total]; as well as self-surrender, praise, prostration, and so forth, and the worship of the Guru. Furthermore, to the east and to the south [is the worship] of Vināyaka.
At the beginning and at the end, Vighneśa, the Lord of the World,
should be worshipped by the gods and by the twice-born for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all rites.
Whoever worships Lord Śiva in this manner, whether in a liṅga or even upon a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila),
attains union with Śiva through that practice within a single year.
And for one who worships the *liṅga*, [the merit lasts] for six months; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Having performed seven circumambulations, the wise man should prostrate himself like a staff.
By circumambulating with a step-by-step gait, one obtains a hundred times the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
therefore, one should always worship [it] for the sake of accomplishing all rites and goals.
One who desires enjoyments obtains enjoyment; one who desires a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom;
one who desires a son obtains an excellent son; and the sick person is liberated from disease.
Whatever desires a person contemplates, those he attains.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa. Śailādi said:
I shall describe the fire-ritual (agnikārya) of Śiva as expounded by Śiva himself.
Having first established [the image] facing east in an auspicious place that has been well-consecrated, // LiP_2,25.1 //
One should carefully lay down three auspicious lines— one oriented eastward and one northward—
upon the field that has been made square, and therein diligently construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
The fire-pit for the daily oblation (nityahoma) shall be provided with three tiers (mekhalā);
these tiers are one cubit in length and measure four, three, and two finger-breadths [in height] respectively.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit (hastamātra) in size, and the womb (yoni) should be one span (prādeśamātra).
One should fashion the womb upon the girdle (mekhalā) so that it resembles a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
O son of Brahmā, one should fashion the navel in the center of the pit according to the prescribed rule, consisting of an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp, measuring one span.
The sixth [rite] is declared to be scraping (ullekhana), and sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is remembered as being performed with the Armour-mantra (varman).
Having gazed at the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Eye-mantra (netra), the wise one should draw six lines.
O best of Brahmins, one should again sprinkle with the *varman* mantra lines extending eastward for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, and lines pointing north for Śiva.
Having churned the fire-drill made from *śamī* and *pippala* wood, sixteen finger-breadths in length,
with the seed-syllable of fire, one should perform the placement of power (*śaktinyāsa*) at the heart with that very same syllable.
Having established the fire according to the prescribed rite, one should cast [the oblation] into it according to the rules,
silently, with auspicious wooden splinters (śakala) from a sacrificial tree, each measuring a span (prādeśa).
One should perform the sprinkling with water in the eight directions,
having strewn [the sacrificial grass] according to the rule, starting from the east and proceeding in due order.
In the east, the tips should indeed face north; in the south, they should face east;
in the west, the tips should face north; and in the north, they should likewise face east.

Having invoked the fire of Indra and the fire of Aindrāgna in the eastern [quarter], it is ordained that the same be done for the southern; above the northern [fire] is the fire of Cāndrāgna, and below it is the fire of Vāruṇāgni.
O observer of noble vows, having placed the vessels in pairs upon the sacrificial grass with their openings facing downward, one should likewise place all the ritual substances to the north.
One should place darbha grass upon that [seat] and place Śiva to the south;
one should worship with the root mantra and thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, he should fill it again with water;
then he should place two *kuśa* blades, each a span in length, upon the water.
One should sprinkle the tips of the *kuśa* grass with the rays of the sun, the Vasu;
having scattered all the vessels and thoroughly sprinkled them according to the rule.
O observer of excellent vows, having taken the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, one should fill it again with water,
properly covering it with other water and *kuśa* grass.
With both hands, one should place the nose-shaped vessel in the northeastern direction;
one should perform the placing of the clarified butter (ājya) auspiciously to the northwest.
One should indeed cause him to take charcoal mixed with ashes while reciting the sakala-mantra;
having led him to the north-west, one should heat clarified butter there.
Having ignited kusa grass in the fire, one should perform the circumambulation three times;
having thrown all of those [blades] there, one should place clarified butter (ājya) in front.
Having washed two *kuśa* blades the size of a thumb according to the prescribed rule,
one should then perform the *paryagni* rite with those same nine [blades] once again.
One should perform the circumambulation with fire once again and then set down that clarified butter;
then one should gradually withdraw the vessel toward the north-west.
Having joined the fire with wood, washed it, and placed it in the western direction,
one should perform the purification of the clarified butter (ājya) using the two strainers together.
Taking them separately with both hands in sequence by means of the stream,
one should [hold] both the thumbs and the ring fingers with the root mantra.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with water, one should cause it to be offered into the fire that is purified by ghee;
O observer of excellent vows, one should fashion a golden *sruk* and *sruva* ladle measuring one *ratni* in length.

Or, according to the rule, both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of silver and endowed with all the required characteristics; or else, they should be fashioned from trees suitable for sacrificial purposes.
O Great Sage, the opening at the base of that handle should be one cubit in length, and its circumference at the root of the staff should be six finger-breadths.
Half of that should be the length of the neck-tube; the opening should be like its base.
The handle should resemble a cow's tail, and the tip of the *sruc* ladle should be level with the nose.
It consists of two joined compartments, filled with pearls and other precious substances,
measuring thirty-six finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width.
The height, however, should be half of that, measured by means of a cord;
furthermore, the mouth should be seven finger-breadths in both width and length.
One-third of that shall be the tip; having made this, one should discard the remainder.
The neck should be two finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.
The altar should be eight finger-breadths in length and width;
in its center, one should make a cavity measuring four finger-breadths.
One should fashion a well-rounded cavity with eight petals and a beautiful pericarp;
around the exterior of the cavity, however, there should be a band measuring half a finger-breadth.
That [portion] in the Brahma-region should be free from indentations and variegated with lotus petals;
the border in that Brahma-region should be two barley-corns in measure.

From the center of the altar, a hole should be dug measuring one *kaniṣṭhā* finger-breadth in width, extending down to the edge of the opening; the depth of the pit should be such that it slopes downward.
The staff should be six finger-breadths long, with a tube at the tip of the staff; three small rods should be made four finger-breadths long, increasing by half a finger-breadth each.
At the base of the staff, there should be a jar (ghaṭa) with a length of thirteen finger-breadths;
the pot (kumbha) should be two finger-breadths wide, and one should know the navel (nābhi) to be ten finger-breadths.
Having done so in the middle of the altar, one should fashion the foot to be two finger-breadths [in height],
with a shape like the back of a lotus, and the foot indeed having the form of a pericarp.
Its back should have a shape resembling an elephant's lip;
for rites such as malevolent magic (abhicāra), one should fashion it from black iron.
O observer of good vows, one should again cleanse the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with a blade of twenty-five-fold grass; having purified the tip with the tip and the middle with the middle.

Having heated the root-mantra with the root-mantra according to the ritual procedure over the fire while reciting the heart-mantra, one should likewise prepare the three vessels: the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the praṇītā vessel, and the prokṣaṇī vessel.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay; otherwise it must not be made at all for rites of pacification, nourishment, or auspicious purposes.
For malevolent rites it should be made of iron, but for pacificatory rites it may be made of clay;
the mouth of the vessels is said to be six finger-breadths wide.
The *prokṣaṇī* vessel is two finger-breadths in height; the *praṇītā* vessel is two finger-breadths higher than that;
the *ājyasthālī* is then [the same], with its height being two finger-breadths greater than the latter.
Those very fuel-sticks with which the oblation is said to be offered shall also serve as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*);
they should have a circumference equal to the middle finger, be straight, free from blemishes, and uniform.
The three enclosing sticks (paridhis) are prescribed to be thirty-two finger-breadths in length;
one should strew [the grass] with thirty blades of darbha, each thirty-two finger-breadths long.
In rites such as those for malevolent magic (abhicāra), the string should be knotted at intervals of four finger-breadths, wound clockwise, and it must be devoid of the installation of the Śiva-fire.
O Brahmin, those that are not soft, but firm, should be taken for rites of sorcery;
they should be complete, well-proportioned, thick, and equal in size to the little finger.
O observer of noble vows, sacrificial fuel-sticks that are straight, unblemished, smooth, and measured at twelve finger-breadths constitute the standard measurement for all ritual acts.
Cow’s ghee is superior to that [other ghee], while that of a Kapila cow is even more excellent;
one should offer oblations until the sruva ladle becomes full.
The measure of grain should be one *akṣa*; for sesame seeds it should be the size of a *śukti*, for barley half of that, and for fruits according to their own natural size.
The quantity of milk, honey, and curd should be like that of the clarified butter;
the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should consist of a ladleful measured by a four-sruva spoon.
Half of that is prescribed for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, or else all the remainder;
one should always offer this into the Śiva-fire for rites of pacification and nourishment.
O illustrious one, rites such as deluding and expelling are performed in the worldly fire;
however, O observer of noble vows, once the Śiva-fire has been generated, all rites may be accomplished.
Having visualized the seven tongues [of fire], one should perform all rites;
or else, all rites are accomplished by means of the tongue alone.
O best of Brahmins, by means of the tongue alone, the practitioner [attains] the fire of Śiva.

Oṃ, to the one of many forms, to the one with the central tongue, to the one of manifold colors, to the one who dwells in the south, north, and center, to the one who bestows the fruits of peace, prosperity, liberation, and so forth—svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Hiraṇyā, who has the luster of refined gold, whose tongue is the Lord (Īśāna), and who bestows knowledge! LiP 2.25.58.
Oṃ, to Kanakā, to her who resembles gold, to the Delightful One, to Indrajihvā, svāhā! LiP_2,25.59.
Oṃ, to the red one, of red color, the tongue of Agni, of manifold colors, who causes hatred and delusion, svāhā! LiP 2.25.60.
Oṃ, to Kṛṣṇā, the tongue of Nairṛta, the slayer, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to the western tongue Suprabhā, who is Muktāphalā, Śāntikā, and Pauṣṭikā. LiP_2,25.62.
Oṃ, svāhā to the manifest one, to the tongue of Vāyu, to the one who eradicates enemies! LiP 2.25.63.
Oṃ, svāhā to Vahni, the radiant one! LiP 2.25.64.
Alternatively, in the rites involving fire,
one should again perform the consecration of the fire (vahnisaṃskāra) according to the rule for occasional (naimittika) ceremonies, making it the fire of Śiva.

Inspection, sprinkling, and striking are performed with the sixth mantra ending in *phaṭ*; sprinkling with water is done with the fourth; digging and scattering are done with the sixth; filling and leveling with the first; sprinkling with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; cutting with the sixth; sweeping and smearing with the fourth;
the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the Nivṛtti-kalā using three [mantras]; the encircling of the pit with the fourth; and the worship of the pit with the first.
The accomplishment of the four lines with the sixth [mantra] ending in *phaṭ* is the "vajrification," and the establishment of the four feet is by the first [mantra] alone;
thus, the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is eighteenfold.

Immediately after the consecration of the fire-pit (kuṇḍasaṃskāra), there is the breaking of the beads (akṣapāṭana) with the sixth [mantra]; the placement of the seat (viṣṭaranyāsa) with the first [mantra], or the invocation of Vāgīśvarī upon the vajrāsana. //25.67//
Oṃ hrīṃ! I invoke Vāgīśvarī, who is dark-complexioned, large-eyed, whose form is intoxicated with youth, and who, being in her season, is the power (śakti) of Vāgīśvara. LiP 2.25.68.
I worship Vāgīśvarī.
*Roṃ Iṃ*, obeisance to Vāgīśvara.

Having honored Vāgīśvarī through the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and stabilization (*sannirodha*), up to the point of worship, one performs the *garbhādhāna* (conception) and *vahnisaṃskāra* (fire-purification) rites.

"I invoke [the deity] who has one face and four arms, who resembles pure crystal, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who holds an axe and a deer, who is adorned with a crown of matted hair, and who is decorated with all ornaments.
*Roṃ iṃ*, obeisance to Vāgīśvara.

Having honored Vāgīśvarī through the rites of invocation, installation, presence, and confinement, up to the point of worship, one performs the consecration of the fire for the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). *LiP_2,25.72*

Having brought fire produced from the *araṇi* wood, or from a magnet, or born of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, into either a copper vessel or an earthen bowl, one should perform inspection, striking, sprinkling, and washing with the first [mantra]. By the first [mantra], there is also the abandonment of the inauspicious flesh-eating fires.
With the first [mantra], one invokes the threefold fire into the stomach, the eyebrows, and so forth; or, by means of the *āgneya* [mantra], one invokes the single-cause form of fire.

With the first [mantra], there is the kindling; with the *puruṣa* [mantra], the *saṃhitā*, and *dhāraṇā*; having veiled it with the *turīya* [mantra] while forming the *dhenumudrā*, one should place both knees upon the ground.

Having gone there, one should place the lifting-vessel (śarāva) upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), circumambulate it clockwise, and offer the *arghya* of kusa grass with the first mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ," directed toward Vāgīśvarī facing oneself through the fourth [mantra] during the placement within the womb-channel (*garbhanāḍī*) by means of the offering of a lotus during the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). Then, with the first mantra, one should offer fuel and kindle the fire; with the first [mantra], the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*); with the *sadyojāta* [mantra], the worship; and with the *vāmadeva* [mantra], the worship.
With the second [mantra], the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is performed; with the third, the worship (pūjana).
