The offering of the limbs and the sprinkling [of water] constitute the expiation from the mouth; with the third [verse], worship is performed by means of the person born from the womb (*garbhaja*) and the *jātakarman*;

with the fourth and the sixth, there is sprinkling for the purification of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Then, with the *kuśāstra* (the mantra of the *kuśa*-grass weapon) belonging to the son of Agni, one performs protection at the mouth. In the fire, the base of the *kuśa*-grass mat is toward the southeast (*īśāna*) and its tip toward the northwest (*vāyavya*), or the base toward the northwest and the tip toward the southeast. This previously mentioned *kuśa*-grass mat and the fuel (*idhma*)—whose tips and bases are smeared with clarified butter—are [prepared].
One should offer oblations with the sixth [mantra] for the removal of saliva.

Having bypassed the five preceding [deities], one should also place the seat-grass (viṣṭara) upon the enclosing-stick (paridhi); furthermore, with the first [mantra], one should worship Hiraṇyagarbha, Hara, and Nārāyaṇa upon that seat-grass.
And one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the world.
One should also worship [the deities] as far as the Vajrāvarta boundary.
Having performed the worship of Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī and so forth, one should dismiss them and then release the oblation.

Then, having performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *srak* and *sruva*—namely, inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and sprinkling with water (*abhyukṣaṇa*) and so forth—as previously described;

and having grasped the *srak* and *sruva* in both hands, one should perform their placement (*saṃsthāpana*) with the first [mantra] and the striking as well. Then, one should perform the tracing (*ullekhana*) of the base of the *darbha* grass upon the *sruc* and *sruva* with the tip [of the grass] three times. One should place the *srak* as Śakti and the *sruva* as Śambhu on the right side upon the *kuśa* grass, [reciting]: "Obeisance to Śakti" and "Obeisance to Śambhu."
Homage! LiP 2.25.79.
Then, with a thread one-quarter [the length] of the anta-sūtra, one should wrap around the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and worship them.
Having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, veiled [the vessel] with the fourth [mantra], and performed protection with the sixth, the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles has already been described.
Furthermore, the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*) has already been described; the acts of inspection, sprinkling, striking, fumigation, and so forth are as before.

One should heat the clarified butter in the northeast or place the vessel of ghee upon the sixth altar. Then, taking the tips of the thumb and ring finger of the left hand and the base of the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, one performs the purification (*utpavana*) with the flames of the fire using a *kuśa* purifier (*pavitra*) one span (*vitasti*) in length.

Having again taken six darbha blades with the fourth mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should perform the immersion of oneself as before using the first mantra ending in *svāhā*, and bind the pair of kuśa-blade purifiers with the first [mantra]; one should place them in the clarified butter—this is the purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).
Holding two blades of darbha grass, one should kindle the fire and cause the clarified butter to circulate three times;
having sprinkled it, one should place it into the fire—this is the *nīrājana* rite.
Taking darbha grass again, inspecting it for insects and the like, sprinkling it with arghya water, and placing the darbha grass into the fire—this is the illumination.
Taking two blades of darbha grass, one should gaze at the clarified butter with the flame of the fire.

Having grasped the *darbha* with its two tips—the first representing the two bright fortnights—one effects the conjunction of the dark fortnights. Having divided the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into three parts, one offers with the first portion of *ājya*: "Svāhā to Agni"; with the second portion of *ājya*: "Svāhā to Soma";
with *ājya*: "Oṃ, Svāhā to Agni and Soma"; and with *ājya*: "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. // LiP_2,25.87 //
Again, having taken it with the thumb, one should consecrate it with the Saṃhitā-mantra ending in "namaḥ."

Having consecrated [the vessel] and performed protection by displaying the *dhenu-mudrā* and applying the *kavaca*, *avaguṇṭhana*, and *astra* mantras, one should then place it within the consecrated area; this is the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*).
With clarified butter and the *mṛgavadana* [formula], one performs the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) of the discus: "To the Śāna-form, beginning with the seed-syllable of the *śakti*, svāhā!
As before, to the Puruṣa-protector, svāhā! To the Aghora-heart, svāhā! To Vāmadeva, the secret one, svāhā! To the Sadyojāta-form, svāhā! Thus is the opening of the faces. (LiP 2.25.90)

"To the form of Īśāna, to the face of Tatpuruṣa, svāhā; to the face of Tatpuruṣa, to the heart of Aghora, svāhā; to the heart of Aghora, to the secret [part] of Vāma, to the form of Sadyojāta, svāhā"—this is the joining of the faces.
"To the form of Īśāna, to Tatpuruṣa as the face, to Aghora as the heart, to Vāmadeva as the secret [part], to Sadyojāta, svāhā"—this is the joining of the faces. (LiP 2.25.91)

"Oṃ *īśānamūrtaye* svāhā! Oṃ *tatpuruṣāya vaktrāya* svāhā! Oṃ *aghorahṛdayāya* svāhā! Oṃ *vāmadevāya guhyāya* svāhā! Oṃ *sadyojātamūrtaye* svāhā!"—thus is the unification of the faces performed. (LiP 2.25.92)
Having thus generated the Śiva-fire, one should perform all rites;
or alternatively, even by means of the tongue alone, one should always perform the rites for pacification and so forth.

O Imperishable One, in rites such as the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna) and others, ten oblations should be offered to the fire for each [rite] five times with the seed-syllable of the womb (yonibīja).
In the Śiva-fire, one should fashion the divine supreme seat as before;
likewise, the invocation, the ritual placement (nyāsa), and the worship should be performed just as for the deity.
Having recited the root mantra once and having bowed to the God of gods,
one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the seed-syllable, as is approved by all.
O great sage, having first sprinkled water and offered that fuel, one should then offer oblations into the midst of the blazing fire.
Having also performed the two āghāra libations with clarified butter alone, O Six-faced One,
one should offer the two ājyabhāga portions according to the rule, using ghee.
The two eyes are the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), and likewise for Agni in the north;
and for Soma in one's own south, O best of the twice-born.
O son of Brahmā, the right eye of the god Śiva, who faces westward, is indeed the fire,
while the left is likewise the moon.
O highly fortunate one, the southern [oblation] certainly comes to pass; there is no doubt about this.
There, ten oblations of clarified butter should be offered with the root mantra itself.
It is likewise prescribed that one should offer the oblation with clarified butter and fuel sticks according to the rules;
then, O observer of good vows, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra.
For all the deities of the enclosures, there are five each as before,
arranged in the order starting from Īśāna and according to the sequence of their seed-syllables (bīja).
The expiation for a cow-slaughter is remembered as being performed with one's own desired end, as previously described;
thus, I have declared the three types of the most auspicious fire-rite.
O Great Sage, one should always act in this manner whenever the occasion arises;
at the end of life, one shall attain heaven and achieve the establishment of the sacred fires.
The practitioner who desires liberation should perform a non-violent fire sacrifice (homa), so that he does not fall into hell as a result of any action whatsoever.
One should contemplate the fire residing in the heart and perform oblations through the sacrifice of meditation upon Śiva,
the Lord of the entire world, who dwells within the bodies of all beings.
Having understood that, one should always offer oblations with devotion through breath control (prāṇāyāma);
for one who offers external oblations becomes a frog upon a stone.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa. Śailādi said:
Or else, one should worship the god Īśāna, Śiva, within the liṅga.
He was a Brahmin, a devotee of Śiva, and entirely devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.

Having taken the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice with the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should indeed smear it over all the limbs, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Wearing the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and facing north, he should sip water using the *brahmatīrtha*;
then, having again composed his body with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," [he should proceed].
And one should worship the God with that mantra and with the *praṇava*;
the worship of the trident-bearing Lord Aghora is superior to all others.
O observer of noble vows, all general sacrifice and fire-rituals,
as well as the specific mantra of that Lord and the meditation upon Aghora, [are prescribed].
The mantra is:

"To those who are not terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible; to all, and to all who are all; let there be salutation to you in your forms as Rudras."
Homage to the non-terrible ones, to the one whose heart is peaceful;
then, svāhā to the terrible ones, to the head of Brahmā who is the self of all;
vaṣaṭ to the most terrible among the terrible, to the crest of Jvālāmālinī.
To all, to all the Śarvas, to Piṅgalakavaca, hūṃ!
Homage be to you who possess the forms of Rudras; to the three eyes, vaṣaṭ!
To the thousand-eyed, impenetrable Pāśupata weapon, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having bathed, sipped water, purified the body, and sprinkled it with the *āgamarṣaṇa* mantra,
one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) according to the rule, offer the *arghya* to the Sun, and worship the Sun.
And likewise, in the worship of Aghora, it is performed equally with the mantra alone;
as well as the purification of the path, the worship at the door, and that of the presiding deity of the site (vāstvadhipa).
Having purified his hand and taken his seat upon an auspicious throne,
he placed [his gaze] upon the lotus at the tip of his nose, his eyes scorched by the fire of the *kṣubhikā*.
Having fanned that ash with the wind and purified it with auspicious ash,
one should fashion the digit of Brahman (brahmakalā) there within the power consisting of nectar.
Having divided Aghora fivefold and again provided it with the five limbs,
one should thus duly perform the placement of both knowledge and action according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) together with the three eyes and having meditated upon the Lord in the excellent seat within the heart,
one should remember the Lord like a lamp between the eyebrows, situated in the fire at the navel.
It is endowed with peace, as well as with the seed, the sprout, the infinite dharmas, and so forth;
it is perfected by the moon, the sun, and fire, and is possessed of the three forms.
Accompanied by Vāmā and the others, and presided over by Manonmanī,
he is seated upon the throne of Śiva, established in his own form, possessing an imperishable appearance and nature.
[He meditated on] Śiva, whose body consists of the thirty-eight kalās and who is endowed with the three principles (tattvas),
the eighteen-armed god who has an elephant hide as his upper garment.
The Supreme Lord, who is non-terrible, wears a lion’s skin as his garment;
he is surrounded by thirty-two powers in the form of the thirty-two syllables.
Adorned with all ornaments and saluted by all the gods,
he wears a garland of skulls as his jewelry and possesses the power over all scorpions and bhūtas.
With a face full like the moon, gentle, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
he bears the crescent moon, is accompanied by Śakti, and has a dark blue form.
In his hands [he holds] a sword, a shield, a noose, a variegated goad adorned with jewels, an elephant-girth,
a bow, the Pāśupata weapon, a staff, and a skull-topped club (khaṭvāṅga), as well as others.
And [the other hands] of Śambhu hold a lute, a bell, a large trident, as well as a divine drum (ḍāmaruka),
a vajra, a mace, a single flaming axe, and a conch-shell.
One should meditate upon and worship the most excellent Supreme Lord, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; furthermore, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).
The entire fire sacrifice (homa) and the various distinctions of mantras are proclaimed as before;
likewise, the offering of the eight flowers and so forth, perfumes and so forth, worship, praise, and the presentation of oblations.
And having prepared the inner offering (antarbali) to the southeast of the sacrificial pit according to the rules,
one should construct the mandala according to the prescribed rite with these mantras in their proper sequence.
To the Rudras, the groups of Mothers, the Yakṣas, the Asuras, the Planets, the Rākṣasas, the Nāgas, the Nakṣatras, the Viśvagaṇas, and the Kṣetrapālas— then, in the direction of Vāyu and Varuṇa,
one should cast the offering for the Kṣetrapālas;
[offering] water for the feet, fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp, O you of good vows.
Having offered the food offering, the mouth-perfume, and so forth as an oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus made the request and then dismissed [the deity], one should perform worship with eight flowers;
for this is common to all forms of worship, O best of sages.
Thus, O observer of noble vows, the worship of Aghora and so forth has been briefly described;
this is the procedure for the worship of Aghora, whether performed at a linga or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Worship of the *liṅga* is unsurpassed and ten million times more meritorious than worship on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
A Brahmin devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* is freed from the consequences of even the most heinous sins.
One would not be stained by even sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
the sight of the Liṅga is meritorious, but touching it is superior to seeing it.
There is nothing superior to worship, O son of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has the supreme worship of Aghora been briefly described.
Even in a hundred million years, it cannot be described in detail.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"We have heard the power of Nandin and the fruit of worshipping the Liṅga."
O Romaharṣaṇa of noble vows, everything is in accordance with the sacred scriptures.
In ancient times, for the benefit of the Kṣatriyas, the Trident-bearer Śiva described the Jayābhiṣeka on the peak of Mount Meru to Manu.
Therefore, O Sūta, best among the wise, you ought to tell us how the sixteenfold great gift (mahādāna) is auspicious.
Sūta said: Having previously performed the *jīvacchrāddha*, the lord Manu Svāyambhuva approached Meru and praised Nīlalohita, the Lord of Gods.
And to him who was disciplined by asceticism, Bhava, being delighted, granted divine vision; through that, Īśāna beheld the Imperishable One.
Having bowed and worshipped according to the prescribed rite, I stood with my palms joined in reverence;
then the God was worshipped and beheld by me just now.
Previously, that which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa was told to Śakra.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, salutations to you, O Sovereign of the universe!
O Mahādeva, this *jīvacchrāddha* has been performed through your grace.
Then the God was worshipped and indeed beheld by me just now;
previously, [the method] that bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa was told to Śakra.
"O Lord of gods, O Master, you ought to explain to me the consecration for victory.
Sūta said:
To him, the divine Mahādeva, the blessed Nīlalohita, [spoke].
The Supreme Lord explained the entire rite of the victory-consecration (*jayābhiṣeka*).
The Blessed One said: "Out of a desire for the welfare of kings, I shall describe the victory-consecration."
For the sake of overcoming untimely death and for victory over all enemies,
when the time of battle has arrived, one should perform this consecration.
Having consecrated his own husband, he should go to fight on the field of battle;
having constructed a pavilion, a water-shed, or even a temporary shed according to the prescribed rite.
A Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas should establish the fire in nine ways;
thereafter, for the sake of the complete consecration, he should cause the laying out of the ritual lines (sūtrapāta).
First, the initial line of colors, and likewise again from the south;
there are two thousand and four hundred [threads] therein.
One should collect the remaining auspicious cells among those cells;
furthermore, one should withdraw a single square from all sides on the outer path.
Having collected the constituent sūtras according to the prescribed rule, one should arrange them separately:
first the sūtra of the eastern color-line, and likewise again the southern color-line.
One should sequentially dissolve the thirty-six [elements], beginning with the east and the south;
likewise, there are seven rows beginning with the east and again those beginning with the south.
Therefore, forty-nine lines are proclaimed;
one should erase nine lines in the center with water mixed with fragrant cow dung.
And there one should draw a beautiful lotus, measuring one cubit,
white, circular, with eight petals, and provided with a pericarp and filaments.
The pericarp, resembling gold, measures eight finger-breadths;
the location for the filaments is said to measure four finger-breadths.
One should place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, respectively,
in the corners beginning with the southeast, using the Praṇava.
One should indeed place the unmanifest and the others in the cardinal directions in the form of limbs;
the fourfold group consists of the Unmanifest, Niyati, Kāla, and Kālī.
Dharma and the others are, in order, white, red, golden, and black;
O you of good vows, their bodies are in the form of swans and possess a golden luster.
Within the power of the support (ādhāraśakti) is the lotus, the cause of creation;
within the digit (kalā) is the mere point (bindu), and beyond that is the form of sound (nāda).
Above the *nāda*, one should meditate upon Śiva, known as the syllable *Āḥ*, the teacher of the world;
and one should contemplate Manonmanī and Mahādeva, who has the luster of a lotus.
Vāmā and the others are indeed located in sequence upon the filaments starting from the east:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Vikaraṇī.
One should install the goddesses Balā, Pramathinī, and Damanī in their respective order,
together with Vāmadeva and the others, using the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) alone.
Homage be to Vāmadeva; homage to the Eldest, the wielder of the trident.
To Rudra, who has the form of Time (Kāla), and to the one who effects the transformation of parts (Kalā-vikaraṇa);
likewise to Bala, and to the subduer of all beings.
"Salutations again and again to the god Manonmanī and to Manonmanī herself;
with these mantras, one should worship the circular mandala according to the prescribed rule."
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure.
In the second enclosure, there are indeed sixteen Śaktis.
And in the third enclosure, there are twenty-four [deities] in sequence;
in the center is the Piśāca path, and the navel-path (nābhivīthi) extends all around.
By these mantras, according to the prescribed rule, the [mantra] of the Piśācas is proclaimed;
it consists of one thousand and eight words and is joined with an eight-spoked [diagram].
One should fashion lotuses in those various distinct places in succession, using śāli rice, nīvāra, wheat, barley, and so forth.
One should prepare [the offering] with rice and sesame seeds, or combined with white mustard seeds,
according to the prescribed rule and at the appropriate time.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus upon them, complete with a pericarp and filaments; it is prescribed that there shall be one āḍhaka of śāli rice for each of the lotuses individually.
Half of that amount should be for rice, and half of that again for barley and other grains;
it is prescribed that one *droṇa* is for the principal jar, and half of that for the rice.
In the center, one should place an āḍhaka of sesame seeds and half of that amount of barley;
then, having sprinkled it with water, one should invoke the lotus with the syllable *praṇava*.
In all of those, one should sequentially place the *praṇava* according to the prescribed rule;
having thus completed this and sprinkled [the area], [one recites] the supreme thousand-word [hymn].
One should have made thousands of auspicious jars, either made of gold or silver, endowed with the characteristics previously described.
The vessels made of copper should be prepared according to the rule with water for the *arghya* offering accompanied by the *praṇava*;
their width at the belly is declared to be twelve finger-breadths.
The navel of that [pedestal] is prescribed to be half of that [height];
the neck, however, has a height of two finger-breadths and a width of four finger-breadths.
The lip is said to be two finger-breadths in height and its projection two finger-breadths;
that which is twice those measurements is proclaimed as the divine Śiva-kumbha.
One should indeed wrap it with a thread at intervals of the size of a barley grain;
having thus covered and sprinkled it, one should place it upon *kuśa* grass according to the prescribed rule.
As before, one should fill [the vessel] with fragrant water using the *praṇava* alone;
then, one should place the auspicious *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī* according to the prescribed knowledge.
In the center of that central lotus, one should place [the image] together with its beard and unbroken grains,
having wrapped it in a pair of cloths and covered it with a lotus.
Having placed Śiva in the Śiva-pitcher with a golden pitcher adorned with various jewels, [one should do so] for each of the thousand pitchers, using the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava.
We know the Puruṣa alone; we meditate upon Mahādeva.
May that Rudra inspire us.
By this mantra, the presence of Rudra is always remembered.
Having established the Goddess within the *vardhanī* vessel with the *gāyatrī* mantra, O Goddess, one should worship her.
Let us know Gaṇāmbikā; let us meditate upon Mahātapā;
may Gaurī inspire us.
In the first enclosure, Vāmā and the others have been proclaimed.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear about the second enclosure.

O observer of noble vows, one should install and worship the sixteen Śaktis here at the beginning, end, and intermediate points of the Indra-array; however, in the center, one should install and worship Subhadrā.
One should worship Bhadrā in the southeast wheel, Kanakāṇḍajā in the south,
and Ambikā in the southwest array, within the central pitcher.
One should worship Śrīdevī in the western quarter, Vāgīśā in the region of the wind (the north-west),
Gomukhī in the northern quarter, and [the central goddess] in the central pitcher.
In the center of the Rudra-arrangement, one should worship Bhadrakarṇī;
in the intermediate directions between Indra and Agni, one should worship the auspicious Aṇimā.
One should place Laghimā upon a lotus between Yama and Agni;
one should worship Mahimā in the center, between the Destroyer of Rākṣasas (Nairṛta) and Varuṇa.
One should worship Prāpti in the middle between Varuṇa and Asura;
one should place Prākāmya upon the lotus in the middle between Varuṇa and Anila.
One should worship by installing Īśitva between Vitteśa and Anila;
one should worship by installing Vaśitva between Vitteśa and Īśāna.
Between Eindreśa and Īśāna, one should worship Kāmāvasāyaka; this is declared as the second enclosure. Now hear of the third enclosure.
One should worship the twenty-four Śaktis within the offering jars and in the midst of the array, according to the prescribed ritual as before.
Dīkṣā and Dīkṣāyikā, Caṇḍā and Caṇḍāṃśunāyikā, Sumati and Sumatyāyī, as well as Gopā and Gopāyikā.
Then, having installed Nanda and Nandāyī, and thereafter Pitāmaha,
Pitāmahāyī, and the others starting from the east according to the prescribed rite, one should worship them.
Having worshipped the auspicious third enclosure according to the prescribed rite,
one should reach the Saubhadra array in the first enclosure in due order.
Having first established the primary [deity] according to the rite, one should then establish the eight Śaktis in sequence;
now hear of the Śaktis in the second enclosure, beginning from the east.
Having worshipped these sixteen, one should display the lotus mudrā:
Bindukā, Bindugarbhā, Nādinī, and Nādagarbhajā.
Śaktikā, Śaktigarbhā, Parā, and Parāparā—
these eight powers are proclaimed to be in the first enclosure.
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍamukhī, Caṇḍavegā, Manojavā,
Caṇḍākṣī, Caṇḍanirghoṣā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
She whose height is the mind, who presides over the mind, who is of the nature of the mind, the object of veneration;
she who captivates the mind, who gladdens the mind, who is the delight of the mind, the Great Sovereign.
In the second enclosure, sixteen [deities] are indeed proclaimed;
the Saubhadra array has been described—now hear from me the Bhadra array.
The eight powers are those of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
Hariṇī, Suvarṇā, Kāñcanī, and likewise Hāṭakī.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Subhagā, Jambunāyikā,
Vāgbhavā, Vākpathā, Vāṇī, Bhīmā, Citrarathā, and Sudhī.
Vedamātā and Hiraṇyākṣī are recorded as being in the second enclosure;
the manifestation named Bhadra has been described—now hear from me that which is named Kanaka.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner,
as well as the mace and the trident, are prescribed in sequence for the first enclosure.
Yuddhā, Prabuddhā, Caṇḍā, Muṇḍā, Kapālinī,
Mṛtyuhantrī, Virūpākṣī, Kapardā, and Kamalāsanā.
Daṃṣṭriṇī, Raṅgiṇī, Lambākṣī, Kaṅkabhūṣaṇī,
Saṃbhāvā, and Bhāvinī— these sixteen are indeed proclaimed.
The Prathakavyūha has been described; now hear from me the one called Ambikā:
she is Khecarī by her own nature, and she is Bhavānī in the form of fire.
Vahninī, Vahninābhā, Mahimā, Amṛtā, and Lālasā—
these eight Śaktis are universally acknowledged as belonging to the first enclosure.
And the goddess Kṣamā, Śikharā, Ṛturatnā, Silā,
Chāyā, Bhūtapanī, Dhanyā, Indramātā, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Tṛṣṇā, Rāgavatī, Mohā, Kāma, Kopa, Mahotkaṭā,
Indra, and the goddess Badhirā— these sixteen are proclaimed.
The manifestation of Ambikā has been described; now listen, O observer of noble vows, to the manifestation of Śrī:
Svarśā, Svarśavatī, Gandhā, Prāṇā, Apānā, and Samānikā.
Udānā and Vyānanāmā are remembered in the first enclosure;
likewise Tamohatā, Prabhāmoghā, Tejinī, and Dahinī.
Bhīmāsyā, Jālinī, Coṣā, Śoṣiṇī, Rudranāyikā,
Varibhadrā, Gaṇādhyakṣā, Candrahāsā, and Gahvarā.
Gaṇamātā and Ambikā, along with all the Śaktis approved by everyone,
are declared to be the sixteen [deities] in the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa) in their proper order.
The Śrīvyūha has been described; O virtuous one, listen now to Vāgīśa:
Dhārā, Vāridharā, Vahnikī, and likewise Nāśakī.
Martyātītā, Mahāmāyā, Vajriṇī, and Kāmadenukā—
thus the eight Śaktis are proclaimed in the first enclosure.
Payoṣṇī, Vāruṇī, Śāntā, Jayantī, and Varapradā; Plāvinī, Jalamātā, Payomātā, and Mahāmbikā.
Raktā, Karālī, Caṇḍākṣī, Mahocchuṣmā, Payasvinī,
Māyā, Vidyeśvarī, Kālī, and Kālikā, in due order.
These sixteen powers alone are proclaimed and accepted by all;
Vāgīśvara is declared to be the Vyūha, and the Gomukha array is also spoken of as a Vyūha.
Śaṅkīnī, Hālinī, Laṅkāvarṇā, Kalkinī,
Yakṣiṇī, Mālinī, Vamanī, and Rasātmanī.
In the first enclosure, eight Śaktis are proclaimed:
Caṇḍā, Ghaṇṭā, Mahānādā, Sumukhī, Durmukhī, and Balā.
Revatī is the first, followed by Ghorā, Sainyā, Līnā, Mahābalā,
Jayā, Vijayā, and also Aparā and Aparājitā.
In the second enclosure, there are indeed sixteen Śaktis;
the Gomukhī array has been described, so now hear from me about Bhadrakarṇī.
Mahājayā, Virūpākṣī, Śuklābhā, Ākāśamātṛkā,
Saṃhārī, Jātahārī, Daṃṣṭrālī, and Suṣkarevatī.
In the first enclosure, eight Śaktis are proclaimed:
Pipīlikā, Puṇyahārī, Aśanī, and Sarvahāriṇī; 2,27.95.
Bhadrahā, Viśvahārī, Himā, Yogīśvarī, Chidrā, Bhānumatī, Chidrā, Saiṃhikī, Surabhī, and Samā.
Sarvabhavyā and Vegā—these are indeed the sixteen Śaktis.
The eight Mahāvyūhas have been declared; now hear of the eight Upavyūhas.
Having surrounded the array of *aṇimā*, in the first enclosure, in due order,
are Indra, Citrabhānu, Vāruṇī, and Daṇḍin.

The *haṃsa*, whose form is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the power of one's own self (*svātmaśakti*), and the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*)—this is declared to be the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*). Now hear about the second enclosure.
The Blessed Keśava, Rudra, the Moon, and likewise the Sun; the Mahātman, as well as the Ātman, the Antarātman, and Maheśvara.
The Supreme Self, the minute individual soul (jīva), Piṅgala, Puruṣa, Paśu,
the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), Bhūtapati, and Bhīma are recorded as being in the second enclosure.
The manifestation of *aṇimā* has been described; now I shall tell you that which is called *laghimā*.
[These are] Śrīkaṇṭha, Anta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and likewise Śaśaka.
Amareśa, Sthitīśa, Dārateśa, and likewise the eighth;
this is declared to be the first enclosure (āvaraṇa). Now hear about the second enclosure.
Sthāṇu, Hara, Daṇḍeśa, Bhauktīśa, Surapuṅgava, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśa, Krūrasena, and Sureśvara;
Krodhīśa, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Śiva himself;
likewise Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, and Caturmukha.
In the second enclosure, sixteen Rudras are proclaimed;
the array of Laghimā has been described—now hear, O observer of good vows, about Mahimā.
Ajeśa, Kṣemarudra, Soma, Aṃśu, Lāṅgalin, Daṇḍāru, Ardhanārī, Ekānta, and Anta; // LiP_2,27.107 //
Pālī, Bhujaṅga, Pinākī, Khaḍkira,
Kāma, Īśa, Śveta, and Bhṛgu are indeed remembered as the sixteen.
The array of majesty has been described; now hear from me the array of attainment:
Saṃvarta, Lakulīśa, Vāḍava, and Hastin.
Caṇḍayakṣa, Gaṇapati, and the high-souled Bhṛguja as the eighth; this is declared to be the first enclosure. Now hear about the second enclosure.
Trivikrama, Mahājihva, Ṛkṣa, Śrībhadra, Mahādeva, Dadhīca, and Kumāra, who is both the supreme and the subordinate.
Mahādaṃṣṭra, Karāla, Sūcaka, Suvardhana,
Mahādhvāṅkṣa, Mahānanda, Daṇḍin, and likewise Gopālaka.
The array of attainment has been fully described; now hear, O observer of noble vows, about sovereign will (*prākāmya*).
The great nāga Puṣpadanta is the bringer of vast bliss.
Śukla, Viśāla, Kamala, Bilva, and Cāruma—these are declared to be the first enclosure; now hear of the second enclosure.
Ratipriya, Sureśāna, Citrāṅga, Sudurjaya,
Vināyaka, Kṣetrapāla, Mahāmoha, and Jaṅgala.
Vatsaputra, Mahāputra, and likewise Grāmadeśādhipa;
the god Sarvāvasthādhipa, Meghanāda, and Pracaṇḍaka.
The messenger of Time (Kāladūta) has been described; this is remembered as the second enclosure.
The array known as Prākāmya has been described; now I shall describe to you Sovereignty (Aiśvarya).
Maṅgalā, Carcikā, Yogeśā, Haradāyikā,
Bhāsurā, Suramātā, Sundarī, and Mātṛkā as the eighth.
Those mentioned in the first enclosure, listen now to those in the second enclosure:
Gaṇādhipa, Mantrajña, Varadeva, and Ṣaḍānana.
Vidagdha, Vicitra, Amogha, and indeed Amogha;
Aśvīrudra, Someśa, and likewise Uttamodumbara.
Nārasiṃha, Vijaya, the lord Indraguha,
and Apāmpati— this is remembered as the second enclosure according to the ritual injunction.
The array known as Aiśvarya has been described; furthermore, Vaśitva is mentioned, as well as Gaganodbhava, Bhavana, Vijaya, and likewise Ajaya.
Mahājaya, Aṅgāra, Vyaṅgāra, and Mahāyaśas are said to be in the first enclosure; now hear [the names] in the second enclosure.
Sundara, Pracaṇḍeśa, Mahāvarṇa, Mahāsura,
Mahāroma, Mahāgarbha, and the first, Kanaka.
Kharaja, Garuḍa, Meghanāda, and Garjaka; Gaja, Chedaka, Bāhu, Triśikha, and Māri. (LiP 2.27.125)
Mastery has been described as the array; now hear of the power of subduing desires:
Vināda, Vikaṭa, Vasanta, and Abhaya.
Vidyunmahābala, Kamala, and likewise Damanaka—this is declared to be the first enclosure; now hear of the second enclosure.
And Dharma is a serpent of exceeding strength, with a massive body and great jaws;
he possesses power, his limbs are smeared with ashes, and he is difficult to conquer and hard to overcome.
Vetāla, Raurava, Durdhara, and Bhoga;
Vajra, Kālāgnirudra, Sadyonāda, and Mahāguha.
The second enclosure has been declared; the Vyūha known as Āvasāyika is the sixteenth Vyūha that has been described. Now listen to the description of the second enclosure.
In the second enclosure and in the Dakṣavyūha are the Śaktis;
there are eight in the first enclosure and sixteen in the outer one.
Manoharā, Mahānādā, Citrā, Citrarathā,
as well as Rohiṇī, Citrāṅgī, Citrarekhā, and Vicitrikā.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
Citrā, Vicitrarūpā, Śubhadā, Kāmadā, and Subhā.
And the goddess Krūrā, Piṅgalā, Khaḍgikā, the virtuous Laṃbikā,
Daṃṣṭrālī, Rākṣasīdhvaṃsī, Lolupā, and Lohitāmukhī.
Sixteen [deities] have been briefly described in the second enclosure; the Dakṣavyūha has thus been fully explained. Now hear from me about the Dākṣavyūha.
Sarvāsatī, Viśvarūpā, Laṃpaṭā, and Āmiṣapriyā; Dīrghadaṃṣṭrā, Vajrā, Laṃboṣṭhī, and Prāṇahāriṇī.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear about the second enclosure:
Gajakarṇā, Aśvakarṇā, Mahākālī, and Subhīṣaṇā.
Vātavegaravā, Ghorā, Ghānāghanaravā, Varaghoṣā, Mahāvarṇā, Sugaṇṭā, and likewise Ghaṇṭikā; // LiP_2,27.138 //
Ghaṇṭaśvarī, Mahāghorā, Ghorā, and likewise Atighorikā—
these sixteen are proclaimed in the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa).
The array of Dākṣī has been fully described; now hear from me the array of the Egg (Aṇḍavyūha).
Atighaṇṭā, Atighorā, Karālā, and likewise Karabhā [are its components].
Vibhūti, Bhogadā, Kānti, and Śaṅkhinī are recorded as the eighth; these are declared in the first enclosure. Now hear concerning the second enclosure.
Patriṇī, Gāndhārī, Yogamātā, Supīvarā,
Raktā, Mālāṃśukā, Vīrā, Saṃhārī, and Māṃsahāriṇī.
Phalahārī, Jīvahārī, Svecchāhārī, Tuṇḍikā, Revatī, Raṅgiṇī, and Saṃgā—these sixteen indeed belong to the second [group]. (LiP 2.27.143)
She is known as Caṇḍavyūhā and is likewise called Caṇḍāvyūhā;
she is Caṇḍī, Caṇḍamukhī, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavegā, and Mahāravā.
Bhrukuṭī, Caṇḍabhū, and Caṇḍarūpā is recorded as the eighth; this is declared to be the first enclosure. Now hear about the second enclosure.
Candraghrāṇā, Balā, Balajihvā, Baleśvarī,
Balavegā, Mahākāyā, Mahākopā, and Vidyutā.
Kaṅkālī, Kalaśī, Vidyut, Caṇḍaghoṣikā,
Mahāghoṣā, Mahārāvā, Caṇḍabhānā, and Aṅgacaṇḍikā.
The array of Caṇḍā has been described; now hear from me the Haravyūha:
the goddess Caṇḍākṣī, Kāmadā, Sūkarī, and Kukkuṭānanā.
Gāndhārī, Dundubhī, Durgā, and Saumitrī is remembered as the eighth;
this is declared the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa). Now hear about the second enclosure.
Mṛtodbhavā, Mahālakṣmī, Varṇadā, Jīvarakṣiṇī,
Hariṇī, Kṣīṇajīvā, Daṇḍavaktrā, and Caturbhujā.
Moving through space, having the form of space, pervading space, the source of auspiciousness;
moving within houses, moving beautifully, consuming poison, and the destroyer of the affliction of poison.
The array of Hara has been fully described; now the array of Harā is being told:
Jaṃbhācyutā, Kaṅkārī, Devikā, and Durdharāvahā.
Caṇḍikā and Capalā are remembered as being in the first enclosure;
likewise Cañjikā, Cāmarī, Bhaṇḍikā, and Śubhānanā.
Piṇḍikā, Muṇḍikā, Muṇḍā, Śākinī, and likewise Śāṅkarī; Kartarī, Bhartarī, Bhāginī, and Yajñadāyinī.
Yamadaṃṣṭrā, Mahādaṃṣṭrā, and Karālā are the Śaktis;
thus has the array of Harā been described. Now hear from me the Śaiṇḍavyūha.
Vikarālī, Karālī, Kālajaṅghā, Yaśasvinī,
Vegā, Vegavatī, Yajñā, and Vedāṅgā is remembered as the eighth.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
Vajrā, Śaṅkhā, Atiśaṅkhā, Balā, and likewise Abalā.
Añjanī, Mohinī, Māyā, Vikaṭāṅgī, and Nalī;
likewise Gaṇḍakī, Daṇḍakī, Ghoṇā, Śoṇā, and Satyavatī.
And Kallolā; thus, in due order, there are exactly sixteen according to the rule.
This is declared to be the Śaiṇḍavyūha; now the Śaiṇḍā array is described.
Danturā, Raudrabhāgā, Amṛtā, Sakulā, Śubhā,
Calajihvā, Āryane-trā, Rūpiṇī, and likewise Dārikā.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
Khādikā, Rūpanāmā, Saṃhārī, and Kṣamāntakā.
Kaṇḍinī, Peṣiṇī, Mahātrāsā, Kṛtāntikā,
Daṇḍinī, Kiṅkarī, Bimbā, Varṇinī, and Amalāṅginī.
Draviṇī and Drāviṇī are indeed the sixteen Śaktis;
thus has been described the most excellent and delightful array of Śauṇḍā.
I shall now describe the first array, which is most beautiful:
Plavinī, Plāvanī, Śobhā, Mandā, and Madotkaṭā.
The Great Goddess Mandākṣepā is remembered in the first enclosure;
she is the goddess Kāmasaṃdīpinī, exceedingly beautiful and captivating to the mind.
Mahāvaśā, Mahāgrāhā, Vihvalā, Madavihvalā,
Aruṇā, Śoṣaṇā, Divyā, Revatī, and Bhāṇḍanāyikā.
Stambhinī, Ghoraraktākṣī, Smararūpā, and Sughoṣaṇā—
this is declared to be the first array, O Svāyambhuva, exactly as it is.
The first array has been described; listen to me as I shall proclaim it:
Ghorā, Ghoratarā, Aghorā, Atighorā, and Aghanāyikā.
Dhāvanī, Kroṣṭukā, and Muṇḍā are proclaimed as the eighth; this is declared the first enclosure. Now hear of the second enclosure.
Terrible, more terrible, and most fearsome, she is praised and perfectly round;
she is the paralyzer, the weeper, the fierce one, possessed of Rudra, immovable, and yet moving.
Mahābalā, Mahāśānti, Śālā, Śāntā, Śivā, Aśivā,
Bṛhatkakṣā, and Mahānāsā— these sixteen are indeed proclaimed.
The first has been fully described; now the array of Manmatha is being told:
Tālakarṇī, Bālā, Kalyāṇī, Kapilā, and Śivā.
Iṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, and Pratijñā are remembered as being in the first enclosure;
likewise Khyāti, Puṣṭikarī, Tuṣṭi, Jalā, Śruti, and Dhṛti.
She is the bestower of desires, the giver of auspiciousness, the gentle one, the radiant, and the mistress of the Kāma-tantra;
she is Dharma, she who is under the sway of Dharma, she whose nature is virtue, the destroyer of sin, and the increaser of righteousness.
The *manmatha* array has been described; now hear from me about the *manmathā*, the *dharmarakṣāvidhānā*, the *dharma*, and likewise the *dharmavatī*.
Sumati, Durmati, Medhā, and Vimalā is remembered as the eighth;
this is declared to be the first enclosure. Now hear about the second enclosure.
Śuddhi, Buddhi, Dyuti, Kānti, Vartulā, Mohavardhinī, Balā, Atibalā, Bhīmā, and likewise Prāṇavṛddhikarī.
The shameless, the pitiless, the dull-witted, the destroyer of all sins,
the tawny, and the extremely distressed— these sixteen are proclaimed.
I have told you my own opinion, and I shall now describe the Bhīmavyūha array;
it is both passionate and dispassionate, causing agitation and increasing sorrow.
Desire, thirst, hunger, and delusion are proclaimed as the eighth;
this is declared the first veil. Now hear about the second veil.
Jayā, Nidrā, Bhaya, Ālasyā, Jalatṛṣṇā, Udarī, Darā, Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇāṅginī, Vṛddhā, Śuddhocchiṣṭāśanī, and Vṛṣā.
Desire, though beautiful, is burnt away; it is a giver of suffering, yet a series of givers of happiness.
This is declared to be the Bhīmavyūha; now the Bhīmāyīvyūha is described.
Ānandā, Sunandā, Mahānandā, Subhaṅkarī,
Vatirāgā, Mahotsāhā, Jitarāgā, and Manoratā.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
Manonmanī, Manaḥkṣobhā, Madonmattā, and Gadākulā.
Mandagarbhā, Mahābhāsā, Kāmānandā, Suvibhvalā,
Mahāvegā, Suvegā, Mahābhogā, and Kṣayāvahā.
Kramiṇī, Kramiṇī, and Vakra are remembered as being in the second enclosure;
thus has the most beautiful array of Bhīmāyī been described to you.
Today I shall describe the Śākuna [astrology], which delights the mind of Svāyambhuva Manu:
Yogā, Vegā, Suvegā, Ativegā, and Suvāsinī.
Devī, Manorathā, Vegā, Jalāvartā, and Dhīmatī—these are declared as the first enclosure; now hear of the second enclosure.
Rodhinī, Kṣobhiṇī, Bālā, Viprā, Aśeṣā, Suśoṣiṇī,
Vidyutā, Bhāsinī, the goddess Manovegā, and Cāpalā.
Vidyujjihvā, Mahājihvā, Bhṛkuṭīkuṭilānanā,
Phullajvālā, Mahājvālā, Sujvālā, and Kṣayāntikā.
The Śākuna array has been described; now hear from me about the Śākunāyā, as well as the Jvālinī, the Bhasmāṅgī, and the Bhasmāntagā.
Bhāvinī, Prajā, Vidyā, and Khyāti is recorded as the eighth;
this is declared to be the first enclosure. Now hear of the second enclosure.
Ullekha, Patākā, Bhogābhogavatī, Khagā,
Bhogabhogavratā, Yogā, Bhogā, and Yogapāragā.
Ṛddhi, buddhi, dhṛti, kānti, smṛti, sākṣācchruti, dharā,
and śākunāyā constitute the Mahāvyūha, which is said to bestow all desires.
O Svāyambhuva, listen to the most beautiful array called Sumati;
it is supreme, desired by others, seen as the highest, immortal, and the destroyer of karmic fruits.
Hiraṇyākṣī, Suvarṇākṣī, the goddess Kapiñjalā in person, and Kāmarekhā—this is what has been declared; now hear of the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Ratnadvīpā, Sudvīpā, Ratnadā, Ratnamālinī,

"May we know that Puruṣa; may we meditate upon Mahādeva;

O best of the twice-born, one should offer the primary oblation with substances as previously described, and with each substance, one should perform a thousand oblations in the presence of the King, accompanied by Īśāna.

The royal insignia are not prescribed for other Kṣatriyas;
furthermore, the measurement for all of them is said to be twelve finger-breadths.
The palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, and vaṭa trees are to be placed in order starting from the east;

Thus has the supreme Jayasecana been briefly described;

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having bathed and having paid obeisance to the God, the Lord of Gods, the Consort of Umā—
With his divine eye, he beheld Rudra, the blue-and-red Ishvara.
Having seen him, he praised Śaṅkara, the giver of boons, with the Rudrādhyāya;
and the god, out of satisfaction, granted him liberation at the end of his reign through his very deeds.
Having spoken once the words "I am yours," he vanished right there;
Manu Svāyambhuva, having paid homage to the bull-bannered god.
He ascended Mount Mahāmeru like the Lord [Śiva] upon a great bull;
there he beheld the god, radiant as gold and endowed with the sovereign power of yoga.
He beheld Sanatkumāra, the granter of boons and the son of Brahmā; he paid homage to that giver of boons, who was devoted to Brahman and whose form was that of Brahman itself.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the one of great splendor offered praise;
and upon seeing Manu, the god, the sage’s hair stood on end with joy.
Out of compassion, Sanatkumāra spoke this, O treasury of mercy;
Sanatkumāra said:
"Having seen [this] from Śaṅkara, the blue-and-red one, the peaceful Lord of All."
Having received the consecration and attained it, he desired to speak;
yet, although he wished to speak, having heard those words of his, [the other] prostrated with palms joined in reverence.
He made this request: "O Lord, how is liberation attained through action?
You ought to explain to us how it is achieved by action alone."
"O Lord, liberation is accomplished through knowledge, or perhaps sometimes through a combination of both.
Then, having heard those words, he who was a treasury of those who know the essence of the Vedas [spoke].
O Sage, the blessed Sanatkumāra attained liberation through action performed in due order, and likewise through mixed action in due order, and finally through knowledge in an instant.
And by the measure of the cities, I attained the state of a camel due to the curse of my lord Nandin;

At times such as the planetary conjunctions (grahaṇa) and so forth, and in auspicious locations,

One should cause a beautiful circular walkway to be constructed, joined with twelve pillars,

Between these two, Endrika and Īśāna, is the principal [form] of the daughter of Brahmā;

The sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) may be hexagonal, triangular, lotus-like, or octagonal according to all measurements, or it may be entirely plain.
It is endowed with four gates, adorned with four archways,
joined by the eight elephants of the quarters, and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass.
It should be endowed with the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) and adorned above with a canopy;

One should perform everything using wood from the *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, and so forth, or exclusively from *khadira*; or else, one should have it all made with that same wood by which the pillar was previously fashioned.
Alternatively, one may fashion it using a mixed method or with bamboo,
measuring eight cubits in length and provided with two additional cubits.
The width of the base of the balance-pillar is considered to be three times its height;

O King, the distance between the two [pillars] is prescribed as six cubits;
the distance between the two pillars themselves is also made four cubits.
The distance between the six pillars situated above the two main pillars should be known as six *vitastis* in width; the diameter and the height should likewise be that same measure.
The height of the two pillars should be equal to the northern door,
measuring thirty-six mātras, while the width should be one *tulā*.
The base (viṣkaṃbha) should be eight mātras in width and joined with a row of barley-corns;
the navel should be thirty-six mātras, and from its construction, it should be auspiciously circular.
One should bind it with a gold band at the top, the bottom, and the middle;
three loops for hanging should be fashioned in the middle of the band.
One should fashion three supports out of copper, or they may be made of brass; one must never have them made of iron.
In the center, a very beautiful support should be fashioned facing upwards;
or one should fasten it to the front of the archway according to the prescribed rite with cords.
A single tongue [of thread] is placed between the two scales,
and a firm, unsurpassed peg is fixed in the middle of the northern side.
Having covered it from above with a canopy, one should properly and firmly apply it;
O Sage, one should have a ring made that is well-proportioned and possesses a hollow.
In the middle of the balance, one should employ a canopy, as well as a suspension by means of a scale-beam, a ring,
or a supporting earring.
It should be very firm in the middle of the balance, measuring nine finger-breadths in length,
and the width of the cloth itself should be five finger-breadths.
One should have two other very firm lumps made from auspicious material;
they should be fashioned five spans in width beneath the sling,
and both should be capable of supporting a thousand palas.
One may construct it with eight hundred palas, or indeed with six hundred;
its width and height should both be four tālas.
The measurement for the pitcher (kalaśa) is prescribed as three and a half tālas;
one should fasten five vessels, which are said to be six units of three mātras each.
It is endowed with four gates, each gate being one finger-breadth in width,
and is provided with earrings that are white, pure, and well-proportioned.
In each pair of earrings, one should fashion a circular chain;
one should join it by means of a supporting loop that hangs down from the chain.
Having set aside a space of one span or four finger-breadths from the ground, one should support [the structure];
both jars should be made beautiful and each one man's height.
Having filled those two with sand, one should place Śiva there;
they should be carefully installed in a pit measuring two cubits.
The wise man should fill it completely on all sides with sand,
and he should construct it by that path so that it attains stability.
Listen to the supreme secret concerning the upper mandala of the altar:
it should be eight finger-breadths in size and adorned with auspicious sprouts.
Strewn with fruits and flowers and provided with incense and lamps,
it should be fashioned in the center of the altar so that it resembles the surface of a mirror.
First, one should draw the maṇḍala, provided with four gates,
complete with primary and secondary ornaments, and endowed with a pericarp and filaments.
One should have a five-colored [image] fashioned, endowed with the appropriate colors and castes;
the vajra is in the eastern sector, and the blazing śakti is in the southeast.
One should draw a staff in the south, and a sword should be drawn in the southwest;
a noose is to be drawn in the west, and a banner indeed in the domain of the wind (the northwest).
A mace should be drawn in the north, and one should draw a trident in the northeast;
to the left of the trident is a wheel, and a lotus is on the right.
Having written it thus, one should thereafter perform the rite of oblation (homakarma);
the primary oblation is offered with the Gāyatrī mantra: "Svāhā to Śakra and to Agni."
To Yama, the lord of the Rākṣasas, to Varuṇa, and to Vāyu;
then to Kubera, to Īśvara, to Viṣṇu, and again to Brahmā.

The oblation should be offered according to the prescribed ritual with the *praṇava* at the end of each mantra, preceded by the invocation of the fire of one's own Vedic school (*svaśākhā*), and accompanied by the *jaya* and other rites.
Then, one should cause all the rites to be performed according to the rules up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
For all *homa*s and especially for the initial *homa*, the fuel-stick (*samidh*) is said to be made of *pālāśa* wood;

O Jātavedas, whose essence is this fuel, blaze up with it and grow; and as you have grown, cause us to increase through progeny, cattle, Vedic splendor, and the enjoyment of food. Svāhā! Bhūḥ! Svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! Svāhā!

One should know Brahmā to be on the right, Viṣṇu on the left, and Śiva, the teacher of the universe, in the center together with the Goddess, surrounded by the hosts of Indra and the other gods.
Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, the god Divākara, Uṣas, Prabhā, as well as Prajñā, Saṃdhyā, and Sāvitrī.
According to the fivefold rite, one should offer a seat, a beautiful vessel, and the *vardhanī* pitcher, circumambulating the great-souled Khakholka.

One should worship, perform fire-offerings, and especially bestow gifts in this manner;
