Having thus performed this extensive ritual procedure for those perfected in the study of the divine [Vedas], and while the fire-oblation (homa) is being carried out, in the central position among the locations starting from the east; LiP_2,28.72.
One should cause the king to ascend according to the prescribed rite with the Rudrādhyāya;
there, O protector of the earth, one should cause the king to break [the vessel] for the duration of one ghaṭikā with focused awareness.
The sacrificer should mutter the mantra known as the Rudra-gāyatrī for half a ghaṭikā or half of that; then he should begin his sitting right there.
Having looked toward the western direction, the wise king, composed in mind and holding a *kūrca* in his hand,
should be adorned with ornaments and carry a sword and a shield.
With the words "Svasti" and so forth, at both the beginning and especially at the end,
the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas should perform the rite for a "holy day" (puṇyāha).
With the most beautiful sounds of the Vedas, such as the words "Victory! and "Auspiciousness!", accompanied by dances, instrumental music, songs, and all manner of splendors.
One should likewise cast gold there in the northwestern direction;
the two ends of the balance should be equal and rounded, so that the weight on the balance remains constant.
The best [image] is said to exceed one hundred niṣkas; the middling is remembered as half of that;
and the lowest shall be half of that again—thus it is ordained as threefold therein.
Then a pair of garments, a turban, earrings, a neck ornament,
a finger-ring, and an ornament for the wrist.
And all of these, at the commencement of a rite of dharma,
one should cause to be given to one who observes the Pāśupata vow and whose limbs are smeared with ashes.
The wise one should give all the previously mentioned ornaments, along with a turban and garments, as a covering cloth to those who perform this rite.
One should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one hundred and fifty, or half of that, to be given;
and for all the yogins, one should cause a separate niṣka to be given.
One should cause the divine implements of the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
however, for the other ascetics, one should cause a separate niṣka to be given.
One should offer gold from a scale-weighing ceremony to Śiva,
as well as a temple, a pavilion, a wall, and likewise ornaments.
Having fashioned and offered a golden-flowered drum and a sword along with its scabbard to Śiva, the wise man should then leave whatever remains.
It should be given to the teachers, especially to those whose limbs are smeared with ashes;
it may be offered with milk, or with curd, or even with all substances together,
or with the *brahmakūrca* mixture, O God, or again with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
There, one should sprinkle the Supreme Lord with a thousand jars,
or even with pure ghee alone, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā.
One should worship the deity with milk, or with curd, or even with all the ritual substances,
or again with the *brahmakūrca* or the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should take cow urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, or cow dung with the Praṇava;
milk with the verse "āpyāyasva," and curd with the verse "dadhikrāvṇo."

One should consecrate him with clarified butter while reciting the *tejo 'si* mantra and with the *īśāna* mantra; and one should indeed consecrate the Lord of Gods with water from a jar containing *kuśa* grass while reciting the *devasya tvā* mantra.
Or one should bathe the Supreme Lord with the entire Rudrādhyāya,
or with a thousand jars using the thousand names of Śambhu.
Whether it be those spoken by Viṣṇu, or those spoken by Taṇḍi, or again those proclaimed by Dakṣa, the foremost of sages; ||| LiP_2,28.93 |||
A great worship should be performed for Mahādeva with devotion;
and a sacrificial fee should always be given to one's own guru, who is a worshiper of Śiva.
And for all [beings], there is the ocean of the body and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the sequence;
likewise for the wretched, the blind, the miserable, the young, the old, the emaciated, and the afflicted.
And one should feed [the brahmins] according to the prescribed rule, and one should also cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, on the procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa gift, in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: "This primordial Tulā, which possesses a universal form, has indeed been described to you."
I shall now describe the second [mantra], Hiraṇyagarbha, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The lower vessel is prescribed to be made of a thousand units of gold;
the upper vessel is half that amount, with an opening just sufficient for entry.
One should likewise fashion this auspicious [image] out of gold, endowed with all ornaments;
one should meditate upon the Goddess, possessed of the three qualities (guṇas), within the vessel below.
One should worship the Goddess Caturviṃśatikā, who embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Agni,
and the twenty-sixth Lord of Umā, who transcends the qualities (guṇas), in the upper vessel.
One should meditate upon the Self as the Primordial Person (Puruṣa), the twenty-fifth principle,
in the center of the previously mentioned location, upon the altar within the mandala.
Having led it inside and placed it in the midst of śāli rice, one should wrap it with new cloths;
having smeared it with a paste of black gram, one should worship it with the five substances.
One should worship with the five [deities] beginning with Īśāna according to the rule;
and the worship of Śiva and the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in sequence as before.
Having recited the goddess Gāyatrī, he himself should enter facing the east,
having duly performed the rites beginning with the conception (garbhādhāna).

Having performed [the preliminary rites] according to the procedure of the sixteen-fold path, the best of Brahmins should perform the sprinkling with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass into the right receptacle.
In the rite of the parting of the hair (sīmantakarma), one should likewise prepare twenty-one portions of water infused with kuśa grass and udumbara fruits in the northeast.
Having adorned a beautiful maiden with thirty niṣkas, one should marry her; then, having likewise offered oblations, one should present her to Śiva.
At the rite of first feeding (annaprāśana), the learned man should feed [the child] with milk-rice (pāyasa) and other such foods;
in this manner, the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the Viśvajit sacrifice are completed.
The rite should be performed by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas using the seed-syllable of Śakti;
all else should be carried out according to the rules, just as in the case of the Tulā-homa.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall fully describe the most excellent mountain of sesame seeds (tilaparvata).
Having performed [the rite] at the previously mentioned place and time, and having worshipped with diligence, // LiP_2,30.1 //
O Sage, on a delightful and level ground that is free from altars,
one should indeed set up a staff measuring ten tālas in height.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water, one should thereafter scatter sesame seeds upon it;
the most excellent of Brahmins should then sprinkle that place with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The wise one should fashion the mandala as before, perfectly symmetrical on all sides;
having established it with new cloths and strewn it with beautiful flowers.
In that [pit], the piling up [of materials] should be performed, especially with loads of sesame seeds;
the height of one cubit (prādeśa) is proclaimed as the best.
O bulls among sages, that which is four finger-breadths shorter than that is the medium size;
the smallest should be equal to the staff, but one should not have it made shorter than the staff.
Having wrapped [the image] all around with new cloths, one should worship it in due order;
having installed Sadyojāta and the other [faces], one should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
And in the eight directions, the previously mentioned forms should be fashioned in sequence;
one should have each one made from three niṣkas of gold in due order.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to the prescribed rule, just as in the case of the Tulābhāra rite;
and the fire-oblation (homa), O best of sages, is declared to be performed exactly as before.
One should worship the Lord of the Gods of gods, who is surrounded by the world-protectors,
situated in the midst of a mountain of sesame seeds, and possessing the form of that mountain of sesame seeds.
And the worship of Śiva should be performed with a thousand-pitcher rite and other ceremonies;
one should show the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, situated in the midst of sesame seeds.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rules and in due order, one should perform the ritual dismissal;
one should cause a mountain of sesame seeds to be given to a poor man learned in the Vedas.
Thus has Tilanaga been described, which is superior to all and supreme.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Gift of the Sesame Mountain," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, [I shall describe] another mountain, subtle and requiring few materials, yet yielding great fruit.
When associated with a mere substance, the middle time is prescribed.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung and scattered garments upon it,
the wise man should place three *bhāras* of auspicious sesame seeds in the middle of that space.
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments;
it should be made with ten niṣkas, or again, with half of that or even half of that.
One should place a lotus in the center of the sesame seeds, and Maheśvara in the center of the lotus;
having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rule, one should worship Vāmā and the others.
One should have the form of Śakti fashioned from gold weighing three niṣkas;
one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) all around, surrounding it with the lords of obstacles (vighneśas).
One should also have images of the Vighneśas fashioned according to the previously mentioned measurement of gold;
having worshipped them in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Recitation, fire-offerings, worship, giving, consecration, and so forth, are to be performed as previously described.
I shall now describe, in brief, the gift of the golden earth.
At the previously mentioned place and time, he should perform [the rite] together with the sages,
according to the characteristics as before, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or in a mandala.
One should have a divine ground constructed, even if it is only one thousand [cubits] in size;
it should be made one cubit high, square, and very beautiful.
It is surrounded by the seven continents, oceans, and mountains;
it is endowed with all sacred fords and possesses Mount Meru at its center.
Alternatively, one should fashion an island in the center consisting of nine sections;
having prepared it without flaw as before, in the middle of the mandala, one should construct an altar.
In accordance with the prescribed rule, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) previously ordained should be given to the devotee of Śiva from the thousand [pieces], consisting of one-seventh of that amount.
One should worship Śiva, the auspicious one, with a thousand jars and other offerings;
the gift of gold and land upon this linga is declared to be supreme.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Gift of the Suvarṇamedinī," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall further describe another supreme Kalpa-tree.
Having thus fashioned [the image] with a hundred niṣkas, it should be endowed with all its branches.
Having fashioned various branches, one should provide supports such as strings of pearls,
and one should arrange the tips of the sprouts with divine emeralds.
The wise man should have sprouts made from coral for the tree,
and he should beautifully adorn its fruits all around with rubies.
The root should be made of sapphire, the excellent trunk of diamond,
the top of the tree of beryl, and the crown of ruby.
O observer of excellent vows, one should indeed make the bulb with gomedaka,
the altar of the tree with sūryakānta, candrakānta, or crystal.
The length of the tree is proclaimed to be one *vitasti*;
likewise, the measurement of the eight branches and their width and height are specified.
One should install the *liṅga* at its base, surrounded by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s),
and having placed the tree within the mandala in the center of the previously mentioned altar.
One should diligently worship the Lord Īśāna and the guardians of the world;
as before, one should perform the recitation of mantras, fire oblations, and other rites, according to the procedure for the Tulā and Bhāra weights.
O King, one should offer a tree to Śambhu, or to yogins, or else to those whose limbs are smeared with ashes; by doing so, a king shall become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Gift of the Kalpa Tree," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
I shall now describe the gift of Gaṇeśeśa in the pavilion previously mentioned.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, who is surrounded by the guardians of the world, ||| LiP_2,34.1 |||

Having fashioned images of Viśveśvara according to the scriptures, adorned with all ornaments, using ten niṣkas of gold, and having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite; ||| LiP_2,34.2 |||
One should perform the oblation as before in eight sacrificial pits with eight officiating priests,
according to the path of the five enclosures and the sequence of the lineage.
Having honored seven Brahmins and likewise one maiden in the north,
he should cause all the mantras to be given in due order with their respective mantras.
Having given [this] in this manner, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Bestowing Gaṇeśeśa," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall fully describe to you the procedure for the golden cow.
It pacifies all sins and destroys the calamities caused by malevolent planets and famine.
It pacifies calamities and wards off all diseases;
one should have it fashioned out of a thousand niṣkas of gold.
Or it may be properly made with half of that, or again with half of that half;
or it may be made with a hundred [units], endowed with all forms and qualities.
One should fashion a divine cow-form, complete with beautiful hooves and endowed with all auspicious marks;
one should place a vajra upon the tips of its hooves and rubies upon its horns.
O best of sages, one should place a divine pearl between the eyebrows;
the breasts should be made of lapis lazuli, and the auspicious tail of sapphire.
A very beautiful topaz should be placed in the position of the tooth;
having fashioned it like a beast, one should make the calf very beautiful.
Having fashioned a maṇḍala adorned with all kinds of jewels using ten gold niṣkas in the center of the previously mentioned altar (vedikā), one should proceed.
Having placed a cow with her calf in the center of that [mandala], one who knows all principles should wrap the cow and her calf there with a pair of garments.
One should again worship the cow, Surabhi, together with her calf, with the Gāyatrī mantra;
then, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules, following the procedure for the single fire (ekāgni).
One should perform the remaining rites as before according to the rules for the fuel-sticks and clarified butter;
the worship of Śiva should be carried out after bathing the liṅga with ghee and other substances.
Having touched a cow with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should offer that auspicious cow to Śiva;
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of thirty niṣkas should be given, O high-minded one.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Cow," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
I shall now proclaim the gift of Lakṣmī, which increases great sovereignty.
The aforementioned rite should be performed upon the mandala on top of the altar in the pavilion.
Having fashioned the image of the illustrious goddess out of gold according to the prescribed rite—using a thousand [palas], or half of that, or again half of that—; 36.2.
One should place Lakṣmī, endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament, within the maṇḍala using one hundred and eight [offerings].
On the southern side of that, one should worship Viṣṇu upon a sacrificial mound;
having worshipped the Queen of the Gods according to the prescribed rite with the Śrī-sūkta.
One should worship Viṣṇu, the teacher of the universe, Hari, with the Viṣṇugāyatrī;
having propitiated the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the fire-oblation as before.
Having kindled the fire according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform oblations of clarified butter;
one should have the most excellent Brahmins offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity].
Having summoned the sacrificer to the ground to the east of her,
he should prostrate himself like a staff with his limbs extended and show that goddess to him.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu situated there, one should worship Śiva as before;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for that is proclaimed to be one-twentieth of it.
Half of that portion should be given to the others as is appropriate;
thereafter, the devotee, especially the yogi, should offer oblations to Śambhu.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Gift of Lakṣmī," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the procedure for the gift of a sesame-cow (tiladhenu).
One should perform the worship of Śiva in the western part of the previously described pavilion.
In front of him, having drawn a beautiful lotus in the middle of the ground,
one should place a beautiful lotus, covered with cloths, in its center.
Having fashioned a sesame-flower, one should then place upon it a golden lotus;
it should be made with thirty niṣkas, or again, with half of that or even half of that.
It should be made with five niṣkas, or again with half of that amount;
having worshipped it according to the prescribed rule with perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order.
O Brahmins, one should place eleven [deities] in the northern quarter of the lotus;
having worshipped them in due order according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should cause garments and upper robes to be given to the Brahmins in due order;
likewise, turbans and adorned earrings should be presented.
Having given golden rings to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite, and having scattered one and ten garments before them; LiP_2,37.7.
Having placed sesame seeds and other offerings separately within those garments,
one should divide a bronze vessel weighing one hundred palas into eleven equal parts.
And a stalk of sugarcane should especially be given to the Brahmins;
one should have it fashioned from gold weighing two niṣkas and placed upon the horn of a cow.
The hooves, however, should be made of silver weighing two niṣkas;
having thus provided each separately, one should cast them into those sesame seeds.
Then, with the eleven Rudra mantras, he should cause [the offerings] to be given to the Rudras;
on the eastern side of the lotus, twelve honored Brahmins [should be seated].
By this very same method, one endowed with faith should likewise cause [the gift] to be given to them with the twelve adhiṣṭhāna mantras.
As before, one should again cause sixteen Brahmins stationed in the southern part to receive [the offerings] with the mantras of the Mūrtis and Vighneśa, as previously described.
The sacrificer must perform all of this in due order;
it may be a gift solely to Rudra, or alternatively, to the Ādityas.
And for the [deities] such as Mūrti and the others, a gift should be given according to the extent of one's wealth;
having placed a lotus, that king or the remaining monarch should have it performed.
And a sacrificial fee must be given, along with an ornament worth five niṣkas.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Sesame-Cow," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O you of noble vows, listen as I describe the gift of a thousand cows.
Having taken a thousand auspicious cows, together with their calves and endowed with all good qualities.
Having worshipped those eight according to the scriptures with great care and effort,
one should then fasten their horns with gold, each with a niṣka.
One should fasten the hooves with silver at the region of the neck;
a beautiful diamond should be set in the ear, fashioned with a niṣka for each.
For the sake of Śiva, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins individually—
ten niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that again.
According to the extent of one's wealth, or even just a single niṣka,
a pair of beautiful garments should be given separately to each brahmin.
Having diligently propitiated cows, one should give away those that are most beautiful;
having thus given according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped Śiva-Saṃkara.
One should recite, according to the rule, this unsurpassed hymn of praise to cows before [the image]:
"May cows always be before me; likewise, may cows be behind us."
"O cows, you always dwell within my heart; I dwell in the midst of the cows.
Having said this and having given [the gift] to the foremost of the twice-born, he should circumambulate them.
One is glorified in the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on that [cow].
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Gift of a Thousand Cows," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: "I shall now describe the gift of a golden horse, which brings about victory."
O you of noble vows, listen; I shall tell you that which is even more excellent than the horse sacrifice.
Having prepared a horse endowed with auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament, [one should perform the rite] one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times.
One should have it fashioned with a divine form, endowed with the five excellences,
possessed of all the primary marks, and complete in all its limbs.
Having stationed that supreme vehicle of Indra, equipped with all weapons and endowed with its own excellent qualities, in the middle of that place, he [placed] the horse.
Considering him to be Uccaiḥśravas, one should worship him with devotion;
and in the eastern direction from him, one should place a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Having worshipped with the thought that he is the Lord of the Gods, one should cause five niṣkas to be given;
and that horse must be bestowed according to the prescribed rite upon a devotee of Śiva.
Having bestowed the golden horse, one should also honor the preceptor according to the extent of one's wealth, or with at least five niṣkas of gold.
One should satisfy the wretched, the blind, the miserable, the helpless, the young, the old, the emaciated,
and the afflicted with gifts of food, and especially the Brahmins.
The man who performs this gift of a horse with devotion shall enjoy celestial pleasures for a long time and become possessed of radiant sovereignty.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Gift of a Golden Horse," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
I shall now describe the gift of a daughter, which is the most excellent among all gifts.
A maiden endowed with auspicious marks and free from all defects.
Having brought about a union between the mother and father, having given them great wealth,
and having then made him his own, he bathed him and gave him a beautiful new garment.
Then, having adorned him with ornaments, one should worship him with perfumes and garlands;
thereafter, one should examine the auspicious omens, such as the lineage, the lunar mansion, and so forth.
Having observed the minds of both and having honored them both with effort,
[the gift] should be given specifically to a *śrotriya* Brahmin who is an ascetic.
To one who has directly studied the Vedas according to the rules and lives as a celibate student (brahmacārī), one should give slaves,
slave-girls, abundant wealth, and especially ornaments.
One should cause fields, wealth, grain, and garments to be given; as many hairs as there are on the body of the maiden, so many [rewards] shall accrue to her progeny.
For that many thousands of years, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Gift of a Daughter," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now I shall describe, in brief, the gift of gold and a bull.
Then, one should have the form of a bull fashioned out of a thousand measures of gold.
Or with half of that, or again with half of that,
or even with one hundred and eight [villages], the wise man [should establish] the bull, who is the embodiment of Dharma.
One should cause a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) in the shape of a crescent moon to be made on the forehead;
it should be fashioned from crystal, and the hoof indeed from silver.
One should fashion the neck with ruby and the hump with gomedaka;
on the neck, one should have a bell-garland made, variegated with jewels.
One should have a bull-emblem (vṛṣāṅka) fashioned there, encircled by small bells and bracelets,
upon the circular mandala on the altar at the previously mentioned place and time.
One should install the lordly bull there facing west in front;
one should worship Īśvara with devotion, mounted upon the bull and bearing the bull as his emblem.
Having worshipped the lord of bulls with the Gāyatrī and having paid homage with a concentrated mind, [one should recite]:
"We know him who has sharp horns; we meditate upon him whose feet are Dharma;
may that Bull inspire us. (LiP 2.41.7)
Having worshipped the bull with this mantra for the increase of dharma,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with ghee, rice, and other offerings, according to the extent of one's means.
A bull, having been honored, should be given to the Brahmins or to Śiva;
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must also be given according to one's means.
He who performs this unsurpassed gift of a bull with devotion becomes an attendant of Śiva and rejoices together with him.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Gift of the Golden Bull," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
I shall now describe, in due order and according to the rules, the gift of an elephant.
Or it should be given to a twice-born man or to Śiva, after first worshipping him as before.
One should have an elephant made, endowed with auspicious marks, either of gold or silver,
weighing one thousand niṣkas or even half of that.
Or one may construct it with half of that half [of the previous size], adorned with all the characteristic marks;
and at the previously mentioned place and time, one should present it to the deity.
Or on the eighth day, it should be offered to Śiva, the Supreme Lord,
to a Brāhmaṇa who is poor, learned in the Vedas, and one who maintains the sacred fires.
Having worshipped Śiva as before, one should give [the gift] with Śiva in mind;
whoever performs this act of giving, being fully absorbed in devotion to Śiva, [attains the highest goal].
Having dwelt for a long time in heaven, he shall become a king, a lord of elephants.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The divine group of eight world-protectors (Lokapālas) is directly most difficult to attain."
It brings about all prosperity, is a secret, and destroys the armies of enemy forces.
It is divine for the protection of one’s own country, it increases elephants and horses,
it brings about the increase of sons, it is meritorious, and it promotes the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
At the previously mentioned place and time, having worshipped Śiva in the center of the mandala upon the altar, according to the rule and in due order.
One should prepare sand altars in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
having duly honored eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Those who have conquered their senses, born of noble lineage, endowed with all auspicious marks, seated facing Śiva, and situated in unstruck celestial garments; ||| LiP_2,43.5 |||
One should worship the Brahmins in due order with garments, divine ornaments, the mantras of the world-protectors, perfumes, flowers, and excellent incense.
One should offer oblations into the fire in the east with the mantras of the world-protectors;
or rather, the fire-ritual should be performed in sequence, offering fuel-sticks and clarified butter.
Having thus performed the rite according to the prescribed injunctions, the preceptor, who is devoted to Śiva,
summons the sacrificer, who is adorned with all ornaments.
Having thus honored them, the twice-born man should then cause wealth to be given to those brahmins individually with their respective mantras, as well as ten niṣkas and ornaments for each.
A separate seat alone should be made with ten niṣkas;
there, the ritual bathing of Śiva should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be bestowed according to the extent of one's wealth.
Thus, the wise person who makes this offering to the Lords of the World with devotion shall remain for a long time among the Lords of the World and become a sovereign ruler of the earth.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.

Having performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa);
indeed, all the ritual substances are to be offered into the two fires according to the rules for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The preceptor should appoint two officiating priests who have mastered the Vedas;
with reference to them, he should cause wealth to be given to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule.
To each of them, one hundred and eight supreme [offerings] should be given individually,
accompanied by garments and ornaments, and endowed with all types of decorations.
For the illustrious Guru alone is indeed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
one should offer gifts to each of them individually and also feed the Brahmins.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.

You should now explain to us the procedure for the *jīvaśrāddha* (the funeral rite for the living).
Sūta said:
I shall describe, in brief, the procedure for the *jīva-śrāddha* (the rite for the living), which is approved by all and was formerly told to Manu by Brahmā, the god of gods.
May the Vasiṣṭhas and the Śiṣṭas, as well as Bhṛgu and the Bhārgavas,
listen with their whole being to this supreme [teaching] which brings about all accomplishments.
O you of excellent vows, I shall explain the sequence of the path of the śrāddha, the sequence of those worthy of the śrāddha, and also the specific details regarding the śrāddha for the living.
On a mountain, by a riverbank, in a forest, or even in a sanctuary,
the *jīvaśrāddha* (living funeral rite) must be performed with diligence at the time of death.
When a *jīvacchrāddha* has been performed, the living person is liberated while still alive—
whether he performs ritual actions or not, and whether he possesses knowledge or lacks it.
Whether he be a learned Vedic scholar or not, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya,
or a Vaiśya— there is no doubt in this matter— that one who has entered the path of Yoga is self-restrained.
Having examined the ground according to rule by its scent, color, taste, and other qualities,
and having carefully extracted any hidden impurities, one should prepare a sacrificial mound of sand upon the earth.
In the center, one should fashion an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit in length,
or alternatively, a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila) measuring one arrow-length (iṣu), repeated as many times as required.

Having smeared [the site] according to the rule, having applied [the ointments], and having established the fire, one should perform the *anvādhāna* rite according to the scripture and enclose it on all sides.
Having worshipped on the sacrificial mound, one should perform oblations in the fire with fuel-sticks and other materials;
first performing the homa with fuel-sticks, and then separately with the sacrificial porridge (caru).
And having extracted all the constituent principles (tattvas) from himself, he should offer oblations individually with clarified butter that has been purified in separate vessels.

on the seventh day, one should also feed the lords of yogins who are worthy of the śrāddha.
And for the brahmins beginning with Śarva, [he should provide] garments, ornaments, and blankets;
as well as vehicles, beds, carriages, and vessels made of bell-metal, copper, and other metals.
Gold, silver, a cow, sesame seeds, a field, and wealth;
as well as a multitude of male and female slaves—these should be given, along with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

furthermore, one should feed a thousand Brahmins along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Or else, one may offer a great caru-oblation to Rudra for three days to a single person who is devoted to yoga, established in the ash-rite, and has conquered his senses.
Thus has the specific distinction regarding all that is enjoined for the *śrāddha* been declared;
whether one should perform it or not when [the ancestor] has died, since he himself is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
He may perform the obligatory and occasional rites or abandon them entirely; even when a relative has died, for him there is neither ritual purity nor impurity.
And there is no doubt that one is purified from birth-impurity (sūtaka) by mere bathing;
this applies even when a son is born later to oneself in one's own field.
Everything must be performed for him; even his son may become a knower of Brahman, should a daughter later be born to that high-souled one from a queen.
She should be known as being like Ekaparṇā, and her observance of vows is like that of Aparṇā; this is certainly so, there is no doubt, even for those born of her lineage.
There is no doubt that the ancestors are liberated even from hell;
by this rite, they are likewise liberated from the karmic debts of their mothers and fathers.
When the twice-born has passed away, one may either bury him in the ground or cremate him;
having performed all the funeral duties for a son, no fault is found.
And by his subsequent karma alone, no further destination for him exists;
all this was told by Brahmā to the sages of purified souls.
Again, it was told to Sanatkumāra by that wise one,
and it was told to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana by the son of Brahmā.
Through the grace of that wise god Vedavyāsa,
this has been known by me and performed solely at his command.
All this secret, which bestows the perfection of Brahman, has been told to you;
O observers of excellent vows, it should be given to the son of a sage, but not to one who lacks devotion.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Śrāddha for the Living," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.

you are indeed the very personified second body of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
