as well as Romaharṣaṇa, were capable of performing such devotion to their guru.
Thus are the extensive verses of Vyāsa on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī;
he alone was a disciple of that one of great splendor, whether equal to him, similar, or distinct.
"You are equal to Vaiśampāyana among the disciples of Vyāsa on this earth;
therefore, you ought to relate everything to us now."
When they had all spoken thus and remained standing right there,
great wonder arose among the sages in his presence.
Then, in the intermediate space, the vast goddess Sarasvatī herself appeared and spoke these words:
"Enough! This question of the sages has been answered."
The entire world consists of the *liṅga*, and everything is established within the *liṅga*;
therefore, having renounced everything else, one should establish and worship it.
With his own long sword fixed upon the path established by the installation of the *liṅga*,
he should quickly pierce through the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and emerge without hesitation.
Upendra, Brahmā, Garuḍa, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera,
and others likewise established Maheśvara, Śiva, in the form of a *liṅga*.
And among their respective factions, those were the foremost, just as the twice-born are:
Brahmā, Hara, and the Lord Viṣṇu; and the goddesses Ramā and Dhara.
Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, Prajñā, Dharā, Durgā, and Śacī;
likewise the Rudras, the Vasus, Skanda, Viśākha, and Śākha.
And the blessed Naigameśa, the world-protectors, and likewise the planets; all the hosts led by Nandin, and the lord Gaṇapati.
All the Pitṛs, the Munis, Kubera and others of great splendor, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sāṃkhyas, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians; LiP_2,46.19 //
The Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, domestic animals, birds, and wild beasts— indeed,
everything from Brahmā down to the stationary objects— is established within the Liṅga.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should establish the immutable Liṅga;
for if one were to worship everything that has been established with effort, one would indeed be worshipping it.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the great sages in heaven then, with palms joined in reverence, became firm in their resolve.
Having prostrated in my mind before you—the most auspicious Śiva, the Lord, the imperishable one who consists of the *liṅga*—[I speak].
The Lord Hari, the unborn master of all gods, the master of the entire universe, along with the Guru himself,
the best of sages, the hosts of attendants, the gods and asuras, and the foremost of men— all these, moreover, are composed of the Śiva-liṅga.
Having heard this, all the sages of the six clans, being composed in mind,
renounced everything and prepared to perform the installation of the deity.
All those of celebrated vows questioned the sinless Sūta with voices faltering with joy regarding the extensive installation of the Liṅga.
Sūta said:
I shall explain to you, in due order and in brief, the installation of the *liṅga*-form [of the deity] for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.

Having diligently fashioned a linga on the earth according to the prescribed rite among all lingas, one should worship a single linga made of stone, which embodies the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
It may be made of gold and jewels, or of silver, or even of copper;
it should be provided with a pedestal and a cord, and its top should be properly extended.
Having purified it, one should devoutly establish this unsurpassed altar together with the pedestal;
for Umā the Goddess is the pedestal, and Maheśvara himself is the liṅga.
By the mere worship of these two, both the Goddess and the God are worshipped;
and by the installation of them, the Lord of Gods is installed together with the Goddess.
Therefore, the best of installers should install a linga that is accompanied by the Vedas.

At the base dwells the Lord Brahmā, and in the middle portion is Viṣṇu; at the top is Paśupati, the unborn Rudra, the supreme form of the Lord of All. Therefore, one should worship or install the liṅga as something most venerable, because this Gaṇapati is worthy of worship by all the foremost of the gods.

Those who constantly worship Maheśvara—the supreme deity among the thirty gods—in the form of a *liṅga* with perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, ablutions, oblations, hymns, mantras, and offerings, become immeasurable beings.
Free from the fear of rebirth, conception, and destruction, they are honored by the foremost of gods and *gandharvas*, revered by the *siddhas*, and saluted by the best of the *gaṇas*.
Therefore, one should install the Supreme Lord with devotion and ritual service,
and especially worship the *liṅga* for the attainment of all goals.
Having worshipped it, one should place the liṅga in the middle of the sacred water upon the seat of Śiva;
then, having covered the liṅga with kūrca-grass, cloth, and other items, [one should worship] again with water-pots.
[The vessels] should be auspicious, containing the Lokapālas and other deities, along with kūrca-grass, unbroken rice (akṣata),
and svastikas and the like made of upturned grass, all wrapped in variegated threads.
One should mark the linga installed by Īśāna on all sides with weapons such as the vajra, provided with cloth coverings and lids.
It was provided with incense and lamps, with canopies spread across the sky,
and adorned with the banners of the world-protectors as well as elephants, buffaloes, and other animals.
With decorated and worshipped [vessels], and a beautiful garland of *darbha* grass endowed with all auspicious characteristics, one should encircle the exterior with it.
Then one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) in water provided with incense and lamps,
for five days, or three days, or even for a single night.
Perfectly accomplished in the study of the Vedas, he [should be honored] with auspicious rites such as dance and song,
accompanied by the tinkling of small bells and the sounds of cymbals and lutes.
The sacrificer, unperturbed and composed, should observe the time;
having raised the svastika, he should meditate upon it within the maṇḍapa endowed with the proper characteristics.
It should be constructed with a sacrificial altar, enclosed by nine fire-pits,
endowed with the previously mentioned ritual procedures, and possessed of all the required characteristics.

It should be provided with eight mandalas and endowed with eight banners in the cardinal directions, along with sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, arranged in order starting from the east.
The principal pit is prescribed as square in the northeast;
alternatively, there may be five pits and a single sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Indeed, with all the implements of sacrifice and ornaments for the worship of Śiva,
one should prepare a great bed in the middle of the altar, fashioned from five types of cotton.
One should fashion [the image] adorned with gold and draped with white cloth;
having thus fashioned it, one should likewise install Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
One should install the liṅga with its head facing east according to the prescribed rite using the Īśāna mantra;
once the installation of the jewels has been performed previously, one should install the water-pot alone.
Having covered the *liṅga* on all sides with two cloths and a tuft of grass (*kūrca*),
when the rite of depositing the jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) has commenced, the nine powers beginning with Vāmā [are to be installed].
One should always install the nine gems, together with gold and other materials combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), even upon a stone slab.
One should indeed install the Brahma-liṅga conjoined with the Śiva-gāyatrī;
or one may also install the imperishable Śiva using the Praṇava alone.
One should likewise assign the portion for Brahmā with the *brahmajajñāna* mantra,
and the Vaiṣṇava portion for the Lord Viṣṇu with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
In the Sūtra endowed with the three principles, one should perform the placement with the Praṇava:
"All obeisance to Śiva," and "Obeisance, Haṃsa, to Śiva."
Or, having cleansed everything with the Rudrādhyāya,
one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) and install the water-pots (kalaśa) all around with the Brahma-mantras.
One should place all [the deities] in the center of the altar according to the procedure previously described;
Śiva in the central jar, and the Supreme Goddess to the south.
One should place Skanda between those two; in a well-decorated Skanda-pitcher, one should place Brahmā, or in the Skanda-pitcher, or likewise Hari in the Īśa-pitcher.
Alternatively, one should place the limbs of Brahmā upon the Śiva-pitcher:
Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
In this manner, one should briefly assign all the Brahmans, as well as the Heart and other limbs along with Ambikā, in the center of the altar, in accordance with the previously stated procedure.
One should place the Goddess in the *vardhanī* vessel after filling it with scented water;
one should then deposit gold, silver, and gems into the *śiva-kuṃbha*.
O observers of good vows, one should also diligently [worship] with the limbs of the Gāyatrī in the Vardhanī vessel;
and in the jar filled with the Brahmakūrca, one should worship the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) in their respective directions.
One should cause new cloth to be offered for each of the eight jars, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, for the gods such as Ananteśa and the others. LiP 2.47.40.
One should place gold, gems, and other materials into the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras);
the oblation should be offered according to the sequence of the faces and according to the sequence of the limbs of the Gāyatrī.
One should perform everything from the Jaya oblation up to the Sviṣṭakṛt as before;
one should sprinkle [the deity] with the Śiva-kumbha, the Vardhanī, and the Vaiṣṇava vessel.
One should especially sprinkle the Supreme Lord with the pitcher of the Grandfather (Brahmā) for the portion of Brahmā,
and with the pitchers of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Being well-composed, one should arrange all the mantras as before;
having performed the ritual bathing, one should worship with offerings consisting of thousands and so forth.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one thousand paṇas should be given as the highest;
for others, half of that or half of that again is prescribed.
Clothing for the principal deity, as well as fields, ornaments, and herds of cattle, should be provided;
furthermore, a festival must be celebrated, followed by oblations, sacrifices, and offerings in due order.
The fire-oblation (homa) is likewise prescribed for nine days, seven days, one day, or three days, after having constantly worshipped Śaṅkara as before.
One should always perform the oblation for the gods, beginning with the Sun, as before; one should worship them both within and outside the fire.
He who thus establishes the liṅga is himself the Supreme Lord;
by him [are established] the hosts of gods, the Rudras, the sages, and likewise the apsarases.
Having been installed and worshipped, they [pervade] the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Installation of the Liṅga," in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
[I shall describe] the installation of all the gods as well, in detail.
Having arranged the sacrificial pits according to their respective measures, one for each [deity].
Having performed the festival, one should establish [the deity] and worship according to the prescribed rite;
for the Sun, the ritual should be performed with five fires or by the sequence of twelve fires.
O you of excellent vows, all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be circular or shaped like lotuses;
there should be a pit in the form of a vulva for Ambā, and one vardhanī vessel is prescribed.
For all the rites of the Śaktis, the Yoni-kuṇḍa is prescribed;
one should diligently fashion the Gāyatrī of Śambhu for all of them as well,
because all are born from a portion of Rudra— I shall tell you this in brief.
The variations of the Gāyatrī: "We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Vāgviśuddha;
may Śiva impel us. (LiP 2.48.5)
We know Gaṇāmbikā; may we meditate upon Karmasiddhi;
may Gaurī inspire us thereto.
Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us toward that.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa;
may that Danti inspire us.
May we know the one with the great army; may we meditate upon the one whose speech is pure; may that Skanda inspire us.
We know him whose horns are sharp; we meditate upon him whose feet are the Vedas;
may that Bull inspire us.
We know him who has the face of Hari; we meditate upon him who has the face of Rudra;
may that Nandin inspire us.
We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva;
may that Viṣṇu inspire us.
We know the Great Mother; we meditate upon her who is the perfection of action;
may that Lakṣmī inspire us.
We know her who has been uplifted; we meditate upon her through Viṣṇu alone;
may that Dharā inspire us.
We know Vainateya; we meditate upon him who has golden wings;
may that Garuḍa inspire us.
We know him who was born from the lotus; we meditate upon him whose face is the Veda;
may that Creator inspire us.
We know her who was born from the mouth of Śiva; we meditate upon her who possesses a divine form;
may she inspire our speech. LiP 2.48.17.
We know the king of the gods; we meditate upon him who holds the thunderbolt in his hand;
may that Śakra inspire us.
We know the one with Rudra’s eyes; we meditate upon the one with the spear in his hand;
may that Fire impel us.
We know Vaivasvata; we meditate upon him who holds a staff in his hand;
may that Yama inspire us.
We know the night-walker; we meditate upon him who holds a sword in his hand;
may that Nirṛti inspire us.
We know him who holds the pure hand; we meditate upon him who holds the noose in his hand;
may that Varuṇa inspire us.
We know the one whose life-force is the serpent; we meditate upon the one who holds a staff in his hand; may he impel our intellect. LiP 2.48.23.
We know the Lord of Yakṣas; we meditate upon him who holds a mace in his hand;
may that Yakṣa inspire us.
Let us know the Lord of All; let us meditate upon Him who holds a trident in His hand; may that Rudra inspire us.
We know Kātyāyanī; we meditate upon Kanyākumārī;
may that Durgā inspire us.
Having thus divided the Gāyatrī according to its respective parts, one should worship them and establish their seat; that seat is known to be the Praṇava.
Alternatively, one should worship Viṣṇu with the Atula-sūkta or the Puruṣa-sūkta,
worshipping Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu in their proper sequence.
One should install them with the Devagāyatrī mantra, having prepared the site according to the prescribed ritual;
Vāsudeva is the primary deity, followed by Saṃkarṣaṇa himself.
For Pradyumna and Aniruddha are indeed manifestations of the Lord's form;
moreover, there are many various [manifestations] here arising from his curse.
In all the cosmic cycles, for the welfare of the worlds, he indeed assumes various forms:
as the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf.
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha, and likewise Kalki,
as well as others, are all manifestations arising from the curse of the Lord Hari.
And having fashioned a *gāyatrī* for them as well, one should install and worship the secret [mantras] of Hari Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods.
The consciousnesses, the machines, and the secret mantras are born from the limbs of the five Brahmās, and they consist of the five elements.
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" is supremely auspicious;
here, the eight syllables of Hari are condensed together with the Praṇava.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa;
salutations indeed to Pradyumna, the primordial principle, and to Aniruddha.
One should install each of the images of the god Śiva, the Supreme Lord Parameṣṭhin, with a single mantra each.
O best of sages, the installation and the worship of the *liṅga* are the same as those for Hari, including the placement of jewels and the auspicious rites (*kautuka*).
O you of good vows, one should have everything performed for a stationary image, and likewise for a mobile one according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform the opening of its eyes with the Netra-mantra.
The circumambulation of the field, as well as that of the grove and the city, and the preliminary consecration of the water, are proclaimed to be performed just as before.
The construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa), as well as the ritual bed, is prescribed;
having performed the oblation in nine pits according to the rule, by means of the ninefold division of the fire.
Alternatively, the divine installation, which has come down through the lineage of tradition, is said to be performed either in five sacrificial pits, or in the principal one alone.
For images made of stone, or for those appearing in a painting, the ritual of water-consecration (jalādhivāsana) is prescribed; this is proclaimed as the procedure for the Lord of Bulls (Vṛṣendra).
In the consecration of a temple,
the consecration of every component of that temple is proclaimed to be performed, just as [the limbs] of a body [are consecrated].
One should also diligently worship Vṛṣa, Agni, Mātṛ, Vighneśa, and Kumāra,
as well as the most excellent Durgā and Caṇḍī, according to the rules with the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should first establish the supreme eightfold enclosure (aṣṭāvaraṇa) of Śambhu, beginning with the east;
one should also duly install the guardians of the world (lokapālas), Gaṇeśa, and the others of Śambhu.
Umā, Caṇḍī, Nandin, Mahākāla, the great sage (Mahāmuni),
Vighneśvara, Mahābhṛṅgin, and Skanda, beginning with the gentle one (Saumya), in due order.
One should diligently install Indra and the other deities in their respective places, as well as Brahmā and Janārdana, and Kṣetreśa within the precincts of the temple.

On the lion-throne, one should indeed install Ananta and the other lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) in sequence with the *praṇava* alone; likewise, the secret limbs (*guhyāṅga*) and so forth should be placed upon the lotus.
Thus has been briefly declared the supreme rite for stabilizing the mobile [deities],
especially for all gods and goddesses.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"The greatness of Aghoreśa has been previously described by you."
O Blessed One, you should deign to explain the worship and the consecration of the deity.
Sūta said:
O eminent sages, the installation must specifically be performed according to the ritual for the liṅga, joined with the Aghora mantra and following the prescribed procedure; there is no other way.
One should perform the fire-worship in such a manner that the worship is exactly as prescribed;
[one should offer] either a thousand oblations, half of that, or one hundred and eight.
Gold should be fashioned from sesame seeds mixed with curd, honey, and clarified butter;
and [the offering] of ghee, parched grain flour, and honey is the cleanser of all suffering.
The oblation of sesame seeds indeed destroys diseases and bestows prosperity;
with a thousand oblations there is great prosperity, and with a hundred, the destruction of disease.
One is undoubtedly liberated from all suffering by means of recitation,
specifically one hundred and eight times at the three periods of the day according to the prescribed rule.

By reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times for six months, the supernatural powers (siddhis) will certainly arise; there is no doubt that they will be attained even by those who rule over the entire circle of the earth.
Fever departs by means of a thousand [offerings]; and he who offers milk performs a sacrifice three times a day for one month, offering a thousand oblations of milk.
Within a month, his supreme and great good fortune is accomplished;
and by performing a year-long fire-offering with honey, clarified butter, and curd, it is likewise accomplished.
By means of an oblation of barley, milk, and ghee, or with unhusked rice grains,
the Blessed Lord Īśa, the Aghora Parameśvara, is indeed pleased.
Through oblations of curd, there is nourishment for kings; through oblations of milk, there is pacification (śāntika);
and by offering ghee for six months, all diseases are destroyed.
Consumption (rājayakṣmā) is destroyed in a year by an oblation of sesame seeds and gold;
through an oblation of barley one gains longevity, and through ghee, victory is then attained.
And for the sake of destroying all forms of leprosy, one should constantly offer ten thousand oblations of rice grains smeared with honey, remaining always disciplined for six months.
Clarified butter, milk, and honey are called the "triple sweet. When offered together, he is satisfied; this indeed destroys hemorrhoids.
It is taught that through the oblation of clarified butter alone, all diseases are destroyed;
likewise, meditation, installation, and worship according to the prescribed rite remove all maladies.
Thus has been briefly described the entire installation and worship of the great-souled Aghora, as it was formerly told by Nandin.
O you of excellent vows, he [taught it] to his disciple Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā.
In the Śrīliṅga Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttarabhāga, the forty-ninth chapter.
The sages said:
"The suppression [of the demons] has been described by that trident-bearing Śiva from his own mouth."
O you of noble vows, you ought to explain that [state] for those who have committed further transgressions.
O highly fortunate Romaharṣaṇa of noble vows, there is nothing— whether worldly or Vedic, revealed in the Vedas (śrauta) or prescribed by tradition (smārta)— that is unknown to you.
Sūta said: O you of excellent vows, in ancient times the son of Bhṛgu spoke of the subjugation of Hiraṇyākṣa by Śukra, the disciple of Aghora, who possesses imperishable splendor.
Through his grace, the powerful lord of the Daityas, Hiraṇyākṣa,
conquered the entire triple world, including its gods, asuras, and humans.
Having produced as his son Gaṇapa, who was Andhaka of beautiful prowess,
he shone in the world after being slain by the divine Varāha.
For one who causes harm to women, children, and especially to cows,
there is no victory on this earth by means of this path.
That goddess Dharā was led to the subterranean realm (rasātala) by that Daitya;
thus, the suppression carried out by that god Aghora proved fruitless.
At the end of a thousand years, he was slain by the Boar;
therefore, for the sake of attaining the state of Aghora, one should never harm Brāhmaṇas.
One should not cause even women or cows to perform this;
I declare to you that which is more secret than the secret, the most hidden, and exceedingly profound.
The best of kings should act against an assassin (ātatāyin),
but they must not act against Brāhmaṇas or against their own sovereign.
When an exceedingly invincible force has arrived and all have been destroyed,
and when an unrighteous battle has ensued, one should perform this unsurpassed rite.
One should act with ruthlessness alone, and one should cause others to act with ruthlessness alone;
there is no doubt that as soon as it is performed, suppression is achieved.

O best of the twice-born, having recited the Aghora mantra of terrible form one hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule with sesame seeds ten times that number.
Having worshipped Dakṣiṇāmūrti according to the prescribed ritual with one hundred thousand white flowers, either at a Bāṇaliṅga or in the sacrificial fire; ||| LiP_2,50.14 |||
There is no other way for one who has mastered the mantra;
furthermore, the master of the mantra himself shall effect the attainments (*siddhi*) and so forth, especially in a cremation ground (*pretasthāna*).
Or even in the place of the mother, a learned Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, or one perfected solely through mantra, being permeated by Śiva [should be honored].
The wise one should perform this rite for his own sake or for that of the king;
the learned practitioner should install eight stakes, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Having fashioned a three-pointed trident with twenty-four prongs at its tip,
he assumes a form that is not terrible (aghoravigraha), his body being composed of the *saṃkalīkṛta* [mantras].
Having meditated upon [the deity] as the destroyer of all, one should perform all rites;
one should also contemplate one's own body as resembling ten million fires of cosmic destruction.
The trident, the skull-bowl, the noose, the staff, the bow,
the arrow, the hand-drum, and the sword— these are the eight weapons in their proper sequence.
Eight-armed, granting boons, blue-throated, and sky-clad,
the Lord is mounted upon the five principles and bears the crescent moon.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, possessing a fierce gaze that inspires fear,
he causes all directions to resound with the great sounds of "huṃ" and "phaṭ."
He has three eyes, his crown is firmly bound with a serpent-noose,
he is endowed with all ornaments, and he is smeared with the ashes of a preta.
He was surrounded by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, ḍākinīs, and rākṣasas,
and he was clad in an elephant hide and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
The god who wears a scorpion as an ornament, whose voice resounds like a dark rain cloud,
who resembles a mountain of blue collyrium, and who has a lion’s skin as his upper garment.
O you of excellent vows, one should thus meditate upon Śiva as Aghoreśa, who is both terrible and more terrible than the terrible,
by means of thirty-six mātrās through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Endowed with the Mahāmudrā, one should perform all rites—
whether at a funeral pyre or in a cemetery— once the mantra has been mastered, according to the prescribed rule.
One should establish them in the middle region, as well as in the directions of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa,
and Kubera, having constructed the sacrificial pits according to the scriptures.
The preceptor should stand at the central pit, while the practitioners indeed occupy the cardinal directions;
having strewn [the sacrificial grass] in reverse order as before, they are equipped with tridents.
Seated in the center of the seat of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), he himself, together with such disciples,
meditated upon the Terrible Lord Aghora, who is conjoined with thirty-two syllables.
Having fashioned an image out of *vibhītaka* wood measuring twelve finger-breadths,
one should place it upon the throne of the king of men, while [the rite] for his enemy is performed with charcoal on Tuesday.
A Brahmin, overcome with anger, should diligently dig up the enemy beneath the sacrificial pit in all the pits,
with his head downward and feet upward.
Having brought charcoal from a cremation ground, one should burn it together with husks;
there, dedicated to celibacy, one should silently establish the fire.
Then, with the Māyūrāstra mantra, one should ignite the fire at the navel;
[one should prepare] a jacket from chaff combined with cotton seeds.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with red garments, especially with various gold objects, together with oils produced from hand-operated presses.
One should perform one thousand and eight oblations in successive order,
beginning on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and proceeding according to the sequence.
Likewise, ending on the eighth lunar day and excluding the locations of the charcoal-mandalas;
when this has been done for the lord of men, his enemies, together with their kinsmen, [shall perish].
Endowed with all manner of suffering, they go to the abode of Yama;
and by means of this mantra, one should likewise take a fingernail in a human skull.
Likewise, human hair, charcoal, chaff, a garment, a scrap of rags, royal dust, or the sweepings from a house; LiP_2,50.39.
The teeth of a venomous serpent, the tusks of a boar, the hooves of cattle, and likewise the teeth and claws of a tiger; LiP_2,50.40.
Likewise, as before, [one should offer] the teeth of black antelopes, of a cat,
of a mongoose, and especially of a boar.
Having consecrated the fangs with this mantra,
O you of excellent vows, one should recite the supreme Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should wrap that skull or fingernail in a cloth from a corpse— whether in a field, a house, a city, a cemetery, or a kingdom.
O you of excellent vows, when the sun is eclipsed while situated in the eighth house from the enemy, or when the moon is eclipsed, [one should act] with this mantra: LiP_2,50.44.
There shall be the destruction of his position and the destruction of his enemy occurs when,
having drawn the enemy of the king, he stands ready to depart.
On the ground, which resembles a mirror and is beautified by a canopy above,
it is provided with four archways and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass.
In a kingdom enriched by the study of the Vedas and manifesting prosperity,
he himself should strike his own head with his right foot.
When this is done, the destruction of the enemies of the lord of men will occur;
for whoever performs a malevolent rite directed toward the ruler of his own kingdom.
That evil-minded man, by destroying himself, would surely ruin his own family;
therefore, one should always protect the king who has come to rule over his own kingdom.
Through mantras, medicinal herbs, rituals, and all other efforts at all times, this secret has been declared; it must not be given to just anyone.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"This supreme method of restraint by her of terrible form has been described to us."
O most excellent of beings, you ought to speak the Vidyā known as Vajravāhanikā.
Sūta said:
There is a [mantra] named Vajravāhanikā, which causes terror to all enemies;
with this one should consecrate the vajra and likewise accomplish it for kings.
Having fashioned a vajra according to the prescribed rule and having consecrated that vajra,
one should install it within that [image] by means of this vidyā and with gold.
Then the wise man, with a concentrated mind, should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times;
he who holds the vajra should offer oblations in a vajra-kuṇḍa with clarified butter and other substances ten times that amount.
One should always protect that vajra and then cause it to be given to the king;
by means of that vajra, indeed, one shall go forth and conquer enemies on the field of battle.
In former times, this knowledge was obtained with great effort by the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself;
likewise, the goddess Vajreśvarī appeared in person for the sake of assisting Śakra.
O you of excellent vows, in ancient times Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord of progeny, having had his son slain by the Lord of the Gods, took away the Soma through his magical power out of enmity toward Indra.
In that sacrifice, the mighty-armed crusher of Viśvarūpa desired whatever oblation was available and prepared by the officiating priests.
"O Śakra, you have killed my son; I will not give you a pleasing portion, for you are unworthy of a share. Viśvarūpa has been slain by you."
Having spoken thus, he deluded the entire hermitage with his illusory power;
then, having pierced through that illusion, the crusher of Viśvarūpa [appeared].
The Lord of Śacī forcibly drank the Soma together with his attendants;
then, filled with rage, Prajāpati took what remained of it.
"O Śatru of Indra, grow strong! Svāhā!"—thus he offered oblations into the fire.
Thereupon, from that [oblation], one known as Vṛtra arose, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
The enemy of the lord of the gods appeared, and the destroyer of Vṛṣa fled;
then the blessed Kirīṭin, in an instant, abandoned heaven.
The thousand-eyed one, overwhelmed by fear, fled along with his hosts;
then the Lord Brahmā, the creator of the universe, joyfully spoke to him.
"Abandoning that vajra, slay him with this," said the subduer of enemies.
Thereupon, the mighty-armed Indra, the lord of the gods, donned his armor along with the deities.
Having slain [them] without effort, he departed, free from all feverish distress;
therefore, this Vajreśvarī-vidyā is the terrifier of all enemies.
The Mandeha Rākṣasas have been eternally conquered by this very vidyā alone;
I shall now fully proclaim that vidyā which liberates one from all sins.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ;
may he impel our intellects.
Oṃ phaṭ! Strike! Huṃ phaṭ! Cut! Split! Strike! Kill, kill! Svāhā!
This Vidyā, known as Vajreśvarī, causes fear to all enemies;
by means of this Vidyā, O best of sages, the withdrawal of Śambhu [is accomplished].
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "We have heard the Brāhmī Vajreśvarī-vidyā, which was of benefit to Śakra."
"We have heard that by her all the affairs of kings are accomplished."
"O Romaharṣaṇa, tell me the application (viniyoga) of this vidyā.
Sūta said:
"It is for subjugation (vaśya), attraction (ākarṣaṇa), and thereafter for inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa)."
Exorcism, immobilization, delusion, as well as striking,
eradication, cutting, killing, and confinement.
One should perform all rites, such as the paralyzing of an army, by means of the Sāvitrī mantra:
"Come, O boon-granting goddess, upon the earth, on the summit of the mountain."
"O Goddess, permitted by the Brahmins, go as you please;
O twice-born ones, one must depart after having performed the ritual dismissal with this mantra, and not otherwise."
Having likewise performed the external rites of counteraction, such as the ritual of gazing (paśyādi),
one should dismiss the fire and, having established another according to the prescribed rule, proceed.
Having invoked the Goddess, he should again recite the mantra and worship her once more;
then he should again perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the sacrificial fire according to the prescribed rite.
Furthermore, one should accomplish all rites according to the prescribed rule by means of the vidyā;
and for the purpose of subjugation, one who desires it should offer three times ten thousand oblations of *jātī* flowers.
O twice-born ones, one should perform attraction with *karavīra* flowers and ghee;
and specifically, one should perform incitement to hatred with *lāṅgalaka* flowers.
Uprooting is said to be performed with oil; paralyzing is traditionally taught to be done with honey;
enchanting is said to be performed with sesame seeds; and striking is done with blood.
Furthermore, the immobilization of a donkey, an elephant, or a camel is performed respectively by means of mustard seed and by means of a goad for the purpose of splitting them apart.
O you of excellent vows, killing and expulsion are accomplished with the seed-syllable of the Rohī plant;
binding is performed with the leaf of a serpent, and after that, the immobilization of an army.
One should know that with realgar the worship of the Supreme Goddess is certain;
through ghee all perfections (siddhis) shall arise, or by means of milk one is purified.
Through sesame seeds there is the destruction of disease, and through lotuses wealth shall arise;
through madhūka flowers one gains beauty, and through sāvitri flowers indeed three times ten thousand [merits].
All [the rites] beginning with Jaya and ending with Sviṣṭakṛt are prescribed as before;
thus has the application been briefly stated, though it is extensive in detail.
Or, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one may recite the mantra alone;
one attains all accomplishments—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, [tell us] the procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas as well."
You ought to speak to us, O Great-minded One, for you are omniscient.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the procedure for conquering death; what is the use of further words?
By means of the Rudrādhyāya, according to the prescribed rite, one should offer a million oblations of ghee in succession.
With sesame seeds mixed with ghee, with lotuses, with effort,
and likewise with dūrvā grass mixed with ghee and cow’s milk, as well as with honey.
One should offer oblations with ghee mixed with *caru*, or even with milk alone; this is proclaimed as the remedy for untimely death.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
With the Tryambaka mantra, [one should worship] the God of gods, Tryambaka.
One should worship [the deity] either in a bāṇaliṅga or, again, in a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) one.
Or else, according to the experts in Āyurveda,
one should worship Śaṅkara with one thousand and eight lotuses (puṇḍarīka) in the proper sequence.
Having worshipped with a thousand lotuses or blue lotuses, and having again offered milk-rice together with ghee and boiled rice; ||| LiP_2,54.3 |||
Mudga-rice mixed with honey, fragrant foods,
and an extensive oblation into the fire, performed duly and in proper sequence.
One should properly recite one million [mantras] with the flowers previously mentioned and especially with sacrificial porridge (caru), and having completed it in due order.
One should indeed feed a thousand Brahmins with appropriate ritual fees;
having given a thousand cows, one should also cause gold to be bestowed.
All this has been told to you in brief, along with its secret meaning,
by Śiva, the God of gods, the All-pervading Lord who wields the most formidable trident.
It was told on the peak of Mount Meru to Skanda of immeasurable splendor;
and by Skanda, the god of gods, it was told to the wise son of Brahmā.
It was spoken directly by Sanatkumāra, who desires the welfare of all the worlds, to the son of Parāśara, having come down through the succession of lineage.
When Śuka had departed for the supreme abode and beheld the three-eyed Rudra,
the illustrious Vyāsa, the supreme seer and lord, was freed from all sorrow.
Having heard of the origin of Skanda and of the greatness of the high-souled one who remains steadfast,
as well as specifically the majesty of the three-eyed Lord and his mantra.
This has indeed been told in many ways to that Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana;
by his very grace, I shall now relate it to you in its entirety.
Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rite, one should mutter the Triyambaka mantra;
one is then liberated from all sins, even those committed throughout seven lifetimes.
Having obtained all that in battle, one shall attain incomparable good fortune;
one who desires a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom through a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) and become happy.
One desiring a son obtains a son by means of a hundred thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt. One desiring wealth should likewise recite it a million times; of this there is no doubt.
Filled with all auspicious things and possessed of all wealth, grain, and the like, he sports with his sons and grandsons; upon death, he is reborn in heaven.
O you of excellent vows, there is no mantra like this one in the world or in the Veda;
therefore, one should always worship the three-eyed God with it.
The fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice shall be eightfold for him who is the lord of the three worlds and of all qualities.
He is the designator of the Vedas, of the gods, and of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
he is also the designator of the phonemes *a*, *u*, and *m*, as well as of their prosodic measures (*mātrās*).
Likewise, Ambā is Soma, Umā is Sūrya, and Mahādeva is Agni; indeed, Aṃbaka is the triad of fires, the three-eyed one.
Just as the exceedingly beautiful fragrance of a tree in full bloom wafts from afar,
so too does the fragrance of that high-souled Śambhu.
Therefore, the Blessed One Sugandha bears fragrance;
and Mahādeva Gāndhāra does so even as a mere plaything for the gods.
In this world, a fragrant wind blows for him in the sky;
therefore, that god is Sugandhi (the Fragrant One), the increaser of prosperity.
From the semen of Śambhu, which was formerly deposited in the womb of Hari,
there arose from that virility the golden egg born of the Unborn (Aja).
Having transcended the moon and sun along with the stars, and the worlds of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Tapas, and Satyaloka, his power indeed flourishes.
The five elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and primordial nature (prakṛti) are indeed the nourishment of that very seed; therefore, he is truly the Increaser of Nourishment (Puṣṭivardhana).
One should worship that god Puṣṭivardhana with clarified butter, milk,
honey, barley, wheat, mung beans, and bilva fruit.
Having offered oblations into the linga according to the rule with white water-lilies, arka flowers, śamī leaves, white mustard seeds, and rice, we worship the God with devotion.
By this truth, may I be released from the bond of fetters through the application of karma,
and from death and imprisonment by your splendor.
Just as ripe *urvāruka* gourds ripen again in due time,
so too has that very time arrived through the diligent effort of that Manu.
Having thus understood the ritual procedure for the mantra, one should worship the Śivaliṅga;
for such a yogin, there is the complete destruction of bonds and the supreme subjugation of death.
O observers of excellent vows, there is no deity equal to Tryambaka, who is endowed with compassion, gracious by nature, and well-pleased; and likewise, his mantra is also such.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should worship Tryambaka, the Lord of Umā,
with great concentration using the Tryambaka mantra.
Even if he has reached any state whatsoever, he is liberated from all sins through meditation on Śiva; of this there is no doubt, for he himself becomes just like Rudra.
Having killed or pierced living beings, or even having consumed [them] unjustly,
one is liberated from all sins by remembering Śiva just once.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"How did the god Tryambaka, the God of gods, whose banner is the bull..."
O observer of noble vows, he should be meditated upon by means of the path of yoga for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
Although I have already heard everything in its entirety, which is equal to the Vedas, you should please explain it all once more in detail and also in brief.

Sūta said: Thus, in ancient times, Nandin, who possesses the splendor of the sun, was questioned by the host of sages on the summit of Mount Meru while he was surrounded by them; this was all told by the Grandfather himself.
The Blessed One, being composed and well-disciplined, spoke in private to that prince, the son of Brahmā, who was bowing before him.
Nandikeśvara said: Thus in ancient times, the Lord Mahādeva, the blue-and-red one (Nīlalohita), was with the daughter of the mountain, the goddess Ambā, his divine consort who shared his single bed.
Questioned on the peak of Kailāsa, his hair standing on end with joy,
the illustrious Goddess said: "How many kinds of Yoga have been taught, and what is its nature?"
"And that divine knowledge which bestows liberation, by means of which living beings are released. The Blessed One said:
"The first is Mantrayoga, and the second is Sparśayoga."
The third is the yoga of existence (bhāvayoga), and the fourth is non-existence (abhāva);
the fifth is proclaimed as the supreme Mahāyoga.
The practice of mantra-yoga is proclaimed as the application of meditation combined with the repetition [of mantras];
it is that which is superior through the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi) and is endowed with the sequence of exhalation (recaka) and so forth.
The mastery of the vital breath (vāyu) is proclaimed to be achieved through the application of both collective and individual methods,
combined with strength, stability, and skillful action, as well as through excellent practices such as dhāraṇā.
Illuminated by the threefold concentration (dhāraṇā) and purifying the threefold division,
the practice established in the state of breath-retention (kuṃbhaka) is proclaimed as the yoga of touch (sparśayoga).
Freed from the touch of mantras and fully relying upon Mahādeva,
he consists of the nature of radiating and withdrawing while abiding in the distinction between the external and internal.
The yoga of contemplation has been fully described as that which bestows purity of mind;
it causes the entire world, both stationary and moving, to dissolve into its constituent parts.
Wherein one contemplates the essential nature as entirely empty and devoid of appearance—
that is declared to be the yoga of non-existence, which brings about the extinction of the mind.
Formless, absolute, pure, independent, and most beautiful; indefinable, ever-luminous, self-known, and all-pervading.
Wherein one's own nature shines forth, that is proclaimed as Mahāyoga;
it is eternally arisen, self-luminous, and emerges from all consciousness.
The stainless and solitary Self is indeed remembered as Mahāyoga;
all [these powers] bestow the *aṇimā* and other siddhis, and all are givers of knowledge.
In these yogas, there is a progressive excellence in successive order;
I am liberated from all attachments, supreme, and like the great ether.
For he is liberated from all obscurations and is inconceivable by his own nature;
this is declared to be the object of knowledge, which cannot even be grasped by the gods.
When the Great One has been perfectly dissolved, self-known and witnessed by oneself, he shines with a body of bliss; by that [means], this is considered the object of knowledge.
It should be given in due order to a disciple who has been tested— a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, is righteous, and is ungrateful to no one.
One should cause it to be given only to one who is devoted to the guru and the deity; otherwise, one should certainly not give it.
[If given otherwise], one is born censured, diseased, and short-lived.

O sinless one, it is the same for the donor as well; therefore, having understood this, one should cause [the gift] to be given by one who is liberated from all attachments, devoted to me, and has me as his supreme goal.
The practitioner should be endowed with knowledge, proficient in the Śrauta and Smārta rites,
devoted to the guru, meritorious in soul, fit for the task, and always intent on yoga.
Thus, O Goddess of slender waist, has been fully described the eternal path of yoga,
which is the nectar of the lotus of all the Vedas and Āgamas.
Having drunk the nectar of yoga, the yogi, the best among the knowers of Brahman, is liberated;
such is the Pāśupata yoga, the unsurpassed sovereignty of yoga.
This should be known as the "Beyond-the-Āśramas" (atyāśrama); by whom is it attained for the sake of liberation?
Therefore, O beloved, [it is attained] by those devoted to the worship of Śiva through their cherished practices.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the Goddess, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull approached Śaṅkukarṇa and united himself with his own self.
Śailādi said: Therefore, O Lord of Yogins, you too should be devoted to the practice of yoga;
for the supreme form of the Self-born is surely the excellent embodiment of Brahman.
Therefore, with every effort, the supreme person seeking liberation should constantly bathe in ashes, being devoted to the Pāśupata yoga.
Then Vaiṣṇavī is to be meditated upon in due order, and after that the supreme Māheśvarī; she alone is to be meditated upon in the proper sequence thereafter.
This very steadfastness of the Lord of Yoga has been described here by means of summary.
Sūta said: Thus was the Pāśupata yoga taught by Nandin, the son of Śilāda, the delighter of his lineage, who was wise and devoted to the practice of smearing himself with ashes.
The blessed Sanatkumāra [taught it] to Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor;
having heard it from him, I too [shall speak it], at the request of those performing the sacrifice.
I have accomplished my purpose; salutations to the Brahmins and to the sacrifices as well.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one; salutations to the sage Vyāsa.
The excellent Laiṅga Purāṇa consists of eleven thousand verses and seven hundred and eight chapters; beyond this is the Ādimāṃśa.
This work, consisting of forty-six chapters, bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa;
then all those sages of Naimiṣa became composed in mind.
With their skin bristling with joy, they bowed down to the Lord Īśāna;
having thus established this eleventh branch of the Purāṇas, the Lord [departed].
The blessed Lord Brahmā, the self-existent, spoke these words:
"Whoever should read or even hear this entire *Liṅga-purāṇa*, from beginning to end..."
Or if he causes the twice-born to hear it, he attains the supreme goal through austerity, sacrifice, charity, and Vedic study.
Whatever vast destination he attains— whether through Vedic knowledge of the scriptures,
or through mixed action, or even through knowledge alone— [that shall be his].
May there be cessation of rebirth for this brahmin, and may he possess eternal devotion toward me, the god Nārāyaṇa; and may there be faith in me, O Great-Souled One.
"The lineage shall possess imperishable knowledge and vigilance in every respect;
such is the command of Brahmā, and therefore everything belongs to that Great Soul."
The sages said: "O Sage, tell us of the perfection attained by Sūta, by ourselves, by these others,
and by Nārada who delights in visiting sacred fords."
And because of this, there is great joy for us, which causes our hair to stand on end.
"May she always be [prosperous] on all sides through the grace of Virūpākṣa.
When the brahmins had spoken thus, the blessed Nārada also [spoke].
With his two hands, whose tips were most beautiful, he touched the charioteer on the skin;
"May it be well with you, O charioteer! May prosperity be yours in the Great God who has the bull as his banner! (LiP 2.55.47)
May you have faith in us, and let there be salutation to that Śiva.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Liṅga Mahāpurāṇa;
this latter half of the Laiṅga is completed.
May it be an offering to Śrī Bhavānī and Śaṅkara.
